p.seg: 1.1 Mèngzǐ went to see King Huì of Liáng.
The king said,
"Venerable sir,
you have not considered a thousand lǐ too far to come here.
Must you have some way to profit my state?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"Your Majesty,
why must you speak of profit?
The king said:
"What will benefit my state?"
The high officials said:
"What will benefit our families?"
The scholars and common people said:
"What will benefit our persons?"
When superiors and inferiors contend with each other for profit
the state will be endangered.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the murderer of its sovereign
will be a noble of a thousand chariots;
in a state of a thousand chariots,
the murderer of its sovereign
will be a noble of a hundred chariots.
To have a thousand out of ten thousand,
or a hundred out of a thousand,
cannot be said to be not considerable.
But if righteousness is put last and profit first,
they will not be satisfied without snatching all.
There has never been a benevolent person who would abandon their parents,
nor has there been a righteous person who would neglect their sovereign.
Your Majesty need only speak of benevolence and righteousness—
why must you speak of profit?"
1.2 Mencius went to see King Hui of Liang.
The king was standing by a pond,
looking at the geese and deer,
and said,
"Do the virtuous also take pleasure in these things?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Only the virtuous can truly enjoy this;
the non-virtuous, even possessing it, cannot enjoy it."
The Book of Songs says:
'When he began the Sacred Tower,
he planned it and founded it;
the people worked at it,
and in no time completed it.
When he began it, he urged no haste;
the people came like children.'
The king was in the Spirit Park,
where the does lay resting,
the does sleek and glossy,
the white birds pure and bright.
The king was by the Spirit Pond,
oh! how the fish leapt about.
King Wén used the people's labor to build a terrace and a pond,
yet the people rejoiced in it,
calling his terrace the Divine Terrace,
calling his pond the Divine Pond,
and delighting in its possession of deer, fish, and turtles.
The ancients shared joy with the people,
therefore they were able to experience true joy.
The "Declaration of Tāng" says:
'When will this sun perish?
I am willing to die together with you.'
When the people wish to perish together with their ruler,
even if he has terraces, ponds, birds, and beasts,
how can he enjoy them alone?"
1.3 King Huì of Liáng said:
"In governing my state,
I exhaust my heart's efforts.
When Hénèi suffers famine,
I transfer its people to Hédōng,
and move grain to Hénèi.
When Hédōng suffers famine
I do likewise."
Observing the governance of neighboring states,
none match the dedication of my efforts.
Yet the people of neighboring states do not decrease,
and my people do not increase.
Why is this?
Mèngzǐ replied:
"The king is fond of warfare,
allow me to use a military analogy.
With the war drums booming,
and the weapons clashing,
they abandoned their armor and trailed their weapons as they fled.
Some stopped after a hundred paces,
some stopped after fifty paces.
If those who retreated fifty paces laugh at those who retreated a hundred paces,
what would you say?"
He said:
"That will not do;
he merely did not run a hundred paces,
but this is also running away."
He said:
"If the king knows this,
then he should not expect his people to be more numerous than those of neighboring states.
If farming seasons are not interfered with, there will be more grain than can be eaten;
If fine nets are not used in ponds and lakes, there will be more fish and turtles than can be eaten;
If axes enter the mountains and forests only at the proper times, there will be more timber than can be used.
Grain and fish and turtles cannot be consumed in their entirety,
timber cannot be used up,
this enables the people to nourish the living and bury the dead without regrets.
Nourishing the living and burying the dead without regrets,
is the beginning of the kingly way.
With a homestead of five mu, if mulberry trees are planted around it,
those who are fifty can be clothed in silk.
In raising poultry, pigs, dogs, and swine, do not neglect their breeding seasons,
so that those who are seventy can eat meat.
With a hundred mu of farmland, do not interfere with the farming seasons,
and a family of several mouths can avoid hunger.
Carefully maintain the teaching in the schools,
inculcating in them the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty,
and grey-haired men will not be seen carrying burdens on the roads.
When those who are seventy wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people are neither hungry nor cold,
yet the ruler does not become a true king,
such a thing has never occurred.
"Dogs and swine eat the food of men, and you do not know to restrict it;
on the roads there are people starving from famine, and you do not know to issue supplies;
when people die, you say:
'It is not I; it is the year.'
How is this different from stabbing a man and killing him, and then saying:
'It is not I; it is the weapon.'"
If the king does not blame the harvest,
then the people of the world will come to him."
1.4 King Huì of Liáng said:
"I wish to receive your instruction with a tranquil mind."
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Is there any difference between killing a man with a club
and killing him with a blade?"
He said:
"There is no difference."
"Using a blade and governing,
is there any difference?"
He said: "There is no difference."
He said:
"In the kitchen there is fat meat,
in the stables there are well-fed horses,
yet the people have hungry looks,
and in the fields lie the starved dead.
This is leading beasts to devour men."
Beasts devour one another,
and men dislike it.
To be the parent of the people,
and to administer the government, yet to be unable to avoid leading on beasts to devour men,
how does such a person fulfill the role of being the parent of the people?
Zhòngní said:
"The one who first made figurines for burial,
should have no descendants!"
Because they resembled humans and were used as such.
How then
could he let these people starve to death?"
1.5 King Huì of Liáng said:
"The State of Jìn,
under Heaven none is stronger than it,
as you, venerable sir, know.
During my reign,
we were defeated in the east by Qí,
where my eldest son died;
we lost seven hundred li of territory to Qín in the west;
and we were humiliated by Chǔ in the south.
I am ashamed of it,
and wish to avenge the dead once and for all.
What should be done to achieve this?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"A territory of a hundred square lǐ
can suffice to make one a true king.
If the king implements benevolent governance towards the people,
reduces punishments,
lightens taxes and imposts,
and ensures deep plowing and thorough weeding;
If the strong, in their days of leisure, cultivate filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and good faith,
serving their fathers and elder brothers at home,
and serving their elders and superiors abroad,
they can be made, with sticks which they have prepared, to oppose the strong mail and sharp weapons of the troops of Qín and Chǔ.
"They rob their people of the farming seasons,
preventing them from plowing and weeding
to support their parents.
Parents suffer from cold and hunger,
while brothers, wives, and children are separated and scattered."
They have sunk and drowned their people,
and Your Majesty goes to punish them.
Who then can oppose Your Majesty?
Therefore it is said,
"The benevolent have no enemy."
I beg Your Majesty not to doubt this!"
1.6 Mencius went to see King Xiāng of Liáng.
Coming out,
he said to someone:
"From a distance, he does not look like a ruler of men;
when you get close to him, you see nothing about him to command awe.
He abruptly asked:
"How can the world be settled?"
"I replied:
"It will be settled through unification."
"Who can unify it?"
I replied:
"One who does not delight in killing can unify it."
"Who will follow him?"
"I replied:
"No one in the world will fail to follow him."
Do you know about young crops?
If there is a drought between the seventh and eighth months,
the seedlings will wither.
When the sky darkens with dense clouds,
and rain pours down abundantly,
then the seedlings will spring up vigorously.
When it is like this,
who can stop it?
Now, the rulers of the world,
there are none who do not delight in killing people.
If there were one who did not delight in killing people,
then all the people in the world would crane their necks to look for him.
If it is truly so,
the people will turn to him,
as water flows downward.
Who can stop such a torrential force?'"
1.7 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"May I hear about the deeds of Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Among the disciples of Zhòngní,
none spoke of the affairs of Huán and Wén,
therefore later generations have no record of them,
and I have not heard of them.
If you insist on having me speak, then perhaps about the way of true kingship?"
He asked:
"What virtue must one possess
to become a true king?"
The reply was:
"By protecting the people, one becomes king,
and no one can oppose him."
He asked again:
"Can someone like me protect the people?"
The reply was:
"Yes."
He said:
"How do you know I am capable?"
The reply was:
"I heard it from Hé Yí:
When Your Majesty was sitting in the hall,
there was a man leading an ox past below it.
The king saw it,
and said:
"Where is the ox being taken?"
The reply was:
"It will be used to consecrate a bell."
The king said:
"Spare it!
I cannot bear to see it trembling with fear,
as if it were innocent yet going to the place of death."
He replied:
"Then shall we abolish the bell-consecration ceremony?"
The other said:
"How can it be abolished?
Use a sheep to replace it!"
I wonder if this actually happened?"
The reply was:
"It did happen."
He said:
"This heart is sufficient to make you a true king.
The common people all think Your Majesty is being stingy,
but I truly know it is because Your Majesty cannot bear to see suffering."
The king said:
"Indeed;
there truly are such commoners.
Although the state of Qí is small and narrow,
why would I begrudge one ox?
It is simply that I cannot bear its frightened trembling,
as if it were without fault yet going to the place of death,
therefore I exchanged it with a sheep."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Do not be surprised that the people consider Your Majesty stingy.
You exchanged a small animal for a large one—
how could they know your true intention?
If Your Majesty pities its innocence as it goes to the slaughter,
then what difference is there between an ox and a sheep?"
The king smiled and said,
"What kind of heart is this indeed?
It is not that I grudged the expense and exchanged it for a sheep.
No wonder the common people call me miserly."
He said:
"It does no harm.
This is the method of benevolence,
for you saw the ox but had not seen the sheep.
The gentleman's attitude toward birds and beasts is that,
having seen them alive,
he cannot bear to see them die;
having heard their cries,
he cannot bear to eat their flesh.
Therefore the gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen."
The king said, saying:
"The Book of Songs says:
'When others have thoughts,
I can measure them.'
This describes you, Master."
I acted in this way,
but upon reflection,
I could not understand my own heart.
When you, Master, spoke of it,
it struck a chord within my heart.
Why is it that this heart is in accord with the way of a true king?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Suppose someone reported to Your Majesty, saying:
'My strength is sufficient to lift three thousand catties,
but insufficient to lift one feather;
my eyesight is sharp enough to examine the tip of an autumn hair,
yet I cannot see a cartload of firewood.'
Would Your Majesty accept this claim?"
The king replied:
"No."
"Now kindness is sufficient to reach animals and birds,
yet the benefits do not extend to the common people.
Why is this alone so?"
Thus, if a feather is not lifted,
it is because no strength is used;
if a cartload of firewood is not seen,
it is because no eyesight is used;
if the people are not protected,
it is because no kindness is used.
Hence, the king's failure to become a true king
is due to not acting,
not because of inability.
The King said:
"What is the difference between not doing something and not being able to do it?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"If someone were to carry Mount Tài under his arm and leap across the North Sea,
and he told people:
'I cannot do it,'
this would truly be a case of not being able to do it.
Breaking off a branch for an elder,
one says to others:
"I cannot do it."
This is a case of not doing it,
not a case of being unable to do it.
The reason why Your Majesty is not a true king,
is not like carrying Mount Tai under one's arm and leaping over the North Sea;
Your Majesty's failure to be a true king
is like refusing to break off a twig.
"Respect the elders in my own family, and extend this respect to the elders in other families;
cherish the young in my own family, and extend this cherishing to the young in other families.
The whole world can be governed as easily as turning something in the palm of your hand."
The Book of Songs says,
'Set an example for your wife,
extend it to your brothers,
and govern the family and state.'
This means applying this same mind to others.
Therefore, extending kindness is sufficient to protect the entire realm,
while failing to extend kindness leaves one unable to protect even wife and children.
The reason why the ancients greatly surpassed others
lay in nothing else
but their skill in extending what they did.
Now your kindness is sufficient to reach animals,
yet your achievements do not extend to the common people—
why is this alone so?
"Weigh, and then know lightness and heaviness;
measure, and then know length and shortness.
All things are so,
but the heart is especially so.
I beg Your Majesty to measure it!"
"Does Your Majesty then delight in raising troops,
endangering officers and men,
and incurring the resentment of the feudal lords,
before feeling satisfied in your heart?"
The king said:
"No;
how would I find pleasure in this?
I wish to seek what I greatly desire."
(Mencius) said:
"May I hear about what Your Majesty greatly desires?"
The king laughed but did not speak.
He said:
"Is it because rich foods are not enough for your mouth?
Or light warm garments not enough for your body?
Or because colorful sights are not enough for your eyes?
Or musical sounds not enough for your ears?
Or because attendants are not enough to serve before you?
All Your Majesty's various ministers are sufficient to provide these,
so how could Your Majesty be for these things?"
Said:
"No;
I do not do this."
Said:
"Then what the king greatly desires can be known."
Wanting to expand your territory,
make Qín and Chǔ pay homage,
stand over the Central Kingdom
and pacify the four barbarians.
To seek what you desire by such means
is like climbing a tree to catch fish."
The king said:
"Is it as serious as that?"
The reply was:
"It is probably even more serious.
To climb a tree in search of fish,
though you may not catch any fish,
there will be no subsequent calamity.
But by acting as you do
to seek what you desire,
and exhausting all your mental and physical efforts to achieve it,
calamity is bound to follow."
The King said:
"May I hear about it?"
Mencius said:
"If the people of Zōu and the people of Chǔ were at war,
which side does Your Majesty think would win?"
The King said:
"The people of Chǔ would win."
He said:
"Thus it is certain that the small cannot match the large,
the few cannot match the many,
the weak cannot match the strong.
Throughout the land
there are nine territories of a thousand square li each,
and Qí possesses but one of them.
To subdue eight with one,
how is this different from Zōu contending with Chǔ?"
Why not return to the fundamental?
"If now Your Majesty were to institute a government and practice benevolent governance,
all the officials under Heaven would wish to stand in Your Majesty's court,
all farmers would wish to till in Your Majesty's fields,
all merchants would wish to store their goods in Your Majesty's marketplaces,
all travelers would wish to journey on Your Majesty's roads,
and all under Heaven who resent their rulers
would wish to come and complain to Your Majesty.
If it is like this,
who can withstand it?"
The king said:
"I am dull-witted,
unable to advance to this level.
I wish that you, Master, would assist my ambition,
and clearly instruct me.
Although I am not quick-witted,
I beg to try it."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Only the scholar is capable of maintaining a constant heart, even though he may lack a constant livelihood.
As for the common people,
if they lack a constant livelihood,
they will lack a constant heart.
And if they lack a constant heart,
there is no depravity to which they will not sink.
When they fall into crime,
then to punish them accordingly
is to entrap the people.
How can a benevolent ruler on the throne
behave in such a way as to entrap the people?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler regulates the people's livelihood
so that it must be sufficient above to serve their parents,
and sufficient below to support their wives and children.
In good years they are always full,
and in bad years they escape death and ruin.
Only then do they drive them toward goodness,
and thus the people follow them with ease.
Now if the people's property is regulated such that,
looking up, it is insufficient to serve their parents,
and looking down, it is insufficient to support their wives and children;
in good years they endure hardship all their lives,
and in bad years they cannot escape death.
In such circumstances, they only fear they will not survive,
so how could they have leisure to cultivate propriety and righteousness?
"If the king wishes to practice this,
why not return to the fundamental solution:
With a homestead of five mu, plant it with mulberry trees,
and those who are fifty can wear silk.
In raising chickens, pigs, dogs, and swine, do not miss their breeding seasons,
and those who are seventy can eat meat.
With a hundred mu of farmland, do not take away the time for farming,
and a family of eight can be free from hunger.
Carefully maintain the teaching in the schools,
inculcate in them the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty,
and grey-haired men will not be seen carrying burdens on the roads.
When the elderly wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people are neither hungry nor cold,
yet one who does not become a true king,
such a thing has never existed.
2.1 Zhuāng Bào went to see Mèngzǐ and said:
"I was received by the king,
and the king told me of his love of music,
but I did not know how to respond."
He then asked:
"What is the significance of loving music?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Wáng zhī hào yuè shèn,
zé Qíguó qí shùjī hū!"
Tā rì,
jiàn yú wáng yuē:
"Wáng cháng yù Zhuāngzǐ yǐ hào yuè,
yǒu zhū?"
The king's countenance changed, and he said:
"I am not capable of appreciating the music of the former kings;
I merely enjoy the popular music of the day."
(Mèngzǐ) said:
"If Your Majesty's love of music is great,
then Qí is nearly well-governed!
The music of today is just like the music of antiquity."
The king said:
"May I hear about it?"
Mencius said:
"Which is more enjoyable - enjoying music alone,
or enjoying music with others?"
The king replied:
"It's not as good as enjoying it with others."
He said:
"Is it more enjoyable to enjoy music with a few people,
or to enjoy music with many people,
which is more enjoyable?"
He replied:
"It is not as good as enjoying it with many people."
I beg to speak to Your Majesty about music.
Now if Your Majesty were here performing music,
and the people heard the sound of Your Majesty's bells and drums,
the notes of pipes and flutes,
they would all raise aching heads and knit their brows, saying to one another:
'Why does our king's love of music
reduce us to such extremity?
Fathers and sons do not see each other,
brothers, wives, and children are separated and scattered.'
Now the king is hunting here,
the people hear the sound of the king's chariots and horses,
see the beauty of the feathered banners,
and all, with aching heads and knitted brows, say to one another:
'Our king's fondness for hunting
—why does it reduce us to such an extreme state?
Fathers and sons do not see each other,
brothers, wives, and children are separated.'
This is for no other reason than that
he does not share joy with the people.
"If now Your Majesty makes music here,
the people, hearing the sound of Your Majesty's bells and drums,
and the notes of your pipes and flutes,
all with delighted countenances look pleased and say to one another:
'Our king is probably free from sickness;
for how else could he make music?'"
Now the king is hunting here,
when the people hear the sound of the king's chariots and horses,
and see the beauty of the feathered banners,
they all joyfully show happy expressions and tell one another:
'Our king is probably free from illness,
how else could he go hunting?'
This is for no other reason than
sharing joy with the people.
If Your Majesty now shares joy with the common people, you will become a true king."
2.2 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"King Wén's hunting park was seventy lǐ square,
is this true?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"There is such a record in the histories."
The other said:
"Was it really so large?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"The people still considered it small."
The king said:
"My park is only forty li square,
yet the people still consider it too large,
why is this?"
It was said:
"King Wén's hunting park was seventy lǐ square,
grass-cutters and fuel-gatherers went there,
pheasant and rabbit hunters went there,
sharing it with the people.
The people considered it small,
wasn't that appropriate?"
When I first arrived at the border,
I inquired about the state's major prohibitions,
and only then dared to enter.
I heard that within the suburban gates
there is a park forty li square,
and killing its deer
is treated as the crime of killing a person.
Thus, an area of forty li was made into a trap within the state.
Is it not fitting that the people considered it too large?
2.3 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"Is there a way to interact with neighboring states?"
Mencius replied:
"There is."
Only the benevolent can serve the small from a position of greatness,
hence Tāng served Gě,
and King Wén served the Hùnyí.
Only the wise can serve the great from a position of smallness,
hence King Tàiwáng served the Xūnyù,
and Gōu Jiàn served Wú.
He who with his great state serves a small one delights in Heaven;
he who with his small state serves a large one stands in awe of Heaven.
He who delights in Heaven will protect the whole world;
he who stands in awe of Heaven will protect his own kingdom.
The Book of Songs says:
"Stand in awe of the majesty of Heaven,
and thus preserve it."
The king said:
"Great are these words!
I have a fault,
I am fond of valor."
He replied:
"I beg Your Majesty not to delight in petty courage.
For one who grasps his sword and glares fiercely, saying:
'How dare he stand against me!'
this is the courage of an ordinary man,
sufficient only to oppose a single person.
I beg Your Majesty to make it greater!"
The Book of Songs says:
"The king blazed with anger,
then marshaled his troops,
to stop the march on Jǔ,
to consolidate Zhōu's blessings,
and to respond to the world."
This was King Wén's courage.
King Wén's single burst of anger
brought peace to the people of the world.
"The Book of Documents says:
'Heaven, having produced the inferior people,
appointed for them rulers,
and appointed for them instructors,
that they might be assisting to God in the loving care of the people.
Throughout the four quarters, whether guilty or innocent, I am the one to deal with them;
how dare anyone under heaven transgress the will of Heaven?'"
When one man acted violently throughout the land,
King Wǔ was ashamed of it.
This was the courage of King Wǔ.
And King Wǔ, with one outburst of anger,
brought peace to the people of the land.
Now if Your Majesty were also to show one instance of anger
and thereby bring peace to the people of the world,
the people would only fear that Your Majesty does not love courage."
2.4 King Xuān of Qí met Mencius at the Snow Palace.
The king said,
"Do the virtuous also have such pleasures?"
Mencius replied,
"Yes.
If the people do not get it,
they will criticize their ruler.
To criticize the ruler for not getting it
is wrong;
for a ruler not to share joy with the people
is also wrong.
He who delights in the joys of the people,
the people will also delight in his joys;
he who worries about the sorrows of the people,
the people will also worry about his sorrows.
Delighting with all under Heaven,
worrying with all under Heaven,
yet failing to become a true king—
such a thing has never occurred.
"Formerly, Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
'I wish to visit Zhuǎnfù and Cháowǔ,
proceed along the sea southward,
and reach Lángyá.
What must I cultivate that I may compare to the tours of the former kings?'"
"Yànzǐ replied:
'An excellent question indeed!
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called a tour of inspection.
A tour of inspection means inspecting what they guard.
When feudal lords attend court before the Son of Heaven, it is called reporting on duties.
Reporting on duties means reporting on their official responsibilities.
There is nothing that is not a matter of concern.
In spring, they inspect the plowing and supplement what is insufficient,
in autumn, they inspect the harvest and aid those in want.
A saying of the Xià goes:
"If our king makes no progress,
how shall we get rest?
If our king makes no excursions,
how shall we get help?
One progress, one excursion—
were the pattern for the princes."
Now it is not so:
the troops march and consume provisions,
the hungry are not fed,
the toilers are not rested.
With glaring eyes they slander one another,
and the people become rebellious.
They defy orders and oppress the people,
eating and drinking as if in a flowing stream.
Indulging in excess and dissipation,
they become a worry to the feudal lords.
To drift downstream and forget to return
is called drifting;
to go upstream and forget to return
is called lingering;
to hunt without satiety
is called excess;
to indulge in wine without satiety
is called dissipation.
The former kings had no excessive pleasures
nor dissolute conduct.
It is for Your Majesty to decide your course of action.'
"Duke Jǐng was pleased,
issued major decrees throughout the state,
and moved out to reside in the suburbs.
Thereupon he began distributing relief and supplying what was lacking."
Summoning the Grand Musician, he said:
"Compose music for me that expresses the mutual delight between ruler and subject!"
These were precisely the "Zhǐzhāo" and "Juézhāo".
The lyrics said:
"How can restraining the ruler be wrong?"
To restrain the ruler
is to love the ruler."
2.5 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"Everyone advises me to dismantle the Bright Hall.
Should I dismantle it, or should I not?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"The Bright Hall is the hall of a true king.
If Your Majesty wishes to practice kingly governance,
then you should not dismantle it."
The king said:
"May I hear about the kingly government?"
He replied:
"Formerly, when King Wén governed Qí,
the farmers paid one-ninth as tax,
officials held hereditary emoluments,
customs and markets were inspected but not taxed,
there were no prohibitions on nets in pools and weirs,
and criminals were punished without implicating their wives and children.
Old and without a wife is called a widower,
old and without a husband is called a widow,
old and without children is called solitary,
young and without a father is called an orphan.
These four kinds of people
are the world's destitute and helpless.
When King Wén issued policies and practiced benevolence,
he always prioritized these four.
The Book of Songs says,
"How fortunate are the rich,
but pitiable are the solitary and alone."
The king said:
"How excellent are these words!"
Mencius said:
"If Your Majesty deems them excellent,
then why do you not put them into practice?"
The king said:
"I have a weakness,
I am fond of wealth."
In reply, he said:
"In former times, Gōng Liú was fond of wealth,
The Book of Songs says:
'They stored grain in their barns,
they wrapped provisions,
in bags and in sacks.
Thinking to gather the people, they made their glory shine.
Bows and arrows were set,
shields, spears, battle-axes, and halberds raised,
and thus they began their march.'
When those at home have full granaries,
and those who travel have well-filled packs,
then it is said, "They can begin their march."
If Your Majesty loves wealth,
let the people be able to gratify the same feeling,
and what difficulty will there be in your attaining the royal sway?"
The king said:
"I have a weakness,
I am fond of beauty."
The reply was:
"In former times, King Tài was fond of beauty,
and loved his consort.
The Book of Songs says:
'The Ancient Duke Dǎnfù, came at dawn galloping his horse,
along the western bank of the river, until he reached below Mount Qí,
and together with Lady Jiāng, came to survey the land for a dwelling.'
At that time,
there were no unmarried women inside,
nor were there any unmarried men outside.
If the king has a fondness for beauty,
let him share it with the common people.
What difficulty would there be for the king?"
2.6 Mencius said to King Xuān of Qí:
"Suppose one of Your Majesty's ministers were to entrust his wife and children
to the care of a friend while he traveled to the state of Chǔ,
and upon his return,
he found his wife and children cold and starving.
What should be done about this?"
The King said:
"He should abandon that friend."
The King asked,
"If a chief justice cannot manage his officials,
what is to be done?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Dismiss him."
Then he asked,
"If the whole kingdom is not well governed,
what is to be done?"
The King turned to his attendants and changed the subject.
2.7 Mencius had an audience with King Xuān of Qí and said:
"When we speak of an ancient state,
we do not mean that it has lofty trees,
but that it has ministers whose families have served for generations.
Your Majesty now has no ministers whom you consider intimate.
Those whom you formerly advanced,
today you do not even know that they have fled."
The king said:
"How can I recognize their lack of talent and dismiss them?"
It was said:
"When a ruler promotes the worthy, if it is unavoidable,
he will cause the lowly to surpass the noble,
the distant to surpass the intimate.
Should this not be done with caution?"
When all those around you say he is worthy,
do not yet approve;
when all the great officers say he is worthy,
do not yet approve;
when the people of the state all say he is worthy,
then examine into the matter;
when you find that he is worthy,
then employ him.
When all those around you say it is not acceptable,
do not listen;
when all the ministers say it is not acceptable,
do not listen;
when all the people of the state say it is not acceptable,
then examine into the case;
if you find it is not acceptable,
then discard it.
If all those around you say he should be executed,
do not listen;
if all the high officials say he should be executed,
do not listen;
if all the people of the state say he should be executed,
then investigate the matter;
if you find he should be executed,
then execute him.
Therefore it is said: the people of the state have executed him.
Only in this way,
can you truly become the parent of the people."
2.8 King Xuān of Qí asked:
"Tāng exiled Jié,
and King Wǔ attacked Zhòu—
did these events occur?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"The records contain them."
The king said:
"May a subject assassinate his sovereign?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"He who violates benevolence
is called a 'violator,'
and he who violates righteousness
is called a 'mutilator.'
A mutilator and violator
is called an 'outcast.'
I have heard of the execution of the outcast Zhòu,
but I have not heard of the murdering of a sovereign."
2.9 Mencius said to King Xuān of Qí:
"When building a great mansion,
you must send the master craftsman to seek large timber.
When the master craftsman obtains large timber,
you are pleased,
considering him capable of fulfilling his responsibility.
But when the carpenter cuts it down to make it smaller,
you become angry,
considering him incapable of fulfilling his responsibility.
When one has studied something in youth,
and wishes to practice it in adulthood,
if the king says:
'Lay aside what you have learned and follow me',
what should one do?
Now suppose there is an uncut jade here,
though it may be worth ten thousand yi,
one must have a jade craftsman carve and polish it.
But when it comes to governing the state,
one says:
'Just put aside what you have learned and follow me,'
then how is this different from teaching a jade craftsman how to carve jade?"
2.10 The people of Qí attacked Yān and conquered it.
King Xuān asked:
"Some advised me not to take it,
while others advised me to take it.
For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots,
and to capture it within fifty days—
human strength alone could not have achieved this.
If I do not take it, there will surely be calamity from Heaven.
What would it be like if I were to take it?"
Mèngzǐ duì yuē:
"Qǔ zhī ér Yàn mín yuè,
zé qǔ zhī.
Gǔ zhī rén yǒu xíng zhī zhě,
Wǔ Wáng shì yě.
Qǔ zhī ér Yàn mín bù yuè,
zé wù qǔ.
Gǔ zhī rén yǒu xíng zhī zhě,
Wén Wáng shì yě.
When a state of ten thousand chariots attacks another state of ten thousand chariots,
with people bringing baskets of food and pots of congee to welcome the king's army,
could there be any other reason?
It is to escape from fire and water.
If the water becomes deeper,
if the fire becomes hotter,
they will simply turn to another ruler.
2.11 The people of Qí attacked Yān,
and captured it.
The various states were planning to rescue Yān.
King Xuān said:
"Many of the states are planning to attack me.
How should I deal with this?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"I have heard of one who governed the world from a territory of seventy li—
Tāng was such a man.
I have never heard of one with a thousand li who stood in fear of others.
The Book of History says:
'When Tāng began his punitive expeditions,
he started with Gé.'
The whole world had confidence in him,
When he marched east,
the western tribes complained;
when he marched south,
the northern tribes complained,
saying,
"Why does he leave us for last?"
The people looked to him,
as in a great drought they look to clouds and rainbows.
Those going to the market did not stop,
nor did those tilling the fields change their tasks.
He punished their ruler and comforted the people,
like timely rain falling.
The people were greatly pleased.
The Book of History says:
'We awaited our sovereign,
when he came, we were revived.'
Now when Yān was oppressing its people,
and you, O king, went forth to punish it,
the people thought that you would deliver them out of the midst of fire and water.
Full of joy, they brought their baskets of food and vessels of drink, and met your majesty's host.
But if you slaughter their fathers and elder brothers,
and put their sons and younger brothers in chains,
if you destroy their ancestral temples,
and remove their precious vessels,
how can such a course be deemed proper?
The world already fears Qí's strength,
and now you have doubled your territory
without practicing benevolent governance,
this will provoke the armies of the world.
Your Majesty should quickly issue an order,
return their old and young,
stop seizing their precious vessels,
consult with the people of Yān,
establish a ruler and then withdraw from there,
then it may still be possible to stop this."
2.12 There was a conflict between Zōu and Lǔ.
Duke Mù asked,
"Thirty-three of my officials have died,
yet none of the common people died for them.
If I punish them,
I cannot possibly punish them all;
if I do not punish them,
then I resent their looking on the deaths of their superiors without rescuing them.
What should be done about this?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In years of calamity and famine,
your people, the old and weak, are left to die in the ditches and gullies,
while the able-bodied scatter in all directions—amounting to nearly a thousand individuals;
yet your granaries are full,
your treasuries overflowing,
and none of your officials report this to you.
This shows negligence from above and cruelty to those below."
Zēng Zǐ said:
"Beware, beware!
What comes from you,
will return to you."
Now the people can finally return it.
Let the ruler not blame them!
If the ruler practices benevolent governance,
then the people will love their superiors
and die for their elders."
2.13 Duke Wén of Téng asked:
"Téng is a small state,
situated between Qí and Chǔ.
Should we serve Qí?
Or should we serve Chǔ?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"This plan is beyond my capability.
If I must speak,
then there is one thing:
Dredge these moats,
build these walls,
defend them together with the people,
and if the people do not flee even when facing death,
then this can be done."
2.14 Duke Wén of Téng asked:
"The people of Qí are about to fortify Xuē,
I am very fearful,
what should be done about it?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In former times, King Tài dwelt in Bīn.
The Dí people invaded it,
so he left and dwelt at the foot of Qí Mountain.
It was not that he chose and took it,
but that he had no alternative.
If one does good,
among later generations of his descendants there is sure to be one who will become a true king.
A nobleman establishes an enterprise and hands down a tradition
so that it can be carried on.
As for achieving success,
that lies with Heaven.
What can you do about that?
Just strive earnestly to do good.
2.15 Duke Wén of Téng asked:
"Téng is a small state;
though we exhaust our strength in serving large states,
we still cannot avoid being attacked.
What course should we take?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In the past, when King Tài dwelt in Bīn,
the Dí people invaded it.
He served them with furs and silks,
but could not avoid it;
he served them with dogs and horses,
but could not avoid it;
he served them with pearls and jades,
but could not avoid it.
Then he gathered the elders and told them:
'What the Dí people desire is our land.
I have heard it said:
A noble man does not use what sustains people to harm people.
Why should you gentlemen worry about having no ruler?
I shall leave here.'
He left Bīn, crossed over Mount Liáng,
and settled at the foot of Mount Qí to dwell there.
The people of Bīn said:
'He is a benevolent man,
we must not lose him.'
Those who followed him flocked like crowds returning to market.
Some said:
'It is a heritage to be guarded,
not something one can decide for oneself.
We should defend it unto death and not leave.'
"I beg you, sir, to choose between these two courses."
2.16 Duke Píng of Lǔ was about to go out,
when his favorite, a man named Zāng Cāng, requested:
"On other days when you go out,
you always inform the officials of your destination.
Now the carriage is already harnessed,
but the officials do not know where you are going.
I venture to ask."
The Duke said:
"I am going to see Mencius."
He said:
"Why does my lord demean himself by taking the initiative to visit a commoner?
Do you consider him worthy?
Propriety and righteousness should emanate from the worthy;
yet Mèngzǐ observed greater mourning for his later deceased parent than for his earlier deceased one.
My lord should not see him!"
The duke said:
"Very well."
Yuèzhèngzǐ entered for an audience and said:
"Why does Your Majesty not receive Mèng Kē?"
The king replied:
"Someone informed me, saying:
'Mèngzǐ observed later mourning rites exceeding the former ones,'
therefore I do not go to see him."
He said:
"What do you mean by 'exceeding proper limits'?
Was it because you first used the rites appropriate to a scholar and then those to a high official?
Or because you first used three tripods and afterwards used five?"
The other replied:
"No;
I referred to the excellence of the inner and outer coffins, the graveclothes, and the coverlet."
He said:
"That cannot be described as exceeding proper limits;
it was a difference between poverty and wealth."
Yuèzhèngzǐ went to see Mèngzǐ and said:
"I told the sovereign about you,
and the sovereign was going to come to see you.
But a favorite named Zāng Cāng dissuaded him,
so the sovereign did not come after all."
He said:
"To act, something impels it;
to stop, something obstructs it.
Acting and stopping are not within human capability.
That I did not meet with the Marquis of Lǔ,
was Heaven's will.
How could the son of the Zāng family
cause me not to meet him?"
3.1 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying,
"If you, Master, were to hold power in Qí,
could we expect achievements like those of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"You are truly a man of Qí,
knowing only Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ."
Someone asked Zēng Xī, saying:
"Who is more virtuous, you or Zǐlù?"
Zēng Xī, looking uneasy, replied:
"He was one whom my late father held in awe."
The person then asked:
"In that case, who is more virtuous, you or Guǎn Zhòng?"
Zēng Xī looked displeased and said unhappily:
'How can you compare me to Guǎn Zhòng?
Guǎn Zhòng enjoyed such exclusive favor from his sovereign,
and administered the state's government for so long,
yet his achievements were so meager;
how can you compare me to such a man?'"
He said:
"Guǎn Zhòng was what Zēng Xī would not do,
and yet you wish me to be like him?"
He said:
"Guǎn Zhòng made his ruler a hegemon,
and Yànzǐ made his ruler illustrious.
Are Guǎn Zhòng and Yànzǐ not even worth emulating?"
The reply was:
"To make Qí a true king,
would be as easy as turning over one's hand."
He said:
"If so,
then my confusion grows even greater.
With King Wén's virtue,
he lived a hundred years before passing away,
yet his influence had not fully spread throughout the world;
King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu succeeded him,
and only then did it become widely established.
Now you speak of achieving kingship as if it were easy—
does this mean King Wén is not worth emulating?"
He said:
"How can King Wén be compared?
From Tāng to Wǔdīng,
there were six or seven generations of wise and sage rulers,
and the world had belonged to Yīn for a long time.
What has long been established is hard to change.
When Wǔdīng received the feudal lords at his court,
he ruled the world as if turning it in his palm.
The time from Zhòu to Wǔdīng was not long,
the old families' remaining customs, lingering influences, and good governance still existed;
moreover, there were Wēizǐ, Wēizhòng, Prince Bǐgàn, Jīzǐ, and Jiāogé,
all worthy men,
who together assisted him,
thus it took a long time before he lost it.
There was not a foot of land that did not belong to him;
there was not a single person who was not his subject;
yet King Wén started with only a territory of a hundred lǐ square;
therefore it was difficult.
The people of Qí have a saying:
'Though one may have wisdom,
it is not as good as seizing the opportunity;
though one may have tools,
it is not as good as awaiting the right time.'
Now it is easy to do so:
In the prosperous ages of Xiàhòu, Yīn, and Zhōu,
no territory exceeded a thousand lǐ square,
yet Qí possesses such territory;
the crowing of cocks and barking of dogs are heard
all the way to its four borders,
and Qí has such a population.
The land need not be further expanded,
the people need not be further gathered.
If one governs with benevolent policies to become king,
none can oppose him.
Moreover, the absence of a true king
has never been more prolonged than at present;
the people's suffering under tyrannical government
has never been more severe than at present.
The hungry are easily fed,
the thirsty are easily given drink.
Confucius said:
"The spread of virtue
is faster than the relay of dispatches through the postal system."
In the present time,
if a state with ten thousand chariots practices benevolent governance,
the people's delight in it
is like being freed from hanging upside down.
Therefore, doing half the work of the ancients
will necessarily achieve double the results,
and only at this time is it so."
3.2 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying,
"If you were to be made a high minister of Qí,
and could carry your principles into practice,
you would not find it difficult to become a hegemon or a true king in doing so.
In such a position, would your mind be perturbed?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"No.
At forty, my mind became unperturbed."
He said:
"If so,
then you surpass Mèng Bēn by far."
He said:
"This is not difficult;
Gào Zǐ attained an unmoved mind before I did."
He said:
"Is there a way to achieve an unmoved mind?"
He said:
"Yes.
In cultivating courage, Běigōng Yǒu
would not flinch if his skin were torn,
nor avert his gaze if his eyes were threatened.
He considered the slightest humiliation from others
as being flogged in the marketplace.
He would not accept even from a commoner in coarse clothes,
nor would he accept from a lord of ten thousand chariots;
he regarded stabbing a lord of ten thousand chariots
as no different from stabbing a commoner in coarse clothes;
he showed no deference to the nobles,
and when harsh words came his way,
he would invariably return them.
Mèng Shīshě's method of cultivating courage,
saying:
"To regard not winning as if it were winning;
to measure the enemy and then advance,
to consider victory and then engage,
this is to fear the three armies.
How could Shě be certain of victory?
He was merely able to be without fear."
Mèng Shīshě resembles Zēngzǐ,
Běigōng Yǒu resembles Zǐxià.
As for the courage of these two men,
it is unknown which is superior,
yet Mèng Shīshě holds to the essential.
Once Zēngzǐ said to Zǐ Xiāng:
'Do you love courage?
I once heard about great courage from the Master:
When upon self-reflection I find I'm not in the right,
even though facing a common man in coarse clothes,
I would be apprehensive;
when upon self-reflection I find I am in the right,
I would go forward even against thousands and tens of thousands.'
Mèng Shīshè's method of maintaining his vital energy
was not as effective as Zēngzǐ's method of maintaining his moral principles."
He said:
"May I ask
about your unperturbed mind and Gàozǐ's unperturbed mind,
can I hear about them?"
"Gàozǐ said:
'If you fail in words,
do not seek it in the mind;
if you fail in the mind,
do not seek it in the vital force.'
If you fail in the mind,
do not seek it in the vital force,
that is acceptable;
if you fail in words,
do not seek it in the mind,
that is not acceptable."
The will is the commander of the vital energy,
and the vital energy is what fills the body.
Where the will arrives,
the vital energy follows;
therefore it is said:
'Maintain your will,
and do not abuse your vital energy.'
"Since it is said: 'The will is primary,
and the vital energy is secondary.'
Why then
does it also say:
'Maintain the will,
and do not abuse the vital energy'?"
He said:
"When the will is unified, it moves the vital energy;
when the vital energy is unified, it moves the will.
Now those who stumble and those who rush forward -
this is due to the vital energy,
yet it conversely moves their mind."
"May I ask in what you excel, Master?"
He said:
"I understand words,
I am good at cultivating my vast, flowing passion-nature."
"May I ask what is meant by your vast, flowing passion-nature?"
He said:
"It is difficult to describe.
As a passion-nature,
it is supremely great and supremely unyielding.
Nourish it with integrity and place no obstacle in its path,
and it will fill the space between Heaven and Earth."
This is a spirit
that, in harmony with righteousness and the Way,
without which, it starves.
It is born from the accumulation of righteousness,
not seized by occasional acts of righteousness.
If in action there is dissatisfaction in one's heart,
then it starves."
Therefore, I say:
"Gàozǐ has never understood righteousness,
because he considers it external."
Be ever intent upon it,
but do not set the mind
forgetting it,
nor help it grow.
Do not be like the man from Sòng:
In the state of Sòng, there was a man who grieved that his sprouts were not growing and pulled them up,
then returned home wearily,
and said to his family:
"I'm exhausted today!
I helped the sprouts grow!"
His son hurried out to look at them,
and the sprouts had all withered."
Few in the world refrain from helping their sprouts grow.
Those who think it futile and neglect them
are the ones who do not weed the sprouts;
those who help them grow
are the ones who pull at the sprouts—
not only is it futile,
but it even harms them.
"What is meant by 'understanding words'?"
It was said:
"When encountering biased words, I understand where they are obscured;
when encountering excessive words, I understand where they are trapped;
when encountering perverse words, I understand where they deviate;
when encountering evasive words, I understand where they are exhausted.
Born in their hearts,
it harms their governance;
manifested in their governance,
it harms their affairs.
Should sages rise again,
they would surely follow my words."
"Zǎi Wǒ, Zǐgòng excel at diplomatic discourse;
Rǎn Niú, Mǐn Zǐ, Yán Yuān excel in discoursing on virtuous conduct.
Confucius combined both abilities,
yet said:
'When it comes to diplomatic rhetoric,
I am incapable.'
Does this mean our Master was already a sage?"
He said:
"Alas!
What kind of talk is this?
Formerly, Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
'Is the Master a sage?'
Confucius said:
'As for being a sage, I cannot attain that.
I learn without satiety and teach without weariness.'"
Zǐgòng said:
"To learn without weariness
is wisdom;
to teach without tiring
is benevolence.
Being both benevolent and wise,
our Master is already a sage."
But Confucius would not claim sagehood for himself—
what does this mean?"
"I have heard it said of old:
Zǐxià, Zǐyóu, and Zǐzhāng
each had one aspect of the sage,
while Rǎnniú, Mǐnzǐ, and Yānyuān
had all aspects in miniature.
May I ask with whom you would rank yourself?"
The reply was:
"Let us leave that for the present."
He asked:
"What about Bóyí and Yīyǐn?"
The reply was:
"They followed different paths.
He would not serve a ruler he disapproved of,
nor command a people he disapproved of;
he would advance when order prevailed,
and withdraw when chaos reigned—
this was Bóyí.
There is no sovereign he would not serve,
there are no people he would not employ;
he advanced when there was order,
he advanced when there was chaos—
such was Yì Yǐn.
He would take office when it was proper to do so,
he would withdraw when it was proper to withdraw,
he would stay long when it was proper to stay long,
he would leave quickly when it was proper to leave quickly—
such was Confucius.
They were all sages of antiquity,
but I have not been able to practice their ways;
as for what I wish,
it is to learn from Confucius."
"Are Bóyí and Yīyǐn on a par with Confucius?"
The reply was:
"No;
since there were living men,
there has never been another Confucius."
"Then were there any points of similarity?"
The reply was:
"There were."
Obtaining a territory of a hundred lǐ and ruling over it,
they were all capable of making the feudal lords pay homage and possessing the empire;
but to commit one unrighteous act,
or kill one innocent person,
in order to gain the empire,
they would not do it.
In this they were alike.
He said:
"May I ask how they differ?"
He replied:
"Zǎi Wǒ, Zǐ Gòng, and Yǒu Ruò,
whose wisdom was sufficient to understand the sage,
were not so base as to flatter one they favored.
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"In my view of the Master,
he was far superior to Yáo and Shùn."
Zǐgòng said:
"Observing their rituals, one understands their governance;
hearing their music, one comprehends their virtue.
From a hundred generations later,
evaluating the kings of a hundred generations,
none can contradict this.
Since the beginning of humankind,
there has never been one like our Master."
Yǒu Ruò said:
"Is this only true for the people?
The qílín among the running beasts,
the fènghuáng among the flying birds,
Mount Tài among the small mounds,
the rivers and seas among the puddles -
they are all of the same category.
The sage among the people
is also of the same category.
Standing out from his kind,
rising above the multitude,
since the beginning of humankind,
there has never been one greater than Confucius.
3.3 Mèngzǐ said:
"One who uses force while feigning benevolence becomes a hegemon,
and a hegemon must possess a large state;
one who practices benevolence through virtue becomes a true king,
and a true king does not depend on having a large state.
Tāng began with only seventy lǐ,
and King Wén with a hundred lǐ."
"Those who use force to make others submit
do not win their hearts' allegiance,
but only their compliance due to insufficient strength;
those who use virtue to make others submit
win their joyful and sincere allegiance from the heart,
just as the seventy disciples submitted to Confucius."
The Book of Songs says:
"From the west, from the east,
from the south, from the north,
none thinks of not submitting."
This is what is meant.
3.4 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence brings honor,
while lack of benevolence brings disgrace;
now if one hates disgrace yet dwells in lack of benevolence,
this is like hating dampness yet dwelling in a low place.
If one hates it,
nothing is better than valuing virtue and honoring scholars,
placing the worthy in positions of authority,
and appointing the capable to offices;"
When a state is at leisure,
seize the moment to clarify its governance and laws.
Even if it is a large state,
it will surely be feared.
The Book of Songs says:
'Before the heavens send down rain and clouds,
I gather roots from the mulberry tree,
to mend my window and my door.
Now you people down below,
who dare to treat me with contempt?'
Kǒngzǐ yuē:
"The author of this poem,
must understand the Way indeed!
One who can properly govern his state,
who would dare to insult him?"
Now that the state is at leisure,
to indulge in pleasure and idleness at this time
is to seek calamity upon oneself.
Calamity and blessing are all sought by oneself.
The Book of Songs says:
'Always strive to accord with the Mandate of Heaven,
and you will seek and obtain abundant blessings.'
The Tai Jia states:
'When Heaven sends down calamities,
there is still hope of weathering them;
when man brings calamities upon himself,
there is no hope of escape.'
This is what is meant."
3.5 Mencius said:
"When the virtuous are honored and the capable employed,
with outstanding individuals in positions of authority,
then all scholars under heaven will be pleased and willing to serve in his court;
when in marketplaces, storage is provided without levying taxes,
and regulations are enforced without warehousing restrictions,
then all merchants under heaven will be pleased and willing to store their goods in his markets;
If tollgates inspect but do not impose taxes,
then all travelers under Heaven will be pleased and willing to take to its roads;
if farmers assist in public fields without paying tax on their own land,
then all farmers under Heaven will be pleased and willing to cultivate its fields;
If there were no taxes on the shops and no additional levies on the households without adult males,
then all the people under heaven would be delighted and wish to become his subjects.
If a ruler can practice these five things,
then the people of neighboring states will look up to him as their parents.
To lead their children to attack their parents—
since the beginning of humankind, no one has ever succeeded in doing so.
Thus,
he will be invincible in the world.
One who is invincible in the world is an official of Heaven.
Yet if such a one does not become a true king,
such a thing has never occurred."
3.6 Mencius said:
"All humans have a heart that cannot bear to see the suffering of others.
The ancient kings had this heart that cannot bear to see the suffering of others,
and thus they had a government that cannot bear to see the suffering of others.
With this heart that cannot bear to see the suffering of others,
practicing a government that cannot bear to see the suffering of others,
ruling the world would be as easy as turning it in the palm of your hand."
The reason for saying that all men have a mind which cannot bear to see the sufferings of others
is this: when men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well,
they all have a feeling of alarm and distress,
not that they may thereby gain the favor of the child's parents,
nor that they may seek the praise of their neighbors and friends,
nor from a dislike to the reputation of having been unmoved by such a thing.
From this perspective,
one who lacks a heart of compassion
is not human;
one who lacks a heart of shame and aversion
is not human;
one who lacks a heart of courtesy and modesty
is not human;
one who lacks a heart of right and wrong
is not human.
The heart of compassion is the seed of benevolence;
the heart of shame is the seed of righteousness;
the heart of courtesy and modesty is the seed of propriety;
the heart of right and wrong is the seed of wisdom.
Humans possess these four beginnings,
just as they have four limbs.
To possess these four beginnings yet claim one is incapable
is to do violence to oneself;
to claim one's ruler is incapable
is to do violence to one's ruler.
All who have these four beginnings within themselves,
knowing to expand and fulfill them completely,
Like a fire just starting to burn,
or a spring just beginning to flow.
If one can expand it,
it will be sufficient to protect all within the four seas;
if one cannot expand it,
it will not suffice to serve one's parents."
3.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Is the arrow-maker less benevolent than the armor-maker?
The arrow-maker only fears that his arrows may not hurt people,
while the armor-maker only fears that they may get hurt.
The same applies to the shaman and the coffin-maker.
Therefore, one must be cautious in choosing one's trade."
Confucius said:
"It is beautiful to dwell in benevolence.
If one chooses not to reside in benevolence,
how can one attain wisdom?"
Now benevolence is heaven's honored rank,
and humanity's peaceful abode.
When none oppose it yet one is not benevolent,
this is unwise.
Without benevolence and wisdom,
without propriety and righteousness,
one becomes a servant of others.
To be a servant yet feel ashamed of servitude
is like an archer being ashamed of making bows
or a fletcher being ashamed of making arrows.
If one feels ashamed of this,
nothing is better than practicing benevolence.
The benevolent person is like an archer:
the archer corrects himself before shooting;
if the arrow is shot but misses the target,
he does not resent those who surpass him,
but turns inward to examine himself.
3.8 Mencius said:
"Zǐlù,
when told he had faults, rejoiced.
Yǔ, upon hearing good words, bowed in gratitude.
The great Shùn was even greater,
sharing goodness with others,
setting aside himself to follow others,
and delighting in drawing from others to cultivate virtue."
From farming, pottery-making, and fishing
to becoming emperor,
there was nothing he did not learn from others.
Taking from others to practice goodness
is to encourage others in doing good.
Therefore, nothing is more important for a noble person than encouraging others in doing good."
3.9 Mencius said:
"Bó Yí would not serve a ruler he did not approve of,
nor befriend anyone he did not approve of.
He would not stand in the court of a wicked man,
nor speak with wicked people.
To stand in the court of a wicked man,
or to speak with wicked people,
was to him like wearing his court robes and court cap and sitting in mud and ashes."
Extending the aversion to evil,
he thought that if standing with a villager
whose cap was not straight,
he would turn away disdainfully,
as if about to be defiled.
Therefore, although feudal lords came with eloquent appeals,
he would not accept them.
Not accepting them
meant he disdained to approach them.
Liǔxià Huì was not ashamed to serve under a corrupt ruler,
nor did he consider it lowly to hold a minor post;
in advancing, he did not conceal his worthiness,
but always acted according to his principles;
when neglected and left without a position, he harbored no resentment,
and in times of hardship and poverty, he did not grieve.
Hence, it is said:
'You are you,
and I am I.
Even if you were to stand naked by my side,
how could you possibly defile me?'
Thus he cheerfully went along with them
without losing himself,
and when pressed to stay, he stayed.
That he stayed when pressed to stay
was because it was beneath him to leave."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Bóyī was narrow-minded,
and Liǔxià Huì was disrespectful.
Narrow-mindedness and disrespectfulness
are paths a gentleman does not follow."
4.1 Mèngzǐ said:
"Favorable weather is not as good as favorable terrain;
favorable terrain is not as good as human harmony.
A city with walls three lǐ in circumference,
and outer walls seven lǐ around,
can be besieged without being captured.
When a city is besieged,
there must be those who have favorable weather;
yet it is not captured—
this shows that favorable weather is not as good as favorable terrain.
The walls are not high enough,
the moats are not deep enough,
the weapons and armor are not sharp and strong enough,
the provisions are not abundant enough;
yet they abandon them and flee,
this shows that geographical advantage is not as important as human unity.
Hence it is said:
To keep the people within bounds does not depend on the borders of the territory;
to secure the state does not depend on the strategic advantages of mountains and rivers;
to awe the world does not depend on the sharpness of weapons and armor.
One who has the Way will have many to support him,
whereas one who has not the Way will have few to support him.
When the support is reduced to the minimum,
even his own relatives will turn against him;
when the support is increased to the maximum,
the whole world will follow him.
With the whole world to follow him,
he can attack the one whom even his relatives have turned against;
therefore, the noble man prefers not to fight,
but when he does, he is sure to win."
4.2 Mèngzǐ was about to go to court to see the king,
when the king sent a messenger to say:
"I had intended to come and see you,
but I have caught a chill,
and cannot expose myself to the wind.
If you were to come to court,
I would make an appearance at court.
I wonder if I might be able to see you?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Unfortunately, I too am unwell,
The next day, he went out to offer condolences at the Dōngguō family.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Yesterday you declined on grounds of illness,
today you go to offer condolences—
is this perhaps not permissible?"
He replied:
"Yesterday I was ill,
today I have recovered—
why should I not offer condolences?"
The king sent someone to inquire about his illness,
and the physician came.
Mèng Zhòngzǐ replied:
"Previously, there was a royal command,
but due to the worry of gathering firewood (i.e., minor illness),
I was unable to attend court.
Now the illness has slightly improved,
and I hasten to go to court,
but I do not know whether I can make it there or not?"
He sent several men to intercept him on the road, saying:
"Please do not return home,
but proceed directly to the court!"
Having no alternative, he went to spend the night at Jǐng Chǒu's house.
Jǐngzǐ said:
"Within, there is the relationship between father and son;
without, there is the relationship between ruler and minister.
These are the great human relationships.
Between father and son, affection is paramount;
between ruler and minister, respect is paramount.
I have seen the king's respect for you,
but I have not seen how you show respect to the king."
He said:
"Alas! What kind of talk is this!
None of the people of Qí discuss benevolence and righteousness with the king,
is it because they consider benevolence and righteousness to be unworthy?
In their hearts they say:
'How is this person worthy of discussing benevolence and righteousness with?' and so on,
then nothing shows greater disrespect than this.
I dare not present anything other than the ways of Yáo and Shùn before the king,
therefore none among the people of Qí respect the king as much as I do."
Jǐngzǐ said:
"No;
that is not what I meant.
The Book of Rites says:
'When a father calls, [one should] not merely answer 'yes';
when summoned by the sovereign's command, [one should] not wait for the carriage to be yoked.'
You were originally going to court,
but upon hearing the king's command, you ultimately did not go,
this seems hardly in accordance with the rites."
He said:
"Is this what is meant?
Zēngzǐ said:
'The wealth of Jìn and Chǔ, I cannot attain;
they have their wealth,
I have my benevolence;
they have their nobility,
I have my righteousness,
in what should I feel lacking?'"
If it were not righteous,
how could Master Zēng have said it?
This is perhaps one way.
There are three universally honored things in the world:
first, noble rank;
second, age;
third, virtue.
In the court, nothing is more esteemed than rank;
in the local community, nothing is more esteemed than age;
in assisting the world and guiding the people, nothing is more esteemed than virtue.
How can one possess one of these and despise the other two?
Therefore, a ruler who is to accomplish great deeds
must have ministers whom he does not summon;
if he wishes to consult with them, he goes to them.
If his respect for virtue and delight in the Way are not like this,
he is not fit to accomplish great deeds.
Thus, Tāng with regard to Yī Yǐn,
learned from him and then made him his minister,
therefore he became king without toil;
Duke Huán with regard to Guǎn Zhòng,
learned from him and then made him his minister,
therefore he became hegemon without toil.
Now under heaven, the lands are similar and virtues are equal,
none can surpass another,
for no other reason
than that they are fond of employing those whom they can teach,
and not fond of employing those from whom they can receive instruction.
Tāng with regard to Yī Yǐn,
Duke Huán with regard to Guǎn Zhòng,
would not dare summon them.
Even Guǎn Zhòng could not be summoned,
how much less one who is no Guǎn Zhòng?"
4.3 Chén Zhēn asked:
"Previously in Qí,
the king offered one hundred jīn of superior gold, yet you did not accept it;
in Sòng,
he offered seventy yì and you accepted;
in Xuē,
he offered fifty yì and you accepted.
If declining it the other day was right,
then accepting it today is wrong;
if accepting it today is right,
then declining it the other day was wrong.
You, Master, must be at one of these extremes.
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Both are correct.
When I was in Sòng,
I was about to embark on a long journey,
and travelers must be given traveling funds;
they offered, saying:
'We present you with traveling funds.'
Why should I not accept them?"
When I was in Xuē,
I had a warning in mind;
they offered a gift, saying:
'We heard of your caution,
so we present this for military provisions.'
Why should I not accept it?
If in Qí,
then there is no justification for it.
To give a gift without justification
is to bribe him.
How can a gentleman be won over by bribery?"
4.4 When Mencius went to Pínglù,
he said to its chief official:
"If one of your spearmen
should three times in one day fall out of rank,
would you dismiss him or not?"
He said:
"Not waiting for three times."
"Then you have also failed in your duties many times.
In years of calamity and famine,
your people—the old and weak are left to die in ditches and gullies,
while the strong and able scatter to the four directions—
number nearly a thousand."
He said:
"This is not something Jùxīn could have done."
He said:
"Suppose someone received another's oxen and sheep
and was to tend them for him,
then he must seek pasture and fodder for them.
If he seeks pasture and fodder but cannot find them,
should he return them to their owner?
Or should he stand by and watch them die?"
He said:
"Then this is Jùxīn's crime."
Another day, he had an audience with the King and said:
"Among those who govern cities for the King,
I know of five individuals.
Among those who recognize their own faults,
only Kǒng Jùxīn does so."
He then recounted the matter to the King.
The King said:
"This then is my fault."
4.5 Mèngzǐ said to Chíwā:
"You resigned from Língqiū
and requested to be the Chief Criminal Judge,
which seemed reasonable,
because in that position you could remonstrate.
Now several months have passed;
have you not been able to remonstrate?"
Chíwā remonstrated with the king but was not heeded,
so he resigned from his post and left.
The people of Qí said:
"The means by which you act for the chán chú
are excellent indeed;
but as for the means by which you act for yourself,
that I do not know."
Gōngdūzǐ reported this.
He said:
"I have heard it said:
Those who hold official positions,
if they cannot fulfill their duties, should resign;
those with responsibility to speak out,
if their counsel is not heeded, should depart.
I hold no official position,
I bear no responsibility to speak out,
so in my coming and going,
am I not completely free and at ease?"
4.6 Mencius served as a minister in Qí,
and was sent to offer condolences in Téng.
The king appointed the official Wáng Huān from Gě as his assistant for the journey.
Wáng Huān met with him morning and evening,
and throughout the return journey between Qí and Téng,
Mencius never spoke with him about official matters.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"The position of a minister of Qí
is not insignificant;
the road between Qí and Téng,
is not short,
yet on your return
you never discussed matters of governance,
why is that?"
He said:
"Since someone has already taken charge of governing it,
what more have I to say?"
4.7 Mèngzǐ went from Qí to bury his mother in Lǔ,
then returned to Qí,
and stopped at Yíng.
Chōng Yú made a request, saying:
"The other day, unaware of my incompetence,
you entrusted me with overseeing the coffin-making.
It was a solemn occasion,
and I did not dare to ask.
Now, I wish to venture a question:
The wood seemed rather fine."
It is said:
"In ancient times, there were no fixed dimensions for inner and outer coffins.
In the middle ages, the inner coffin was seven inches thick,
and the outer coffin matched it.
This applied from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
not merely for the sake of appearance,
but to fully express the feelings of the human heart.
If it cannot be obtained,
it cannot bring pleasure;
if there is no wealth,
it cannot bring pleasure.
When obtained and with wealth,
the ancients all used it,
why should I alone not do so?
Moreover, compared to the deceased,
not letting the soil touch their skin,
wouldn't that alone bring comfort to people's hearts?
I have heard it said:
A noble person does not stint on their parents for the sake of the world."
4.8 Shěn Tóng asked in his private capacity:
"Is Yān fit to be invaded?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yes;
Zǐ Kuài had no right to give Yān to another,
nor had Zǐ Zhī the right to receive Yān from Zǐ Kuài.
There is an official here,
and you are pleased with him,
without informing the king
you privately give him your emoluments and rank;
as for this scholar,
he also receives them from you privately without the king's command,
would that be acceptable?
How is this different from that?"
The people of Qí attacked Yān.
Someone asked:
"Did you encourage Qí to attack Yān,
is that true?"
He replied:
"No;
Shěn Tóng asked 'Can Yān be attacked?'
I responded to him:
'It can,'
and so they went ahead and attacked it.
If he were to say: 'Who is fit to attack it?'
then one should respond to him:
'One who is Heaven's appointed officer
is fit to attack it.'
Suppose there is a murderer,
and someone asks:
'Is it permissible to kill a person?'
Then one should respond:
'It is permissible.'
If they then ask:
'Who may execute him?'
Then one should respond:
'The judge,
may execute him.'
But now using Yan to attack Yan,
4.9 The people of Yān rebelled.
King Xuān of Qí said:
"I feel deeply ashamed before Mèngzǐ."
Chén Jiǎ said:
"Your Majesty should not worry about this.
Does Your Majesty consider yourself compared to Duke of Zhōu
who was more benevolent and wise?"
The King said:
"Oh!
What kind of talk is this!"
It was said:
"The Duke of Zhōu sent Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn,
but Guǎn Shū used Yīn to rebel;
if he knew and still sent him,
this shows lack of benevolence;
if he didn't know and sent him,
this shows lack of wisdom.
Benevolence and wisdom
were not fully possessed by the Duke of Zhōu,
how much less by the king?
I beg to see him and explain this matter."
He went to see Mèngzǐ and asked:
"What kind of person was Zhōu Gōng?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"An ancient sage."
The questioner continued:
"He appointed Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn,
yet Guǎn Shū used Yīn to rebel, is this true?"
Mèngzǐ answered:
"Yes."
Someone asked:
"Did the Duke of Zhōu know he would rebel
yet still appointed him?"
The reply was:
"He did not know."
"Then can even a sage make mistakes?"
The answer:
"The Duke of Zhōu was the younger brother;
Guǎn Shū was the elder brother.
The Duke of Zhōu's error,
wasn't it quite natural?"
The noble person of antiquity,
when having faults, would correct them;
the noble person of today,
when having faults, would indulge them.
The noble person of antiquity,
their faults were like eclipses of the sun and moon,
which all people could see;
and when they reformed,
all people looked up to them.
The gentlemen of today,
do they merely comply with it?
They even go so far as to make excuses for it.
4.10 Mencius resigned from his position as a minister and prepared to return home.
The king went to see Mencius,
saying:
"Previously, I wished to see you but could not;
I was very pleased to have you serve in the same court;
now you are abandoning me and returning home—
I wonder if I may continue to see you after this?"
Mencius replied:
"I did not dare to ask,
but it is certainly my wish."
Another day, the king said to Shí Zǐ:
"I wish to establish Mèngzǐ in the central region of the state and grant him a residence,
providing for his disciples with ten thousand zhōng of grain,
so that all the officials and people of the state may have a model to emulate.
Why don't you convey this for me!"
Shí Zǐ then relayed this through Chén Zǐ to inform Mèngzǐ,
and Chén Zǐ conveyed Shí Zǐ's words to Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Indeed;
but how could Shí Zǐ know it is unacceptable?
If I were seeking wealth,
why would I decline a hundred thousand to accept ten thousand—
is that seeking wealth?"
Jìsūn said:
"How strange
Zǐshū Yí is!
He wished to be in charge of governance himself;
when not employed,
he should have let it rest at that,
yet he also made his sons and younger brothers high ministers.
Who among men does not desire wealth and honor?
But he alone, in the midst of wealth and honor,
privately monopolized it."
In ancient times, when markets were held,
people would exchange what they had
for what they lacked,
with officials managing the affairs.
There was a mean fellow, however,
who would invariably seek out a vantage point to climb,
looking left and right,
in order to monopolize the market's profits.
Everyone considered them base,
so they were taxed accordingly.
The taxation of merchants
began with these base men."
4.11 Mèngzǐ left Qí,
and lodged at Zhòu.
There was someone who wished to persuade the king to detain him,
who sat down and spoke.
Mèngzǐ did not respond,
but leaned on a low table and lay down.
The visitor was displeased and said:
"I, your disciple, fasted and purified myself overnight before daring to speak,
yet you, Master, lie down and do not listen.
I beg never to dare see you again."
Said:
"Sit!
I will speak plainly to you.
In the past, Duke Mù of Lǔ
had no one by Zǐsī's side,
then he could not keep Zǐsī content;
Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng
had no one by Duke Mù's side,
then they could not secure their own positions.
You plan for the elder,
yet fall short of Zǐsī;
do you reject the elder?
Or does the elder reject you?
4.12 Mencius left Qí.
Yǐn Shì said to someone:
"If he did not realize that the king could not become a Tāng or Wǔ,
then he lacks discernment;
if he did realize it was impossible,
yet still came,
then he was seeking emolument."
Traveling a thousand li to see the king,
yet departing without meeting him,
lingering for three nights before leaving Zhòu—
why such delay?
A scholar would be displeased by this."
Gāo Zǐ reported this.
He said:
"How could Yǐn Shì understand me?
Traveling a thousand lǐ to see the king
was what I desired;
not meeting him, I therefore left—
how could that be what I desired?
I had no alternative.
After staying three nights before leaving Zhòu,
in my heart I still thought it was too hasty.
The king may perhaps change!
If the king does change,
then he will certainly recall me.
When I left Zhòu,
and the king did not send anyone to pursue me,
I then felt a vast and determined will to return home.
Although I am so,
how could I abandon the king!
The king is capable of doing good;
if the king were to employ me,
then not only would the people of Qí be at peace,
but all the people under heaven would be at peace.
May the king perhaps change his ways!
This I daily hope for!
How could I be like those petty men?
If one remonstrates with his sovereign and it is not accepted,
then he becomes angry,
with resentment showing on his face,
and upon leaving, exhausts his strength for the day before stopping to rest?"
Yǐn Shì heard this,
and said:
"I am truly a petty man."
4.13 Mencius left Qí,
and Chōng Yú asked him along the way:
"You seem to have an unhappy expression, Master.
The other day I heard from you, Master:
'A noble person does not complain against Heaven,
nor does he blame others.'"
He said:
"That was one time,
and this is another.
Every five hundred years a true king should arise,
and in between there should be men famous in their generation.
From the Zhou dynasty down to the present,
more than seven hundred years have passed.
Judging from the number of years,
it is indeed more than time."
Heaven does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world;
if it did wish to bring peace and order to the world,
in the present time,
who is there besides me to do it?
Why should I be unhappy?"
4.14 Mencius left Qí and resided in Xiū.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Is it the way of antiquity to hold office without accepting an official salary?"
Mencius replied,
"No, it is not.
In Chóng,
I had the opportunity to meet the king,
but upon withdrawing, I felt the desire to leave,
not wishing to change my mind,
so I did not accept the offer.
Subsequently, there came military orders,
making it impossible to request departure.
To remain long in Qí
was not my intention.
5.1 When Téng Wéngōng was crown prince,
he was going to Chǔ,
and passing through Sòng, he visited Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ expounded on the innate goodness of human nature,
and in his speech always referred to Yáo and Shùn.
When the crown prince returned from Chǔ,
he visited Mèngzǐ again.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Does the heir apparent doubt my words?
The Way is one and that is all.
Chéng Jiàn said to Duke Jìng of Qí:
"He is a man,
I am a man too;
why should I fear him?"
Yán Yuān said:
"What kind of man was Shùn?
What kind of man am I?
He who strives will be like him."
Gōngmíng Yí said:
"King Wén was my teacher;
how could the Duke of Zhōu deceive me?"
Now Téng, if we take its long parts to make up for its short ones,
will be nearly fifty lǐ square,
and can still be made into a good state.
The Book of Documents says:
"If medicine does not cause dizziness,
the disease will not be cured."
5.2 When Duke Dìng of Téng passed away,
the heir apparent said to Rǎn Yǒu:
"Previously, Mèngzǐ once spoke with me in Sòng,
and it has remained unforgettable in my heart.
Now unfortunately, we have encountered this great misfortune.
I wish to send you to inquire of Mèngzǐ,
and then proceed with the affairs."
Rán Yǒu went to Zōu
and asked Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is this not excellent!
In mourning for one's parents, one should indeed exert oneself to the utmost."
Zēngzǐ said:
'In life,
serve them according to ritual;
in death,
