bury them according to ritual,
and sacrifice to them according to ritual—
this may be called filial piety.'
The rituals of the feudal lords,
I have not studied them;
nevertheless,
I have heard about them.
The three-year mourning,
the coarse mourning garments,
the eating of congee,
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
the three dynasties all shared this practice.
Rǎnyǒu returned with the message,
and it was decided to observe the three-year mourning.
The paternal and maternal uncles and all the officers did not wish it to be so,
and therefore they said:
"Among our ancestral state of Lǔ, none of the former princes observed this practice;
neither did any of our former princes observe it.
As for you to turn to it in your own person
is not proper.
Moreover, the Record says:
'In mourning and sacrifices, follow the ancestors.'
It says:
'I have received this tradition.'
Telling Rán Yǒu, he said:
"In the past, I never studied or inquired,
but delighted in galloping horses and testing swords.
Now, my elders and the hundred officials do not find me sufficient,
and I fear I cannot fully perform the great matter.
You, go ask Mèngzǐ for me!"
Rán Yǒu again went to Zōu
to ask Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yes;
this cannot be sought from others.
Kǒngzǐ yuē:
"Jūn hōng,
tīng yú zhǒngzǎi,
chuò zhōu,
miàn shēnmò,
jíwèi ér kū,
bǎiguān yǒusī
mò gǎn bù āi,
xiān zhī yě."
When those above have preferences,
those below are sure to follow them more excessively.
The virtue of the superior man
is like the wind;
the virtue of the inferior man
is like the grass.
When the wind blows over the grass,
it is sure to bend. This depends on the ruler.
Rán Yǒu returned with his report.
The crown prince said:
"Indeed;
this truly depends on me."
Residing in the mourning hut for five months,
there were no orders or prohibitions issued.
All officials and clan members
found it acceptable,
and said it showed understanding.
When it came to the burial,
people from all directions came to observe it.
The grief in their countenances,
the sorrow in their weeping,
greatly pleased the mourners.
5.3 Téng Wéngōng asked about governing a state.
Mèngzǐ said:
"The people's affairs cannot be delayed."
The Book of Songs says:
'By day you gather thatch,
by night you twist ropes;
hurry to mend your roofs,
soon you will sow all grains.'
It is a rule for the people,
that those who have constant means of livelihood have constant hearts,
while those who lack constant means of livelihood lack constant hearts.
If they lack constant hearts,
they become dissipated and depraved,
and there is nothing they will not do.
When they thus fall into crime,
to follow them up and punish them
is to entrap the people.
How can a benevolent person in authority
be capable of entrapping the people?
Therefore, a wise ruler must be respectful, frugal, and courteous to his subordinates,
and take from the people according to regulations.
Yánghǔ said:
'To be wealthy is to be without benevolence;
to be benevolent is to be without wealth.'
The Xià dynasty allotted fifty mǔ and collected tribute,
the Yīn dynasty allotted seventy mǔ and used the zhù system,
the Zhōu dynasty allotted one hundred mǔ and used the chè system,
but in reality, all took one-tenth.
Chè is
to take away;
zhù is
to borrow.
Lóngzǐ said:
'In governing the land, nothing is better than the zhù system,
and nothing is worse than the gòng system.'
The gòng system
averages the harvest of several years to fix the amount.
In a year of good harvest,
when grains are scattered about in abundance,
taking more is not considered oppressive,
yet they take less;
in a year of bad harvest,
when even manuring the fields is insufficient,
they still insist on taking the full amount.
As parents of the people,
if they cause the people to toil with weary looks,
and throughout the year labor incessantly,
yet unable to nourish their own parents,
and have to borrow to make up the deficiency,
so that the old and young are left to die in ditches and gullies,
where is their role as parents of the people?
Now, the system of hereditary emoluments
has long been practiced in Téng.
The Book of Songs says:
'Rain falls on our public fields,
and then reaches our private ones.'
Only the aid system had public fields.
From this we can see,
even the Zhōu dynasty practiced the aid system.
They established xiáng, xù, and xiàoxiào to educate them.
Xiáng means nurturing,
xiào means teaching,
xù means archery.
In the Xià dynasty, it was called xiào,
in the Yīn dynasty, it was called xù,
in the Zhōu dynasty, it was called xiáng;
the term xué was common to all three dynasties,
all serving to illuminate human relationships.
Human relations are clarified by those above,
and the common people are affectionate below.
When a true king arises,
he will certainly come to adopt these models,
thus making them the teacher of kings.
The Book of Songs says:
'Although Zhou was an ancient state,
its mandate was renewed.'
This refers to King Wén.
If you strive to practice this,
you too shall renew your kingdom!
He sent Bì Zhàn to inquire about the well-field system.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Your ruler is about to practice benevolent governance,
and having chosen you for this mission,
you must exert yourself!"
Now benevolent governance must begin with defining boundaries.
If boundaries are not correctly defined,
the well-field system will not be equal,
and grain salaries will not be fair.
Therefore, tyrants and corrupt officials must neglect their boundaries.
Once the boundaries are properly set,
the distribution of land and regulation of emoluments
can be settled with ease.
"The state of Téng, with its narrow and small territory,
must have gentlemen,
and must have commoners.
Without gentlemen, there would be none to govern the commoners;
without commoners, there would be none to support the gentlemen.
I propose that in the countryside
the system of one-ninth assistance be adopted,
while in the capital
a tax of one-tenth be levied by self-assessment.
Officials below the rank of qīng must have sacrificial fields,
with fifty mǔ for sacrificial fields;
additional men receive twenty-five mǔ.
Neither death nor relocation takes one beyond the township,
where fields within the same well-field system are shared,
coming and going, they befriend each other,
keeping watch and aiding one another,
in sickness and ailment, supporting each other,
thus the common people are affectionate and harmonious.
A square li forms a well-field,
each well-field consists of nine hundred mu,
of which the central portion is the public field.
Eight families each have a private holding of one hundred mu,
and together they cultivate the public field.
When the public work is completed,
then they dare to attend to their private affairs.
This is how the countrymen are distinguished.
This is the general outline;
as for modifying and perfecting it,
that depends on the ruler and you.
5.4 There was one Xǔ Xíng, who advocated the doctrines of Shénnóng.
Coming from Chǔ to Téng,
he went to the gate and informed Duke Wén,
saying,
"People from afar
have heard that you, Prince, are practicing a benevolent government,
Duke Wén gave him a place to stay.
His disciples numbered several tens,
all wearing coarse clothes,
making sandals and weaving mats for a living.
Chén Liáng's disciple Chén Xiàng and his younger brother Xīn
carrying plows on their backs came from Sòng to Téng.
He said:
"I have heard that you practice the government of a sage,
this makes you a sage as well,
and I wish to become a subject of a sage."
Chén Xiàng, upon meeting Xǔ Xíng, was greatly delighted,
and completely abandoned what he had learned to study under him.
Chén Xiàng visited Mèngzǐ,
and conveyed Xǔ Xíng's words, saying:
"The ruler of Téng is indeed a worthy ruler;
however,
he has not yet understood the true Way.
A worthy person works alongside the people to eat,
cooking his own meals while governing.
But now Téng has granaries and treasuries,
which means he exploits the people to support himself.
How can he be considered worthy?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Xǔzǐ bì zhǒng sù ér hòu shí hū?"
Yuē:
"Rán."
"Xǔzǐ bì zhī bù ránhòu yì hū?"
Yuē:
"Fǒu;
Xǔzǐ yì hè."
"Xǔzǐ guàn hū?"
Yuē:
"Guàn."
He asked:
"What do you wear on your head?"
The reply was:
"A plain silk cap."
He asked:
"Did you weave it yourself?"
The reply was:
"No;
I exchanged grain for it."
He said:
"Why does Xǔzǐ not weave himself?"
He replied:
"It would interfere with farming."
He said:
"Does Xǔzǐ use a pot and steamer for cooking,
and iron tools for farming?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Did you make them yourself?"
He replied:
"No;
I exchanged grain for them."
"When exchanging grain for tools and utensils,
this doesn't harm the potters and smiths;
when potters and smiths exchange tools and utensils for grain,
how could this harm the farmers?"
Moreover, why does Master Xǔ not engage in pottery and smithing,
so that he can take everything from his own house and use it?
Why does he busily trade with the various artisans?
Why is Master Xǔ not afraid of trouble?"
The reply was:
"The work of the various artisans
certainly cannot be done while farming."
"Then, can governing the world alone be done while tilling the fields?
There are the affairs of the great men,
and there are the affairs of the small men.
Moreover, for a single person's needs,
the products of all the various artisans must be available.
If one must make everything oneself before using it,
this would lead the whole world onto a path of hardship."
Therefore it is said:
'Some labor with their minds,
and some labor with their strength.
Those who labor with their minds govern others;
those who labor with their strength are governed by others.
Those who are governed by others support them;
those who govern others are supported by them.
This is a principle universally recognized.'
"In the time of Yáo,
the world was not yet settled,
floods flowed unchecked,
spreading across the land,
plants grew thick and lush,
birds and beasts multiplied,
the five grains did not ripen,
birds and beasts oppressed humans,
paths of animal hooves and bird tracks
crisscrossed the Middle Kingdom."
Yáo alone was troubled by this,
so he raised Shùn to spread governance.
Shùn appointed Yì to oversee fire,
and Yì set the mountains and marshes ablaze with fierce fires,
causing birds and beasts to flee and hide.
Yǔ dredged the nine rivers,
channeled the Jì and Tà rivers to flow into the sea,
cleared the Rǔ and Hàn rivers,
and redirected the Huái and Sì rivers to empty into the Yangtze,
after which the central lands could be cultivated for food.
At that time,
Yǔ spent eight years away from home,
passing by his own door three times without entering;
even if he had wished to farm,
could he have done so?
"Hòujì taught the people to sow and reap,
cultivating the five grains;
when the five grains ripened, the people were nourished."
It is a principle of human nature that
with ample food, warm clothing,
and comfortable living without education,
one becomes little different from beasts.
The sages were concerned about this,
so they appointed Xiè as Minister of Education,
to teach human relationships:
between father and son, there should be affection;
between ruler and subject, there should be righteousness;
between husband and wife, there should be distinction;
between elder and younger, there should be order;
between friends, there should be trust.
Fàng Xūn said:
'Labor for them and attract them,
correct them and straighten them,
assist them and protect them,
so that they may find their own way,
and then further uplift and morally cultivate them.'
Such is the sage's concern for the people—
how could he have leisure for farming?
"Yáo considered his failure to obtain Shùn as his own anxiety;
Shùn considered his failure to obtain Yǔ and Gāoyáo as his own anxiety.
Now, he who considers the poor management of his hundred acres as his own anxiety
is a farmer.
To share wealth with others is called benevolence;
to teach others what is good is called loyalty;
to find the right person for the world is called true virtue.
Therefore, to give the world to someone is easy,
but to find the right person for the world is difficult."
Confucius said:
"How great was
Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is truly great,
and only Yáo modeled himself upon it.
So boundless was he that the people could find no name for him!
How perfect was Shùn as a ruler!
So majestic was he that he possessed the empire but did not interfere with it!"
Yáo and Shùn governed the world,
how could they have had no use for their minds?
They simply did not apply them to tilling the land.
"I have heard of using the Xià ways to transform the barbarians,
but never of being transformed by the barbarians."
Chén Liáng
was a native of Chǔ,
who admired the ways of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
and went north to study in the Central States.
Among the northern scholars,
none could surpass him.
He was what is called an outstanding scholar.
You brothers
served him for decades,
yet when your master died, you turned against him!
In the past, after Confucius passed away,
beyond the three-year mourning period,
his disciples prepared their baggage to return home.
They entered and bowed to Zǐgòng,
faced each other and wept,
all losing their voices,
and only then returned home.
Zǐgòng went back,
built a hut by the burial ground,
lived alone for three years,
and only then returned home.
One day, Zǐxià, Zǐzhāng, and Zǐyóu,
because Yǒuruò resembled the sage,
wished to serve him as they had served Confucius,
and pressed Zǐzēng to do so.
Zǐzēng said:
'It cannot be;
the Jiāng and Hàn rivers washed him,
the autumn sun scorched him,
so brilliantly white that nothing can surpass it.'
Now, a man with the jabbering tongue of the southern barbarians,
who rejects the ways of the ancient kings,
you, forsaking your teacher, study from him;
this is indeed different from Zēngzǐ.
I have heard of leaving the dark valley
to move up to the tall trees,
but never of descending from the tall trees into the dark valley.
The "Odes of Lǔ" says:
"The Róng and Dí tribes were repelled,
the Jīng and Shū tribes were punished."
The Duke of Zhōu was then repelling them,
yet you study this,
which shows you are not good at adapting to change."
"If we follow Master Xǔ's way,
then market prices will be uniform,
and there will be no deceit in the state;
even if a child of five chi goes to the market,
no one will deceive them."
If the length of cloth and silk is the same,
then their prices are similar;
if the weight of hemp thread and silk floss is the same,
then their prices are similar;
if the quantity of the five grains is the same,
then their prices are similar;
if the size of shoes is the same,
then their prices are similar.
He said:
"Things are inherently unequal,
this is their natural condition;
some differ by double or fivefold,
some by ten or hundredfold,
some by thousand or ten-thousandfold.
You equate and uniform them,
this would throw the world into chaos.
If large shoes and small shoes are sold at the same price,
who would make the large ones?
Following Xǔ Xíng's way of thinking,
people would lead one another to practice deceit.
How can this bring order to the state?"
5.5 Mòzhe Yí Zhī
sought an interview with Mèngzǐ through Xú Pì.
Mèngzǐ said:
"I was indeed willing to see him,
but now I am still ill.
When I recover,
I will go to see him.
Master Yí need not come!"
Another day, he again sought to see Mencius.
Mencius said:
"Now I can see him.
If one is not straightforward, the Way will not appear;
I shall be straightforward with him.
I have heard that Master Yí is a Mohist,
and the Mohists in managing funerals
consider frugality as their principle;
Yízǐ sought to change the world with his ideas,
believing nothing else was worthy of honor;
yet when he buried his parents with lavish rites,
he served them with what he deemed base."
Xúzǐ reported this to Yízǐ.
Yí Zǐ yuē:
"The Way of the Confucians
in ancient times
said 'like protecting an infant.'
What does this statement mean?
I take it to mean that love has no distinctions of degree,
yet its application begins with one's kin."
Xúzǐ told Mèngzǐ about it.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Does Yízǐ truly believe
that a person's affection for their elder brother's child
is like their affection for a neighbor's newborn infant?
There is a reason for this.
When an infant crawls and is about to fall into a well,
it is not the infant's fault.
Now, in the production of things, Heaven
appoints one root for them,
but Yí Zǐ would have two roots.
Anciently, there were some who did not inter their parents.
When their parents died,
they took them and threw them into a ditch.
Another day passing by it,
foxes had eaten it,
flies and gnats were swarming upon it.
His forehead broke into a sweat,
and he looked away, unable to bear the sight.
This sweat was
not shed for others to see,
but an expression from his heart reaching his face.
He returned, took a basket and spade, and covered the body.
The covering it
was certainly right,
and thus when a filial son or benevolent man covers his parent,
it is undoubtedly in accordance with the proper way."
Xúzǐ informed Yízǐ of this.
Yízǐ was thoughtful for a short time and then said,
"He has instructed me."
6.1 Chéndài said:
"Not seeing the feudal lords
seems rather petty;
now if you were to see them once,
on a grand scale you could make them true kings,
on a small scale you could make them hegemons.
Moreover, the Record says:
'Bend a foot to straighten eight,'
this seems something that could be done."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Xī Qí Jǐnggōng tián,
zhāo yú rén yǐ jīng,
bù zhì,
jiāng shā zhī.
'Zhìshì bù wàng zài gōuhè,
yǒngshì bù wàng sàng qí yuán.
What did Confucius find commendable in that?
He found commendable the refusal to go unless summoned in the proper way.
If one were to go without waiting for a proper summons,
what would be the point?
Moreover, the idea of bending one foot to straighten eight feet
is spoken of in terms of advantage.
If it is for the sake of advantage,
then would it also be acceptable to bend eight feet to straighten one foot
if that were advantageous?
Formerly, Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào
sent Wáng Liáng to drive for his favorite Xī,
but by the end of the day, they had not captured a single bird.
The favorite Xī reported back, saying:
"He is the poorest workman in the world."
Someone told Wáng Liáng of this.
Liáng said:
"I beg to try again."
Only after being pressed did he consent,
and in one morning they captured ten birds.
Bì Xī reported back, saying:
'He is the finest craftsman in the world.'
Jiǎnzǐ said:
'I will have him take charge of your chariot driving.'
He told this to Wáng Liáng.
Liáng was unwilling,
saying:
'When I drive according to the rules
of proper charioteering,
I do not catch a single bird all day;
but when I drive improperly,
I catch ten in one morning.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Without breaking his pace,
he releases his arrow as if piercing through.'
I am unaccustomed to sharing a chariot with petty men,
I beg to decline."
A charioteer would be ashamed to be compared with an archer;
even if by comparison he could capture game
piled up like hills and mounds,
he would not do it.
If one bends the Way to follow others,
what is the point?
Moreover, you are mistaken:
one who has twisted oneself
has never been able to straighten others."
6.2 Jǐng Chūn said:
"Are not Gōngsūn Yǎn and Zhāng Yí
truly great men?
When they are angry, the feudal lords tremble;
when they are at peace, the world is quelled."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"How can this be considered a great man?
Have you not studied the rites?
When a young man is capped,
his father gives him instructions;
when a young woman is married,
her mother gives her instructions,
As she escorted her to the gate,
she admonished her, saying:
"When you go to your husband's home,
you must be respectful and cautious,
do not disobey your husband!"
To regard compliance as the correct standard
is the way of a wife and concubine.
Dwell in the broadest dwelling of the world,
stand in the most correct position of the world,
walk the great path of the world;
when achieving one's aspirations, share them with the people;
when not achieving them,
walk one's path alone.
Wealth and honor cannot corrupt,
poverty and lowliness cannot shift,
power and force cannot bend—
this is what is called a great man."
6.3 Zhōu Xiāo asked:
"Did the gentlemen of antiquity take office?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"They did."
The Record states:
"When Confucius was without a sovereign to serve for three months,
he appeared anxious and uneasy,
and when leaving a state's borders, he always carried with him gifts of introduction."
Gōngmíng Yí said:
"The ancients,
if three months passed without serving a ruler,
would go to offer condolences."
"Going to offer condolences after three months without serving a ruler—
isn't that too hasty?"
He replied:
"When a scholar loses his official position,
it is like a feudal lord losing his state."
The Book of Rites says:
'The feudal lords plow the fields
to supply the sacrificial grains;
their wives raise silkworms and reel silk,
to make the ritual garments.
If the sacrificial animals are not perfect,
the grains are not pure,
or the garments are not complete,
they dare not perform the sacrifices.
Even officials who have no land
likewise do not perform sacrifices.'
If the sacrificial animals, vessels, and garments are not complete,
one dare not perform the sacrifice;
then one dare not feast,
is that not also sufficient for condolence?
"When leaving one's state, one must carry presents for interview.
Why is that?"
The reply was,
"An officer's taking office
is like a farmer's plowing.
Would a farmer, because he leaves his state,
discard his plow and hoe?"
He said:
"Jìn is also a state where one can take office,
yet I have never heard of seeking office with such urgency.
If seeking office is so urgent,
why is it that the noble man finds it difficult to take office?
What is the reason?"
It is said:
"When a boy is born, people wish him to have a wife;
when a girl is born, people wish her to have a husband.
This feeling is shared by all parents.
All people have this sentiment.
If, without waiting for the command of parents
and the words of a matchmaker,
they bore holes in the wall to peep at each other,
or leap over the wall to follow each other,
then parents and fellow countrymen all despise them."
The ancients never did not wish to take office,
but they also hated doing so improperly.
To go forward improperly
is like boring holes and creeping through crevices.
6.4 Péng Gèng asked, saying,
"With several tens of carriages following behind,
and several hundred attendants accompanying you,
is it not excessive to go eating from one feudal lord to another?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Fēi qí dào,
zé yī dān shí bùkě shòu yú rén;
rú qí dào,
zé Shùn shòu Yáo zhī tiānxià
bù yǐwéi tài,
zǐ yǐwéi tài hū?"
He said:
"No;
for a scholar to eat without working,
is not permissible."
He said:
"If you do not exchange products and services,
using surplus to make up for deficiency,
then farmers will have surplus grain,
and weavers will have surplus cloth;
if you do exchange them,
then carpenters, craftsmen, and carriage makers can all obtain food from you."
Here is a man who,
at home is filial,
abroad is respectful to elders,
guards the Way of the former kings,
awaiting later learners,
yet cannot get sustenance from you;
why do you honor carpenters and carriage-makers
but slight those who practice benevolence and righteousness?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Carpenters and carriage-makers
have the intention of seeking food;
does a gentleman in practicing the Way
also have the intention of seeking food?"
He said:
"Why do you base it on their motives?
If they have merit for you,
you may feed them and so feed them.
Moreover, do you feed based on motives?
Or do you feed based on merit?"
He replied:
"I feed based on motives."
He said:
"Suppose there is a man here
who breaks tiles and defaces walls,
his intention being to seek food.
Would you feed him?"
The reply was:
"No."
He then said:
"Then you do not feed people based on their intentions,
but rather based on their accomplishments."
6.5 Wàn Zhāng asked:
"Sòng is
a small state;
now it is about to implement benevolent governance,
but Qí and Chǔ dislike this and attack it.
What should be done?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Tāng jū Bó,
yǔ Gě wéi lín,
Gě Bó fàng ér bú sì.
Tāng shǐ rén wèn zhī yuē:
'Hé wéi bú sì?'
Yuē:
'Wú yǐ gōng xīshēng yě.'"
Tāng sent people to present him with cattle and sheep.
Gé Bó consumed them,
but still did not use them for sacrifices.
Tāng again sent someone to ask him,
"Why do you not perform sacrifices?"
He replied,
"I have nothing to provide the sacrificial offerings."
Tāng sent the people of Bó to go and plow for them,
with the old and weak supplying food.
The Earl of Gé led his people
to intercept those who had wine, food, millet, or rice,
seizing it from them.
Those who would not hand it over
were killed.
There was a child bringing millet and meat as provisions;
he was killed and it was taken from him.
The Book of History says:
"Gé Bó made an enemy of those who brought provisions."
This refers to this case.
Because he killed this child, Tāng launched a punitive expedition against him,
and all within the four seas said:
"It was not to enrich the world,
but to avenge the common man and woman."
"Tāng began his punitive expeditions
starting with Gé."
He fought eleven campaigns and was invincible under heaven.
When he marched east,
the western barbarians complained;
when he marched south,
the northern barbarians complained,
saying:
"Why does he put us last?"
The people looked up to him,
as in a great drought they look up for rain.
Those who were going to the markets did not stop;
those who were weeding made no change in their operations.
While he punished their rulers,
he consoled the people.
His coming was like a timely fall of rain:
and the people were delighted.
The Book of Documents says:
"We wait for our sovereign;
when the sovereign comes, may there be no more punishments!"
"Those who refused to acknowledge their allegiance,
we marched east to chastise,
bringing peace to their men and women.
They presented us with their dark and yellow silks,
requesting to be introduced to our King Zhōu to receive his favor,
and pledged their allegiance to the great state of Zhōu."
Their gentlemen filled their baskets with dark and yellow silks
to welcome their gentlemen,
and their common people brought baskets of food and pots of congee
to welcome their common people;
they saved the people from fire and water,
only removing the oppressors.
The Great Declaration says:
'Our military might is to be displayed,
invading their territories,
then seizing their cruel ones,
killing and attacking to expand our influence,
bringing glory to Tāng.'
It is only that he does not practice benevolent government.
If he were to practice benevolent government,
all within the four seas would lift up their heads
and look to him,
wishing to have him as their sovereign.
Though Qi and Chu are large,
what would there be to fear from them?"
6.6 Mencius said to Dài Bùshèng:
"Do you wish for your king to become good?
Let me tell you clearly.
Suppose there is a high official of Chǔ here,
who wishes his son to speak the language of Qí.
Should he have a man of Qí teach him,
or a man of Chǔ teach him?"
He replied:
"Have a man of Qí teach him."
He said:
"If one man from Qí teaches him,
while a crowd of men from Chǔ clamor around him,
even if you beat him daily to make him speak the language of Qí,
it will be impossible to achieve.
But if you place him for several years in the neighborhood of Zhuāng and Yuè,
even if you beat him daily to make him speak the language of Chǔ,
it will likewise be impossible to achieve."
Mèngzǐ said of Xuē Jūzhōu,
"He is a good man."
If he were made to live in the king's palace,
and all those in the king's palace,
whether old or young, lowly or noble, were like Xuē Jūzhōu,
with whom would the king do what is not good?
If all those in the king's palace,
whether old or young, lowly or noble, were not like Xuē Jūzhōu,
with whom would the king do what is good?
What can one Xuē Jūzhōu alone
do for the King of Sòng?"
6.7 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying,
"What is the principle
of not visiting the feudal lords?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"In ancient times, unless one was in the service of a prince, one did not go to see him.
Duàngānmù leaped over a wall to avoid the prince,
and Xiè Liǔ shut his door and would not admit him.
These, however, are extremes.
When a prince is urgent,
then it is permissible to see him."
Yánghuò wished to see Confucius
but disliked being discourteous.
When a senior official bestows a gift upon a scholar,
if the scholar cannot receive it at his home,
he should go to the official's gate to pay his respects.
Yánghuò spied on when Confucius was away from home
and sent him a steamed piglet as a gift.
Confucius in turn spied on when Yánghuò was away
and went to pay his respects.
At that time,
Yánghuò took the lead,
how could one avoid meeting him?
Zēngzǐ said:
'Raising the shoulders and forcing a flattering smile,
is more exhausting than laboring in the summer fields.'
Zǐlù said:
'Speaking without being in agreement,
observing his countenance
flushed with shame,
is something I, Yóu, cannot understand.'
From this we can see,
the cultivation of the noble person,
can be known indeed.
6.8 Dài Yíngzhī said:
"To collect one tenth as tax,
and abolish the levies on goods at passes and markets—
this year we are still unable to do it,
but I would like to lighten the taxes,
and wait until next year,
then abolish them completely.
What do you think?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Jīn yǒu rén rì rǎng qí lín zhī jī zhě,
huò gào zhī yuē:
'Shì fēi jūnzǐ zhī dào.'
Yuē:
'Qǐng sǔn zhī,
yuè rǎng yī jī,
yǐ dài láinián
ránhòu yǐ.'
Rú zhī qí fēi yì,
sī sù yǐ yǐ,
hé dài láinián?"
6.9 Gōngdūzǐ said:
"People outside all say that you, Master, are fond of disputation.
May I ask why this is?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"How could I be fond of disputation?
I am compelled to do so."
The world has existed for a long time,
alternating between order and chaos.
In the time of Yáo,
the waters flowed backward,
overflowing across the Central Kingdom.
Snakes and dragons dwelt in it,
and the people had nowhere to settle;
those in lowlands built nests,
those in highlands made cave dwellings.
The Book of History says:
'The deluge warns us.'
The deluge means a great flood.
They appointed Yǔ to control it.
Yǔ dug channels and conducted the waters to the sea,
drove the snakes and dragons into the marshes;
the waters flowed through the land,
as seen in the Jiāng, Huái, Hé, and Hàn rivers.
When dangers and obstacles were removed,
and the harm from birds and beasts to people disappeared,
then people could live on the level ground.
"After Yáo and Shùn passed away,
the Way of the sages declined,
tyrants arose one after another,
they destroyed houses to create ponds and lakes,
leaving the people with no place to rest;
they abandoned farmland to make parks and hunting grounds,
depriving the people of clothing and food.
Heretical doctrines and violent deeds emerged again,
parks, ponds, lakes, and marshes became numerous
and birds and beasts flocked there.
By the time of King Zhòu himself,
the world fell into great chaos again.
The Duke of Zhōu assisted King Wǔ
in executing Zhòu, and they campaigned against Yǎn
for three years to punish its ruler.
They pursued Fēilián to a coastal corner and put him to death,
eliminating fifty states.
They drove away tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants, banishing them far off,
and the world was greatly pleased.
The Book of Documents says:
'How illustrious were the plans of King Wén!
How glorious were the achievements of King Wǔ!
They assisted and enlightened us, their descendants,
so that all are correct and without defect.'
"When the world fell into decay and the Way declined,
perverse doctrines and violent deeds arose.
There were instances of ministers assassinating their rulers,
and of sons murdering their fathers.
Kǒngzǐ was alarmed,
and composed the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Spring and Autumn Annals concern the affairs of the Son of Heaven;
therefore Kǒngzǐ said:
"Those who understand me
will do so because of the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Those who condemn me
will do so because of the Spring and Autumn Annals!"
When sage kings ceased to arise,
the feudal lords acted wantonly,
and unemployed scholars indulged in irresponsible discussions,
The words of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí fill the world.
The words of the world
either go to Yáng, or go to Mò.
The Yáng school advocates egoism,
which is to deny the sovereign;
the Mò school advocates universal love,
which is to deny the father.
To deny father and sovereign
is to be like birds and beasts.
Gōngmíng Yí said:
"In the kitchen there is fat meat,
in the stables there are fat horses;
yet the people have hungry looks,
and in the countryside there are corpses of the starved;
this is leading beasts to devour men."
If the doctrines of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí are not extinguished,
the doctrines of Confucius will not be made manifest.
These perverse teachings mislead the people,
and block up the path of benevolence and righteousness.
When benevolence and righteousness are blocked up,
it leads to beasts preying on humans,
and humans will devour one another.
I am fearful of this,
so I defend the Way of the former sages,
oppose the doctrines of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí, and banish excessive statements,
ensuring that perverse doctrines cannot arise.
If they arise in one's mind,
they harm one's actions;
if they arise in one's actions,
they harm governance.
Even if a sage were to rise again,
he would not change my words.
"In ancient times, Yǔ controlled the floods
and the world was pacified,
the Duke of Zhōu subdued the barbarian tribes,
drove away fierce beasts
and the common people were tranquil,
Confucius completed the 'Spring and Autumn Annals'
and rebellious ministers and villainous sons were afraid."
The Book of Songs says:
"The Róng and Dí tribes are to be resisted,
the Jīng and Shū states are to be punished,
then none dare to oppose us."
Those who acknowledge neither father nor sovereign
are what the Duke of Zhōu would resist.
I also wish to rectify people's hearts,
put an end to perverse doctrines,
oppose deviant conduct,
and banish licentious words,
so as to carry on the legacy of the three sages.
How could I be fond of argument?
It is simply that I have no alternative.
Those who are able to refute the doctrines of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí
are disciples of the sages."
6.10 Kuāng Zhāng said:
"Is Chén Zhòngzǐ not truly a man of integrity?
He lived in Wòlíng,
and went without food for three days,
until his ears could hear nothing,
and his eyes could see nothing.
There was a plum tree by a well,
with more than half of its fruits eaten by grubs.
He crawled over, intending to eat them;
after swallowing three times,
his ears could then hear, and his eyes could see."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Among the scholars of the state of Qí,
I must regard Zhòngzǐ as the greatest.
Nevertheless,
how can Zhòngzǐ be considered incorruptible?
To fulfill Zhòngzǐ's principles of conduct,
one would have to become an earthworm to be acceptable.
Now the earthworm eats the dry soil above,
and drinks from the yellow springs below."
The house in which Zhòngzǐ dwells,
was it built by a Bó Yí,
or was it built by a Dào Zhí?
The grain he eats,
was it planted by a Bó Yí,
or was it planted by a Dào Zhí?
This cannot be known."
He said:
"What harm is there in that?
He himself weaves sandals and his wife spins hemp,
and they exchange these for it."
Another said:
"Zhòngzǐ
belongs to a noble family of Qí;
his elder brother Dài
receives a salary of ten thousand zhōng from Gé;
He considered his elder brother's emolument to be an unrighteous emolument
and therefore would not eat of it,
and he considered his elder brother's residence to be an unrighteous residence
and therefore would not dwell in it.
Avoiding his elder brother and leaving his mother,
he lived in Yùlíng.
One day when he returned home,
someone had presented his elder brother with a live goose.
He knitted his brows and said:
"What is the use of this cackling creature?"
On another day, his mother killed the goose
and gave it to him to eat.
Just then his elder brother came in from outside
and said:
"This is the meat of that cackling creature."
He went out and vomited it up.
He would not eat food provided by his mother,
but he would eat food provided by his wife.
He would not live in his brother's house,
but he lived in Wūlíng.
Was this extending
his principle to its fullest extent?
As for a man like Zhòngzǐ,
he would have to become an earthworm to fully carry out his principles."
7.1 Mèngzǐ said:
"With the eyesight of Lílóu
and the skill of Gōngshūzǐ,
without compasses and squares,
one cannot form squares and circles;
with the hearing of Shī Kuàng,
without the six pitch-pipes,
one cannot correctly adjust the five notes;
with the way of Yáo and Shùn,
without benevolent governance,
one cannot bring peace and order to the world."
Now there are those with benevolent hearts and reputations
yet the people do not receive their blessings,
who cannot be models for later generations—
this is because they do not practice the Way of the former kings.
Therefore it is said:
'Goodness alone is insufficient for governance,
laws alone cannot implement themselves.'
The Book of Songs says,
"Do not err, do not forget,
but follow the ancient statutes."
Those who err
while following the laws of the former kings have never existed.
The sage, having exhausted the power of his eyes,
proceeded to apply the compass, square, level, and line,
to produce squares, circles, levels, and straight lines,
which are inexhaustible in their use;
having exhausted the power of his ears,
he proceeded to apply the six pitch-pipes to rectify the five notes,
which are inexhaustible in their use;
having exhausted the power of his mind,
he proceeded to govern with a government that cannot bear to see suffering,
and his benevolence overspread the kingdom.
Therefore it is said:
To build high, one must rely on hills and mounds;
to dig deep, one must rely on rivers and marshes;
to govern
without relying on the ways of the former kings,
can it be called wise?
Thus, only the benevolent should hold high positions.
If the unbenevolent hold high positions,
this is to spread their evil among the multitude.
When those above lack moral principles to guide them,
and those below have no laws to abide by,
when the court does not believe in the Way,
and artisans do not trust in standards,
when gentlemen violate righteousness,
and commoners break the laws,
the survival of the state
is merely a matter of luck.
Therefore it is said:
When the city walls are not complete,
and the weapons and armor are not abundant,
these are not the calamities of a state.
When the fields and wilds are not opened up,
and goods and wealth are not accumulated,
these are not the harms of a state.
If those above have no propriety,
and those below have no learning,
then rebellious people will arise,
and the state's downfall is not far off.
The Book of Songs says:
'When Heaven is about to send down calamity,
do not be so garrulous.'
Garrulousness
is like being frivolous.
Serving one's ruler without righteousness,
acting without propriety in advancing or retiring,
and speaking in ways that run counter to the Way of the ancient kings—
this is what is meant by being frivolous.
Therefore it is said:
To demand what is difficult from one's ruler is called respect,
to set forth what is good and repress his perversities is called reverence,
to say that one's ruler cannot do what is good is called robbery.
7.2 Mèngzǐ said:
"Compass and square
are the ultimate standards for squares and circles;
the sage
is the ultimate standard for human relationships.
If one wishes to be a ruler,
let them fulfill the Way of a ruler;
if one wishes to be a minister,
let them fulfill the Way of a minister.
Both simply need to emulate Yáo and Shùn
and that is all.
He who does not serve his sovereign as Shùn served Yáo,
does not respect his sovereign;
he who does not rule his people as Yáo ruled them,
injures his people.
Confucius said,
"There are two ways:
that of benevolence and that of non-benevolence, and that is all."
When a ruler oppresses his people excessively,
he will be assassinated and his state perish;
if not excessively,
he will be endangered and his state weakened.
He will be named
"Yōu" or "Lì",
and even if he has filial sons and affectionate grandsons,
they cannot change this for a hundred generations.
The Book of Songs says:
"The mirror of the Yin is not far off,
it is found in the age of the Xia sovereign."
This expresses the meaning.
7.3 Mencius said:
"The Three Dynasties obtained the world through benevolence,
and lost the world through lack of benevolence.
The same principle applies to the rise and fall, survival and demise of states.
If the Son of Heaven is not benevolent,
he cannot preserve the empire;
if the feudal lords are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their states;
if the ministers and great officers are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their ancestral temples;
if the scholars and common people are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their own bodies.
Now to dislike death and ruin
yet to delight in unrighteousness
is like disliking drunkenness
yet forcing oneself to drink.
7.4 Mencius said:
"When you love others and they are not affectionate to you,
reflect on your own benevolence;
when you govern others and they are not orderly,
reflect on your own wisdom;
when you treat others with propriety and they do not respond,
reflect on your own respectfulness."
When one fails to achieve desired outcomes,
one should always reflect and seek the cause within oneself.
When one's own character is upright,
the world will turn to them.
The Book of Songs says:
"Always accord with the Mandate of Heaven,
and seek abundant blessings for yourself."
7.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"People have a constant saying, all saying:
'The world, the state, the family.'
The foundation of the world lies in the state,
the foundation of the state lies in the family,
the foundation of the family lies in the individual."
7.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"Governing is not difficult;
it lies in not offending the great families.
What the great families admire,
the whole state admires;
what the whole state admires,
the whole world admires;
thus abundantly does moral teaching overflow throughout the four seas."
7.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"When the Way prevails in the world,
the less virtuous serve the more virtuous,
the less worthy serve the more worthy;
when the Way does not prevail in the world,
the small serve the great,
the weak serve the strong.
Both these cases
are of Heaven's ordaining.
Those who obey Heaven are preserved;
those who defy Heaven perish.
Duke Jǐng of Qí said:
"Since we can neither give orders,
nor receive them,
we are cut off from the world."
He shed tears and gave his daughter in marriage to Wú.
Now, when a small state imitates a large state
yet feels ashamed to receive its commands,
it is like a disciple feeling ashamed to receive instructions from his master.
If they are ashamed of this,
there is nothing better than to follow King Wén.
By following King Wén,
within five years if it is a large state,
or seven years if it is a small state,
it is sure to hold sway over the empire.
The Book of Songs says:
'The descendants of Shāng,
their number is beyond a hundred thousand.
Since God has commanded,
they become subjects of Zhōu.
They submit to Zhōu,
for the Mandate of Heaven is not constant.
The officers of Yīn are elegant and diligent,
assisting in the ceremonies at the capital.'
Confucius said:
"Humaneness cannot be achieved through numbers. If
a ruler loves humaneness,
he will be invincible in the world."
Now, to desire invincibility in the world
without practicing humaneness
is like grasping something hot without cooling it with water.
The Book of Songs says:
"Who can grasp something hot
and not cool it with water?"
7.8 Mencius said:
"Can one speak with the unvirtuous?
They regard danger as safety and profit from disasters,
delighting in the very things that lead to their downfall.
If one could speak with the unvirtuous
and be heeded,
then how could there be
any ruined states or collapsed families?"
A child was singing:
"When the Cānglàng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat-strings therein;
When the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet therein."
Confucius said:
"My children, listen to this!
When clear, then wash your hat-strings;
When muddy, then wash your feet.
This distinction comes from the water itself."
A person must first insult themselves,
then others will insult them;
a family must first destroy itself,
then others will destroy it;
a state must first attack itself,
then others will attack it.
The "Tai Jia" says:
"When Heaven sends down calamities,
it is still possible to escape them;
when we bring calamities upon ourselves,
it is impossible to survive."
This is what is meant.
7.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"The reason Jié and Zhòu lost the world
was because they lost the people;
the reason they lost the people
was because they lost their hearts."
There is a way to gain the empire:
gain its people, and you gain the empire;
there is a way to gain the people:
gain their hearts, and you gain the people;
there is a way to gain their hearts:
gather for them what they desire,
and do not impose
what they dislike
upon them—that is all.
"The people's turning to benevolence is
like water flowing downward,
or wild beasts fleeing to the wilderness.
Thus, those who drive the fish into the deep waters
are the otters;
those who drive the sparrows into the thickets
are the sparrowhawks;
and those who drive the people to Tāng and Wǔ
were Jié and Zhòu."
If the ruler of the kingdom were fond of benevolence,
all the feudal lords would drive the people to take refuge with him.
Though he wished not to become sovereign,
he could not avoid it.
Those among the present princes who wish to be sovereign
are like those who, having a seven years' sickness, have to seek for the mugwort of three years.
If one does not accumulate virtue,
one will never attain it.
If one does not set one's mind on benevolence,
one will end up in sorrow and disgrace,
leading to downfall and death.
The Book of Songs says,
'How can they be good?
They will only drag each other down to drowning.'
This is what is meant."
7.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"One who is self-destructive
cannot be spoken with;
one who is self-abandoning
cannot be accomplished with.
Speaking contrary to ritual and righteousness
is called self-destruction;
being unable to dwell in benevolence and follow righteousness in oneself
is called self-abandonment."
Benevolence is
the peaceful abode of man,
righteousness is
the correct path of man.
To leave the peaceful abode vacant and not dwell in it,
to abandon the correct path and not follow it,
how lamentable!
7.11 Mencius said:
"The Way lies in what is near,
yet people seek it in what is distant;
duty lies in what is easy,
yet people seek it in what is difficult.
If everyone would love their parents and respect their elders,
the world would be at peace."
7.12 Mencius said:
"If one occupies a subordinate position
and fails to win the confidence of his superior,
he cannot govern the people effectively.
There is a way to win the confidence of one's superior:
if one is not trusted by his friends,
he will not win the confidence of his superior.
There is a way to be trusted by friends.
If one fails to please his parents,
he will not be trusted by friends.
There is a way to please one's parents.
If one, upon self-reflection, is found to be insincere,
he will not please his parents.
There is a way to be sincere in oneself.
If one does not understand what is good,
he will not be sincere in himself.
Therefore, sincerity is
the Way of Heaven;
to reflect on sincerity is
the Way of humanity.
There has never been one
who, having reached the utmost sincerity, failed to influence others;
without sincerity,
there has never been one able to influence others."
7.13 Mencius said:
"Bóyí avoided Zhòu,
dwelling by the shores of the North Sea.
Hearing that King Wén had arisen,
he rose up and said:
'Why not return to him!
I have heard that the Lord of the West knows well how to care for the aged."
Tàigōng avoided Zhòu,
dwelling by the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Hearing of King Wén's rise,
he exclaimed:
"Why not return there!
I have heard that the Earl of the West excels at caring for the elderly."
The two elders
were the most venerable in the world, and they came to him,
which means the fathers of the world came to him.
When the fathers of the world came to him,
where could their sons go?
If any feudal lord were to practice the government of King Wén,
within seven years,
he would surely govern the whole world."
7.14 Mèngzǐ said:
"Qiú, as
the steward of the Jì family,
was unable to reform their virtue,
yet doubled the grain tax compared to former days.
Confucius said:
'Qiú
is no disciple of mine.
My young disciples, you may beat the drum and assail him.'"
From this perspective,
if a ruler fails to practice benevolent governance
yet enriches himself,
he is one rejected by Confucius.
How much more is it to wage war for it?
They fight to seize land,
and the dead fill the plains;
they fight to capture cities,
and the dead fill the cities.
This is what is called leading the land to devour human flesh.
Death is not enough for such a crime.
Thus, those skilled in warfare should suffer the severest punishment;
those who form alliances among the feudal lords come next;
those who open up wastelands
and take charge of the land come next."
7.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"In a person,
nothing is better than the pupils of the eyes.
The pupils cannot conceal one's wickedness.
If the mind is upright,
then the pupils are clear;
if the mind is not upright,
then the pupils are dull.
Listen to his words,
and observe the pupils of his eyes—
how can a man hide his true character?"
7.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"The respectful do not insult others,
the frugal do not seize from others.
A ruler who insults and seizes from others,
fears only that people will not submit to him,
how can he be considered respectful and frugal?
Can respect and frugality be conveyed merely by one's tone of voice and smiling countenance?"
7.17 Chúnyú Kūn said:
"When men and women give and receive things, they should not touch each other's hands -
is this according to propriety?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"It is according to propriety."
Someone asked:
"If your sister-in-law is drowning, should you reach out a hand to save her?"
The reply was:
"If you do not rescue a drowning sister-in-law,
you are a wolf or a jackal.
That men and women should not touch in giving and receiving
is a matter of ritual;
but when a sister-in-law is drowning, to reach out a hand to save her
is a matter of expediency."
He said:
"Now the world is drowning,
yet you, Master, do not rescue it,
why is this?"
He replied:
"When the world is drowning,
one rescues it with the Way;
when a sister-in-law is drowning,
one rescues her with hands.
Do you wish to rescue the world with your hands?"
7.18 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Why does a gentleman
not teach his own son?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Because circumstances make it impracticable.
Teaching must be done with correctness;
when correctness fails,
it is followed by anger.
When anger follows,
then it actually causes injury instead."
"You, sir, teach me with rectitude,
but you yourself do not act with rectitude."
This would mean father and son are wounding each other.
When father and son wound each other, it is terrible indeed.
In ancient times, people exchanged sons to teach them,
so that between father and son there would be no demanding goodness.
To demand goodness leads to estrangement,
and estrangement brings about the greatest misfortune."
7.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"Of services, which is the greatest?
The service of parents is the greatest.
Of preservations, which is the greatest?
The preservation of one's character is the greatest.
I have heard of
one who, not having lost his character,
was able to serve his parents;
I have not heard of one,
who, having lost his character, was able to serve his parents.
Who does not have duties to perform?
But the duties of serving one's parents
are the root of all duties.
Who does not have a life to guard?
But the guarding of one's own person
is the root of all guarding.
Zēngzǐ supported Zēngxī,
and there was always wine and meat;
when about to clear away the leftovers,
he would always ask to whom they should be given;
if asked whether there was any left,
he would always say, "There is."
When Zēng Xī died,
Zēng Yuán supported Zēngzǐ,
there was always wine and meat;
when about to clear away the leftovers,
he did not ask to whom they should be given;
when asked if there was any left,
he said:
"There is none."
It is intended to restore advancement.
This is what is called nourishing the mouth and body.
As for someone like Zēngzǐ,
he can be said to have nourished the will.
Serving one’s parents like Zēngzǐ did
is acceptable."
7.20 Mencius said:
"It is not worthwhile to censure men,
nor to discuss about a government's faults;
only a great man can rectify the evil in the sovereign's heart.
When the sovereign is benevolent, none will fail to be benevolent;
when the sovereign is righteous, none will fail to be righteous;
when the sovereign is correct, none will fail to be correct.
Once the sovereign is rectified, the state will be settled."
7.21 Mèngzǐ said:
"There is unexpected praise,
and there is damaging criticism that seeks perfection."
7.22 Mèngzǐ said:
"When a person speaks too easily,
it is simply because they bear no responsibility."
7.23 Mèngzǐ said:
"The trouble with people
is their fondness for being teachers of others."
7.24 Yuèzhèngzǐ followed Zǐ'áo to Qí.
Yuèzhèngzǐ went to see Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Have you also come to see me?"
He replied:
"Master, why do you say such words?"
He said:
"How many days have you been here?"
The reply was:
"Since yesterday."
He said:
"Since yesterday,
then my saying these words
was indeed appropriate, was it not?"
The reply was:
"My lodging was not yet settled."
He said: "Have you heard that one should
first settle in the lodging
before seeking an audience with the elder?"
He replied:
"I am at fault."
7.25 Mèngzǐ said to Yuèzhèngzǐ:
"You followed Zǐ'áo here,
merely for food and drink.
I did not expect that you, who study the Way of the Ancients,
would do so for food and drink."
7.26 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are three forms of unfilial conduct,
of which having no descendants is the worst.
Shùn married without informing his parents
because he feared having no descendants.
A noble person considers this as if he had informed them."
7.27 Mèngzǐ said:
"The substance of benevolence
is serving one's parents;
the substance of righteousness
is obeying one's elder brothers;
the substance of wisdom
is knowing these two and not departing from them;
The essence of rites
is to regulate and adorn these two things;
the essence of music
is to delight in these two things.
When delight arises,
it cannot be stopped;
being unstoppable,
one unconsciously begins to tap feet
and wave hands in dance.
7.28 Mèngzǐ said:
"When all under heaven greatly rejoiced
and were about to submit to him,
to regard all under heaven rejoicing and submitting to him
as mere grass and weeds—
only Shùn was like this.
If one does not gain the affection of his parents,
he cannot be considered a true man;
if he does not obey his parents,
he cannot be considered a true son.
Shùn fully fulfilled the way of serving his parents,
and Gǔsǒu became content.
Gǔsǒu becoming content
transformed the world;
Gǔsǒu becoming content
established the proper relationship between fathers and sons throughout the world.
This is what is called great filial piety."
8.1 Mencius said:
"Shùn was born in Zhūféng,
moved to Fùxià,
and died in Míngtiáo,
being a man of the Eastern Yi.
King Wén was born in Qízhōu,
and died in Bìyǐng,
being a man of the Western Yi."
The lands are separated by
over a thousand li;
the eras are divided by
over a thousand years.
When achieving their ambitions and governing the Central Kingdom,
they matched like tallying tokens,
whether earlier sages or later sages,
their principles were one and the same."
8.2 When Zǐchǎn governed the state of Zhèng,
he used his own carriage to ferry people across the Zhēn and Wěi rivers.
Mèngzǐ said:
"He was kind but did not understand governance.
In the eleventh month of the year, footbridges are completed;
in the twelfth month, carriage bridges are finished,
and the people do not suffer from crossing rivers.
The gentleman levels his governance,
and it is permissible for his actions to avoid others;
how can he assist everyone?
Therefore, those who govern
and try to please every person
will find the days insufficient.
8.3 Mencius said to King Xuān of Qí:
"If a ruler regards his ministers as his hands and feet,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as their belly and heart;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as a mere fellow countryman;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dirt and weeds,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as a bandit and enemy."
The king said:
"According to the rites,
one should wear mourning for a former ruler.
Under what circumstances should one wear mourning for him?"
It is said:
"When one's remonstrances are practiced and words heeded,
the benefits descend to the people;
if for some reason one must depart,
then he is escorted beyond the borders,
and preparations are made at his destination beforehand;
if after three years of absence he does not return,
only then are his fields and homestead reclaimed.
These are called the three courtesies.
When such is the case,
then mourning garments are worn for him."
Now, as a minister,
when I remonstrate, my advice is not followed;
when I speak, my words are not heeded;
the benefits do not reach the people;
if I have a reason to leave,
the ruler seizes and detains me,
and further obstructs me in the place I go;
on the day of my departure,
he confiscates my fields and homestead.
This is what is called an enemy.
With an enemy, what loyalty is there to be observed?"
8.4 Mèngzǐ said:
"If scholars are killed though they have committed no crime,
then high officials may leave;
if the people are slaughtered though they have committed no crime,
then scholars may move away."
8.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"If the ruler is benevolent, none will be unbenevolent;
if the ruler is righteous, none will be unrighteous."
8.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"The courtesy that is not courtesy,
the righteousness that is not righteousness,
the great man does not practice."
8.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"The virtuous nurture the non-virtuous,
the talented nurture the untalented,
therefore people delight in having virtuous fathers and elder brothers.
If the virtuous were to abandon the non-virtuous,
the talented were to abandon the untalented,
then the distance between the virtuous and the unworthy
would not be measurable by even an inch."
8.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"Only when a person refrains from certain actions
can they then accomplish meaningful deeds."
8.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"When one speaks of others' faults,
what should one do about the future troubles?"
8.10 Mencius said:
"Zhòngní never went to extremes."
8.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"The great person
does not necessarily make their words trustworthy,
nor their actions necessarily resolute,
but only follows where righteousness lies."
8.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"The great person
is one who does not lose the heart of a newborn child."
8.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"Providing for the living
is not sufficient to be considered a great affair;
only sending off the dead can be considered a great affair."
8.14 Mencius said:
"The noble person deeply cultivates it with the Way,
desiring to acquire it through self-attainment.
Having acquired it through self-attainment, one abides in it peacefully;
abiding in it peacefully, one draws from it deeply;
drawing from it deeply, one finds its source wherever one turns,
therefore the noble person desires to acquire it through self-attainment."
8.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"Extensive learning and detailed explanation of it
are meant to lead back to stating its essentials."
8.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who use goodness to subdue others
have never been able to subdue them;
but those who use goodness to nurture others
can then subdue the whole world.
One who rules the world without winning its heartfelt submission
has never existed."
8.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"Words without substance
are inauspicious.
The substance of inauspiciousness
is embodied by those who obstruct the worthy."
8.18 Xú Zǐ said:
"Zhòngní often praised water,
saying:
'Water,
water!'
What did he find in water?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Yuán quán hǔnhǔn,
bù shě zhòuyè,
yíng kē ér hòu jìn,
fàng hū sìhǎi.
Yǒu běn zhě rúshì,
shì zhī qǔ ěr.
If it lacks a foundation,
during the months of July and August
when rain gathers,
all ditches and channels will be filled;
yet their drying up
can be expected to happen quickly.
Thus, when reputation exceeds reality,
a noble person feels ashamed of it."
8.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"That by which humans differ from birds and beasts
is very slight;
common people discard it,
while the gentleman preserves it.
Shùn understood the nature of all things,
discerned human relationships,
and acted from benevolence and righteousness,
rather than performing acts of benevolence and righteousness."
8.20 Mencius said:
"Yǔ detested fine wine and loved good words.
Tāng held fast to the Mean,
and appointed the worthy without fixed rules.
King Wén looked upon the people as if they were wounded,
and gazed upon the Way as if he had not seen it.
King Wǔ did not neglect the near,
nor forget the distant.
The Duke of Zhōu thought of combining
the ways of the three ancient kings,
to practice the four kinds of governance;
when there was anything not matching,
he would look up and ponder it,
continuing through the night into the day;
if fortunately he attained it,
he would sit waiting for the dawn.
8.21 Mèngzǐ said:
"When the traces of the true kings vanished,
the Book of Songs ceased to be made;
after the Book of Songs ceased to be made,
then the Spring and Autumn Annals were composed.
The "Chéng" of Jìn,
the "Táowù" of Chǔ,
and the "Chūnqiū" of Lǔ,
are one and the same:
their events concern Duke Huán of Qí
and Duke Wén of Jìn,
their style is that of historical records.
Confucius said:
"As for their underlying principles, I, Qiū, have privately adopted them."
8.22 Mèngzǐ said:
"The influence of a noble man
lasts for five generations before it is cut off,
the influence of a petty man
lasts for five generations before it is cut off.
I did not have the opportunity to be a direct disciple of Confucius,
I have privately learned from him through others."
8.23 Mèngzǐ said:
"When it is permissible to take,
and also permissible not to take,
taking would injure integrity;
when it is permissible to give,
and also permissible not to give,
giving would injure generosity;
when it is permissible to die,
and also permissible not to die,
dying would injure courage."
8.24 Féng Méng learned archery from Yì,
mastered all of Yì's techniques,
and thought that in all the world only Yì surpassed himself,
whereupon he killed Yì.
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"This too is Yì's guilt."
Gōngmíng Yí yuē:
"It would seem he had no guilt."
Yuē:
"Slight though it may be,
how can he be without guilt?"
The people of Zhèng sent Zǐzhuó Rúzǐ to invade Wèi,
and Wèi sent Yǔgōng Zhīsī to pursue him.
Zǐzhuó Rúzǐ said:
"Today my illness has flared up,
I cannot hold a bow,
I am doomed to die!"
He asked his servant:
"Who is pursuing me?"
His servant replied:
"It is Yǔgōng Zhīsī."
He said:
"I shall live."
His servant said:
"Yǔgōng Zhīsī
is an expert archer of Wèi;
why do you, Master, say you shall live,
what does it mean?"
He replied:
"Yǔgōng Zhīsī learned archery
from Yǐngōng Zhītuō,
and Yǐngōng Zhītuō learned archery from me."
Fū Yǐn Gōng Zhī Tuó,
is an upright man,
so those he befriends must be upright as well.
When Yǔ Gōngzhī Sī arrived,
he said:
"Why is it that you, Master, are not holding your bow?"
The other replied:
"Today my illness has flared up,
so I cannot hold a bow."
He said:
"I learned archery from Yǐn Gōng Zhī Tuō,
and Yǐn Gōng Zhī Tuō learned archery from you, Master.
I cannot bear to use the Way of the Master
to harm the Master in return.
Nevertheless, today's matter
is the affair of my lord,
and I dare not neglect it."
He drew an arrow, tapped it against his chariot wheel,
removed its metal arrowhead,
shot four arrows, and then turned back."
8.25 Mèngzǐ said:
"If Xīzǐ were covered with filth,
people would all cover their noses and pass by her;
even if there is an ugly person,
who fasts, abstains, and bathes,
then they may sacrifice to the Lord on High."
8.26 Mencius said:
"When people in the world discuss human nature,
they merely base it on its original state.
This original state
takes what is beneficial as its foundation.
What we dislike about the wise
is their forcing of interpretations.
If the wise
were like Yǔ directing the flow of water,
then we would have no dislike for wisdom.
Yǔ's management of the waters
was by doing nothing contrary to their nature.
If the wise also did nothing contrary to nature in their actions,
then their wisdom would be great indeed.
Heaven is so high,
the stars are so distant,
yet if we seek out their inherent principles,
the solstices of a thousand years hence
can be determined while sitting.
8.27 When Gōng Xíngzǐ had the funeral of his son,
the Right Minister went to offer condolences.
Upon entering the gate,
some came forward to speak with the Right Minister,
while others went to the Right Minister's position
to speak with him.
Mèngzǐ did not speak with the Minister of War,
who said displeasedly:
"All the gentlemen have spoken with Huān,
yet Mèngzǐ alone does not speak with Huān,
this is slighting Huān."
Mèngzǐ heard of this,
and said:
"According to the rites,
at court one should not cross positions to speak with others,
nor step over steps to bow to one another.
I wished to practice the rites,
yet Zǐ'áo considered me negligent -
is this not strange?"
8.28 Mèngzǐ said:
"What distinguishes the gentleman from others
lies in his heart-mind.
The gentleman preserves benevolence in his heart-mind,
and preserves propriety in his heart-mind.
The benevolent love others,
the courteous respect others.
He who loves others
is constantly loved by them;
he who respects others
is constantly respected by them.
Suppose there is a person here,
who treats me with rudeness and perversity.
Then a noble man will certainly examine himself:
I must have been lacking in benevolence,
I must have failed in courtesy;
how else could such a thing happen to me?
If upon self-examination I find that I have been benevolent,
and upon self-examination I find that I have been courteous,
When such unreasonable treatment is encountered,
a noble person must reflect upon themselves,
thinking, "I must have been unfaithful."
After self-reflection, if they find they have been faithful,
yet the unreasonable treatment persists,
the noble person says:
"This is merely a reckless person.
In that case, what difference is there between them and an animal?
Why should one bother with an animal?"
Therefore, the noble person has lifelong worries,
but not a single morning's calamity.
As for what they worry about, it is this:
Shùn was a human being,
and I, too, am a human being.
Shùn became a model for the world,
worthy of being passed down to later generations,
while I have yet to avoid being just a common villager.
This is indeed something to worry about.
How to address this worry?
Simply by emulating Shùn.
As for what the gentleman worries about, there is none.
He does nothing that is not benevolent,
and takes no action that is not in accordance with ritual.
If there should be a sudden calamity,
then the gentleman does not worry about it."
8.29 When Yǔ and Jì lived in an age of peace,
they passed by their own gates three times without entering,
and Confucius praised their worthiness.
When Yánzǐ lived in an age of disorder,
he dwelt in a mean narrow lane,
having only a single bamboo dish of rice,
a single gourd dipper of drink;
other men could not have endured the distress,
but Yánzǐ did not allow his joy to be altered by it,
and Confucius praised his worthiness.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yǔ, Jì, and Yán Huí followed the same Way.
When Yǔ thought of anyone drowning in the world,
he felt as if he himself had caused it;
when Jì thought of anyone starving in the world,
he felt as if he himself had caused it,
therefore
they were so urgently concerned.
Had Yǔ, Jì, and Yánzǐ exchanged places,
they would have acted the same way."
If people in the same room are fighting,
to intervene and rescue them,
even with disheveled hair and cap strings untied,
is permissible;
if neighbors are fighting,
to rush with disheveled hair and cap strings untied to rescue them,
would be unwise;
even closing the door is permissible.
8.30 Gōngdūzǐ said:
"Kuāng Zhāng,
the whole state calls him unfilial,
yet you, Master, associate with him,
and moreover treat him with courtesy.
May I ask why?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Súshì suǒwèi bú xiào zhě wǔ,
duò qí sì zhī,
búgù fùmǔ zhī yǎng,
yī bú xiào yě;
bóyì hào yǐnjiǔ,
búgù fùmǔ zhī yǎng,
èr bú xiào yě;
Being fond of wealth,
and selfishly attached to his wife and children,
so as not to attend to the nourishment of his parents—
this is the third kind of unfilial conduct.
Following the desires of his ears and eyes,
so as to bring his parents to disgrace—
this is the fourth.
Being fond of bravery, fighting, and quarrelling,
so as to endanger his parents—
this is the fifth.
Is Zhāngzǐ guilty of any one of these?
Now Zhāngzǐ,
father and son reproved one another for goodness
and did not get along.
To reprove one another for goodness
is the way of friends.
If father and son reprove one another for goodness,
this is the greatest injury to affection.
As for Zhāngzǐ,
did he not desire to have the relationships of husband and wife, parent and child?
Because he had offended his father,
he could not be near him,
so he sent away his wife and kept his son at a distance,
and never received support from them all his life.
His intention was that
if he did not do this,
it would be a great offense,
and this is what Zhāngzǐ was about.
8.31 Zēngzǐ lived in Wǔchéng,
when Yuè invaders came.
Someone said:
"The invaders are approaching,
why not leave?"
He replied:
"Do not let anyone stay in my house,
lest they damage the firewood and trees."
When the invaders retreated,
he said:
"Repair my walls and house,
I shall return."
The invaders retreated,
and Zēngzǐ returned.
The attendants said:
"We have treated you, sir, with such
loyalty and respect,
yet when the bandits arrived,
you were the first to leave, setting an example for the people;
and when the bandits retreated, you returned.
This is hardly acceptable."
Shěn Yóu Xíng said:
"This is not something you understand.
Formerly,
when Shěn Yóu had the disaster of Fù Chú,
the seventy followers of the Master
took no part in it."
Zǐsī lived in Wèi,
and there was an army from Qí.
Someone said:
"The army is coming,
why not leave?"
Zǐsī said:
"If Jí leaves,
with whom will the ruler defend the state?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī followed the same path.
Zēngzǐ was a teacher,
like a father or elder brother;
Zǐsī was a minister,
of humble status.
Had Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī exchanged places,
both would have acted the same way."
8.32 Chǔ Zǐ said:
"The king sent someone to observe you, sir,
to see if you are truly different from others."
Mèng Zǐ replied:
"How could I be different from others?
Yáo and Shùn were the same as everyone else."
8.33 There was a man of Qí who had one wife and one concubine living together in his house.
When their husband went out,
he would always return only after having eaten and drunk to his fill.
His wife asked with whom he ate and drank,
and he said they were all wealthy and noble people.
His wife told his concubine, saying:
"When our husband goes out,
he is sure to eat and drink his fill before returning;
when we ask about those with whom he eats and drinks,
they are all wealthy and noble people,
yet no distinguished person has ever come here.
I shall spy on where our husband goes."
She rose early,
and stealthily followed her husband to where he was going.
Throughout the whole city, there was no one who would stand and talk with him.
At last, he came to the graveyard among the tombs in the eastern outskirts,
and went to those who were sacrificing,
begging for what they had left.
Not getting enough,
he looked around and went to another group.
This was the way he sought to satisfy his hunger.
His wife returned home,
told his concubine, saying:
"A husband is
he whom we look up to for our entire lives,
yet now he is like this."
Together with his concubine, she slandered their husband,
and they wept together in the courtyard,
while the husband remained unaware of this.
Proudly he came in from outside,
boasting before his wife and concubine.
From the perspective of a noble person,
the means by which people seek wealth, rank, and advancement,
would cause their wives and concubines not to feel ashamed, nor to weep together,
are indeed very few.
9.1 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
'When Shùn went into the fields,
he cried and wept to the pitying heavens.
Why did he cry and weep?'
Mèngzǐ replied,
"He was full of discontent and yearning."
Wàn Zhāng yuē:
" 'Fùmǔ ài zhī,
xǐ ér bú wàng;
fùmǔ wù zhī,
láo ér bú yuàn.'
Ránzé Shùn yuàn hū?"
It is said:
"Cháng Xī asked Gōngmíng Gāo, saying:
'Regarding Shùn going to the fields,
I have already received your instruction;
but weeping and crying to compassionate Heaven,
and to his parents,
I do not understand.'
Gōngmíng Gāo said:
'This is not something you can comprehend.'
Now, Gōngmíng Gāo considered that a filial son's heart
could not be so indifferent,
I strive to cultivate the fields,
merely fulfilling my duties as a son.
If my parents do not love me,
what can I do about it?
The Emperor sent his nine sons and two daughters,
along with officials, cattle, sheep, and fully stocked granaries,
to serve Shùn in the midst of the farmlands.
Many scholars of the world went to him,
and the Emperor planned to transfer the entire empire to him.
To be disobedient to one's parents,
is like a poor man having nowhere to turn.
The scholars of the world delight in him,
which is what men desire,
yet it is not enough to dispel his sorrow;
Beauty is what people desire,
yet marrying the two daughters of the emperor
was not enough to relieve sorrow;
wealth,
is what people desire,
yet possessing all under heaven
was not enough to relieve sorrow;
nobility,
is what people desire,
yet being honored as the Son of Heaven
was not enough to relieve sorrow.
Being pleased by others,
beauty, wealth, and honor—
none of these are sufficient to dispel sorrow.
Only obedience to parents
can dispel sorrow.
When young, one cherishes their parents;
upon knowing attraction, one admires the young and beautiful;
with a wife and children, one dotes on them;
in service, one is devoted to the ruler,
and if not favored by the ruler, one's heart burns with anxiety.
The greatest filial piety is lifelong cherishing of parents.
At fifty, still cherishing them—
this I have witnessed in the great Shùn."
9.2 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"The Book of Songs says:
'How does one take a wife?
One must inform one's parents.'
If these words are true,
none should have exemplified them better than Shùn.
Why then did Shùn take a wife without informing
his parents?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Gào zé bùdé qǔ.
Nánnǚ jū shì,
rén zhī dà lún yě.
Rú gào, zé fèi rén zhī dà lún,
yǐ duì fùmǔ,
shìyǐ bù gào yě."
Wàn Zhāng yuē:
"Shùn zhī bù gào ér qǔ,
zé wú jì dé wén mìng yǐ;
Dì zhī qī Shùn ér bù gào,
hé yě?"
Yuē:
"Dì yì zhī gào yān
zé bùdé qī yě."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"Shùn's parents sent him to repair the granary,
then removed the ladder,
and Gǔ Sǒu set the granary on fire.
They sent him to dredge the well,
and when he came out,
they proceeded to cover him up.
The image says:
'The plans to cover the sovereign were all my achievement;
the oxen and sheep go to my parents,
the granaries go to my parents,
the shields and spears are mine,
the lute is mine,
the bow is mine,
and my two sisters-in-law shall attend to my resting place.'
Xiàng then went into Shùn's palace,
where Shùn was sitting on his bed playing the lute.
The commentary says:
"I was deeply distressed and longed for you."
He looked ashamed.
Shùn said:
"All these ministers and common people,
I leave them for you to govern."
Did Shùn not know that Xiàng intended to kill him?"
He said:
"How could I not know?
When Xiàng was sorrowful, I too was sorrowful;
when Xiàng was joyful, I too was joyful."
He said:
"Then was Shùn pretending to be joyful?"
He said:
"No;
Once someone gave a live fish as a gift to Zhèng Zǐchǎn,
Zǐchǎn ordered the pond keeper to raise it in a pond.
The pond keeper cooked it,
then reported back, saying:
"When I first released it, it appeared listless;
after a while it became lively;
then it swiftly swam away."
Zǐchǎn said:
"It has found its proper place!
It has found its proper place!"
The keeper of the fish pond left,
and said:
'Who says Zǐchǎn is wise?
I have already cooked and eaten it,
and he said:
"It has met its proper end,
it has met its proper end."'
Thus a gentleman can be deceived by what is right,
but cannot be misled by what is contrary to principle.
Since he came with the way of loving his elder brother,
I therefore sincerely believed and rejoiced in it.
How could it be false?"
9.3 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
'Xiàng's daily endeavor was to murder Shùn.
When [Shùn] was made the Son of Heaven,
he banished [Xiàng].
Why was this?'
Mèngzǐ said,
'He enfeoffed him;
some say, he banished him.'
Wàn Zhāng said:
"Shùn exiled Gōnggōng to Yōuzhōu,
banished Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
executed the Sānmiáo at Sānwēi,
and put Gǔn to death at Yǔshān.
When these four criminals were punished,
the whole world submitted."
It is to punish the unvirtuous.
Xiàng was extremely unvirtuous,
yet he was enfeoffed in Yǒubì.
What crime did the people of Yǒubì commit?
Should a virtuous person really act like this—
punishing others when they are at fault,
but enfeoffing his own brother?
It is said:
"A benevolent person, regarding his younger brother,
does not harbor anger,
does not retain resentment,
but simply loves him dearly."
To be close to him,
one wishes him to be noble;
to love him,
one wishes him to be wealthy.
Enfeoffing him in Yǒubì,
was to make him wealthy and noble.
If one is the Son of Heaven himself,
while his brother remains a commoner,
can that be called being close and loving him?"
I venture to ask,
"Some say he was banished.
What does this mean?"
The reply was:
"Xiàng could not govern his state,
so the Son of Heaven appointed officials to administer it
and collect its tribute taxes for him,
hence it is called banishment.
How could he be allowed to oppress those people?"
Although,
one wishes to see him constantly,
so he comes in an uninterrupted stream,
"Without waiting for tribute,
he attends to governance in Yǒubì."
This is what is meant."
9.4 Xiánqiū Méng asked, saying:
"There is a saying,
'A man of great virtue
cannot be treated as a subject by the sovereign,
nor as a son by the father.'"
Shùn stood facing south,
Yáo led the feudal lords
to pay homage to him facing north,
and Gǔsǒu also faced north
to pay homage.
When Shùn saw Gǔsǒu,
his countenance appeared troubled.
Confucius said:
"At this time,
the world is in peril,
precariously so!"
I wonder if these words are truly accurate?
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Bù;
cǐ fēi jūnzǐ zhī yán,
Qí dōng yěrén zhī yǔ yě.
Yáo lǎo ér Shùn shè yě.
《Yáo Diǎn》yuē:
'Èrshí yòu bā zǎi,
Fàngxūn nǎi cúluò,
bǎixìng rú sàng kǎobǐ,
sān nián,
sìhǎi è mì bā yīn.'"
Kǒngzǐ yuē:
"Tiān wú èr rì,
mín wú èr wáng."
Shùn jì wéi tiānzǐ yǐ,
yòu shuài tiānxià zhūhóu
yǐ wéi Yáo sān nián sāng,
shì èr tiānzǐ yǐ."
Xiánqiū Méng yuē:
"Shùn zhī bù chén Yáo,
zé wú jì dé wén mìng yǐ.
