The Book of Songs says:
"Under the vast sky,
all is the king's land;
within the sea's boundaries,
all are the king's subjects."
Since Shùn had become the Son of Heaven,
may I ask how Gǔsǒu could not be his subject?
He said:
"This poem
does not refer to this;
it speaks of toiling in the king's service
and being unable to support one's parents.
It says:
'All these are the king's affairs,
yet I alone am burdened with toil.'"
Therefore, when interpreting the Book of Songs,
one should not let the literary form distort the meaning of the words,
nor let the words distort the intended thought.
By using one's understanding to infer the intended thought,
that is the way to grasp it.
If one relies solely on the words,
The poem "Yún Hàn" says:
"Of Zhōu's remaining common people,
not a single one was left."
If this saying is true,
then Zhōu had no survivors.
The ultimate of filial piety,
is nothing greater than honoring one's parents;
the ultimate of honoring one's parents,
is nothing greater than supporting them with the whole world.
To be the father of the Son of Heaven,
is the ultimate honor;
to be supported with the whole world,
is the ultimate support.
The Book of Songs says:
'Forever cherish filial thoughts,
filial thoughts become the norm.'
This is what is meant.
The Book of Documents says:
'When reverently attending to Gǔsǒu,
trembling with awe and caution,
Gǔsǒu also became truly agreeable.'
Is this not a case where a father cannot but treat his son as a son?"
9.5 Wàn Zhāng said:
"Yáo gave the empire to Shùn,
is that so?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"No;
the Son of Heaven cannot give the empire to another."
"Then when Shùn possessed the empire,
who gave it to him?"
He said:
"Heaven gave it to him."
"When Heaven gives it to him,
does it do so with explicit instructions?"
He replied:
"No;
Heaven does not speak,
but reveals it through actions and events only."
He asked:
"When revealing through actions and events,
how does it do so?"
It is said:
"The Son of Heaven can recommend a person to Heaven,
but cannot make Heaven give him the empire;
the feudal lords can recommend a person to the Son of Heaven,
but cannot make the Son of Heaven give them a feudal state;
the high officials can recommend a person to the feudal lords,
but cannot make the feudal lords give them an office.
In ancient times, Yáo recommended Shùn to Heaven,
and Heaven accepted him;
he presented him to the people,
and the people accepted him;
Therefore it is said,
'Heaven does not speak,
but reveals itself through actions and events only.'
It was said:
"May I ask, when he is recommended to Heaven,
and Heaven accepts him;
when he is presented to the people, and the people accept him,
how is this so?"
The reply was:
"If he is made to preside over the sacrifices,
and the hundred spirits enjoy them,
this is Heaven accepting him;
When he was put in charge of affairs,
and the affairs were well administered,
the common people felt at ease with him,
this shows that the people accepted him.
Heaven gave the throne to him,
and men gave it to him;
therefore it is said,
"The Son of Heaven cannot give the world to another."
Shùn served as Yáo's minister
for twenty-eight years,
which was not something that could be achieved by human effort alone,
but was the work of Heaven.
When Yáo passed away,
and the three-year mourning period was completed,
Shùn withdrew to avoid Yáo's son
south of the Southern River.
The feudal lords of the world who came to pay homage,
did not go to Yáo’s son but to Shùn;
those who had lawsuits,
did not go to Yáo’s son but to Shùn;
those who sang praises,
did not sing praises for Yáo’s son but for Shùn,
therefore it is said,
'It is Heaven’s will.'
Only after this did he come to the Central Kingdom,
and ascend the Son of Heaven's throne.
Yet to dwell in Yáo's palace,
and force Yáo's son aside,
is usurpation,
not Heaven's grant.
The Great Declaration says,
"Heaven's seeing comes through our people's seeing;
Heaven's hearing comes through our people's hearing,"
this expresses it.
9.6 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Some people say,
'With Yǔ virtue declined,
for he did not transmit the throne to a worthy,
but transmitted it to his son.'
Is this so?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it is not so;
If Heaven bestows it on the worthy,
then it is bestowed on the worthy;
if Heaven bestows it on the son,
then it is bestowed on the son.
In ancient times, Shùn recommended Yǔ to Heaven,
and after seventeen years,
Shùn passed away.
When the three-year mourning period ended,
Yǔ withdrew to avoid Shùn's son
in Yángchéng,
yet the people of the world followed him,
just as after Yáo's demise
they did not follow Yáo's son but followed Shùn instead.
Yǔ recommended Yì to Heaven,
after seven years,
Yǔ passed away,
when the three-year mourning period ended,
Yì withdrew in favor of Yǔ's son
to the northern side of Jīshān.
Those who came to pay homage
and those involved in litigation
did not go to Yì but went to Qǐ,
saying,
"He is our sovereign's son."
Those who sang praises
did not sing praises for Yì but sang praises for Qǐ,
saying,
"He is our sovereign's son."
Dānzhū was unworthy,
and Shùn's son was also unworthy.
Shùn served as Yáo's minister,
and Yǔ served as Shùn's minister
for many years,
bestowing benefits upon the people for a long time.
Qǐ was worthy,
able to respectfully inherit and continue Yǔ's way.
Yì served as Yǔ's minister
for few years,
bestowing benefits upon the people for not long.
Shùn, Yǔ, and Yì
lived far apart in time.
Whether their sons were worthy or unworthy
was all due to Heaven,
not something that human effort could achieve.
What is done without anyone doing it
is Heaven.
What comes without anyone bringing it
is destiny.
A commoner who possesses the empire
must have virtue like Shùn and Yǔ,
and moreover have the Son of Heaven recommend him;
therefore, Zhòngní did not possess the empire.
One who inherits the empire through succession,
whom Heaven would cast aside,
must be like Jié and Zhòu;
therefore, Yì, Yīyǐn, and Zhōugōng
did not possess the empire.
Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng in ruling the world as king,
after Tāng's death,
Tài Dīng did not ascend the throne,
Wài Bǐng reigned for two years,
Zhòng Rén reigned for four years,
Tài Jiǎ overturned Tāng's established laws and punishments,
Yī Yǐn exiled him to Tóng.
In the third year,
Tàijiǎ repented of his faults,
blaming and reforming himself,
dwelling in Tóng, he turned to benevolence and moved toward righteousness.
After three years, having listened to Yīyǐn's instructions to himself,
he returned to Bó.
The reason Zhōu Gōng did not possess the empire,
is similar to Yì under the Xià,
and Yī Yǐn under the Yīn.
Confucius said,
"Táng and Yǔ abdicated,
while the Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu inherited,
but the principle is the same."
9.7 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Some people say,
'Yǐ Yǐn sought to attract Tāng by his knowledge of cookery.'
Was this the case?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
It was not so.
Yī Yǐn farmed in the wilderness of Yǒushēn,
and delighted in the ways of Yáo and Shùn.
If it was not righteous,
if it was not the Way,
he would not even glance at the wealth of the entire world offered to him;
he would not look at a thousand teams of horses tethered for him.
If it was not righteous,
if it was not the Way,
he would not give others even a single blade of grass,
nor take a single blade of grass from others.
Tāng sent someone with gifts to invite him,
but he said disdainfully:
"What use have I for King Tāng's invitation gifts?
Wouldn't I rather remain in my fields and
there delight in the Way of Yáo and Shùn?"
Tāng sent messengers three times to invite him,
whereupon he changed his mind and said:
'Rather than dwelling in the fields
and thereby delighting in the ways of Yáo and Shùn,
would it not be better for me to make this ruler a sovereign like Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better for me to make this people subjects like those of Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better for me to witness it with my own eyes?
When Heaven produced this people,
it caused those with first knowledge to awaken those with later knowledge,
and those with first awareness to awaken those with later awareness.
I
am one of Heaven's people who has first awareness;
I shall use this Way to awaken this people.
If I do not awaken them, who will?"
He thought that if there were any common man or woman in the world
who did not enjoy the benefits of Yáo and Shùn's benevolent rule,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
He took upon himself the heavy responsibility for the world in this manner,
so he went to Tāng
and persuaded
him to attack the Xià dynasty
and save the people.
I have never heard of one who could correct others while being crooked himself,
let alone one who could bring order to the world while humiliating himself.
The actions of the sages differ from one another;
some are distant, some are close;
some depart, some do not depart;
they all return to purifying themselves, that is all.
I have heard that he sought out Tāng with the way of Yáo and Shùn,
but I have not heard of him using butchering and cooking.
The "Yī Xùn" says:
"Heaven's punishment began its attack from the Mù Palace,
but I initiated it from Bó."
9.8 Wàn Zhāng asked:
"Some say
that when Confucius was in Wèi, he stayed with Yōng Jū,
and when in Qí, he stayed with the eunuch Jí Huán.
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"No,
it is not so;
it was fabricated by busybodies."
In Wèi,
he stayed with Yán Chóuyóu.
The wife of Mí Zǐ and the wife of Zǐlù
were sisters.
Mí Zǐ said to Zǐlù:
"If Confucius would stay with me,
he could obtain the position of a minister of Wèi."
Zǐlù reported this.
Confucius said:
"It depends on fate."
Confucius advanced according to propriety,
and withdrew according to righteousness,
whether obtaining office or not obtaining it, he said,
"It is fate."
But to serve Yōngjū and the eunuch Jí Huán,
this is to have neither righteousness nor fate.
Confucius was displeased in Lǔ and Wèi,
encountered Sīmǎ of Sòng Huán,
who intended to intercept and kill him,
so he disguised himself and passed through Sòng.
At this time Confucius was in distress,
stayed with Chéngzǐ the Minister of Works,
and served as an official to Zhōu, the Marquis of Chén.
I have heard that to observe a minister at court,
one considers those he associates with;
to observe a minister from afar,
one considers those who host him.
If Confucius had stayed with Yōngjū and the attendant Jí Huán,
how could he have been Confucius?"
9.9 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Some say,
'Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself
to a cattle keeper of Qín
for the skin of five sheep to feed oxen,
in order to seek out Duke Mù of Qín.'
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it is not so;
it was made up by busybodies."
Bǎilǐ Xī was
a man of Yú.
The people of Jìn used the jade from Chuíjí
and the steeds from Qūchǎn
to borrow a path through Yú to attack Guó.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated,
but Bǎilǐ Xī did not.
Knowing that the Duke of Yú could not be remonstrated with, he left for Qín.
He was already seventy years old;
yet he never realized that gaining the favor of Duke Mù of Qín by feeding oxen was disgraceful—
can this be called wise?
When remonstrance was impossible and he did not remonstrate,
can this be called unwise?
Knowing that Duke Yú was about to perish
and leaving him beforehand,
this cannot be called unwise.
When he was recommended in Qín,
he knew that Duke Mù could achieve great deeds with him
and became his minister—
can this be called unwise?
As minister of Qín
he brought glory to his ruler throughout the world,
leaving a legacy for later generations—
could this be done by one who was not virtuous?
To sell oneself to accomplish his ruler's aims
is what even self-respecting villagers would not do—
how could we say a virtuous man would do it?"
10.1 Mencius said:
"Bó Yí would not look upon an evil sight with his eyes,
nor listen to an evil sound with his ears.
He would not serve a sovereign whom he did not approve,
nor command a people whom he did not approve.
When good order prevailed in the government, he would take office;
when disorder prevailed, he would retire.
Where tyrannical government is enforced,
where unruly people dwell,
he could not bear to reside.
To live among the villagers,
he felt as if he were sitting in filth and ashes
while wearing court robes and a court cap.
During the time of Zhòu,
he dwelled by the shores of the Northern Sea,
awaiting the purification of the world.
Therefore, those who have heard of the ways of Bó Yí,
the corrupt become honest,
and the timid become resolute.
Yī Yǐn said:
"What ruler is unworthy of service?
What people are unworthy of being governed?"
He would advance in times of orderly rule,
and advance in times of chaotic rule,
He said:
"When Heaven gave birth to this people,
it made those who first apprehend
enlighten those who later apprehend,
and made those who first awaken
enlighten those who later awaken.
I am
one of Heaven's people who awakened first.
I shall use this Way to enlighten this people."
He considered that if there were common men and women in the world
who did not share in the benefits of Yáo and Shùn's benevolent rule,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
Such was the weight of responsibility he took upon himself for the world.
Liǔxià Huì
was not ashamed to serve a corrupt ruler,
nor did he decline a minor office.
In advancing, he did not conceal his worthiness,
but always acted according to his principles.
When neglected and cast aside, he bore no resentment;
in poverty and distress, he felt no despair.
When living among the villagers,
he was content and reluctant to leave.
"You are you,
I am I.
Even if you were to stand naked by my side,
how could you defile me?"
Therefore, those who hear of the character of Liǔxià Huì
make the mean generous,
and the frivolous, earnest.
"When Confucius left Qí,
he departed with the rice he was washing;
when he left Lǔ,
he said,
'I am taking my departure slowly—
this is the way to leave the land of one's parents.'
He would hasten when it was proper to hasten,
delay when it was proper to delay,
retire when it was proper to retire,
and take office when it was proper to take office—
this was Confucius."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Bóyí
shì shèngrén zhī qīngzhě yě,
Yīyǐn
shì shèngrén zhī rènzhě yě,
Liǔxià Huì
shì shèngrén zhī hézhě yě,
Kǒngzǐ, shì shèngrén zhī shízhě yě."
Confucius is said to have epitomized the highest achievement.
To epitomize the highest achievement means
to begin with the sound of a bell and end with the resonance of a jade chime.
The sound of a bell
represents the beginning of order;
the resonance of a jade chime
represents the completion of order.
The beginning of order
is the work of wisdom;
the completion of order
is the work of sagehood.
Wisdom is like skill;
sagehood is like strength.
It is like shooting from beyond a hundred paces:
the arrow's reaching the target
is due to your strength,
but hitting the mark
is not due to your strength.
10.2 Běigōng Qǐ asked, saying,
"The royal house of Zhōu arranged the ranks of nobility and the amount of their emoluments;
how was this done?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"The particulars of that arrangement
cannot be learned,
for the feudal lords, disliking them as injurious to themselves,
have all made away with the records of them.
Nevertheless,
I have learned the general outline of them.
The Son of Heaven holds one rank,
the Duke holds one rank,
the Marquis holds one rank,
the Earl holds one rank,
the Viscount and Baron share one rank,
making five ranks in total.
One rank for the sovereign,
one rank for the high ministers,
one rank for the senior officials,
one rank for the upper-grade scholars,
one rank for the middle-grade scholars,
one rank for the lower-grade scholars,
making six ranks in total.
The system of the Son of Heaven,
his domain is a thousand li square,
the dukes and marquises each have domains of a hundred li square,
the earls seventy li,
the viscounts and barons fifty li,
making four grades in all.
Those who cannot reach fifty li,
do not have direct access to the Son of Heaven,
but are attached to the feudal lords,
are called dependencies.
The high ministers of the Son of Heaven
receive land equivalent to that of a marquis,
the grand masters
receive land equivalent to that of an earl,
and the senior officials
receive land equivalent to that of a viscount or baron.
A large state with a territory of a hundred square li,
the ruler's emolument is ten times that of a minister,
the minister's emolument is four times that of a senior official,
the senior official's emolument is double that of a high-ranking scholar,
the high-ranking scholar's emolument is double that of a middle-ranking scholar,
the middle-ranking scholar's emolument is double that of a low-ranking scholar,
the low-ranking scholar and commoners serving in government receive the same emolument,
which is sufficient to replace their income from farming.
A secondary state has a territory of seventy lǐ,
its ruler's emolument is ten times that of a minister,
a minister's emolument is three times that of a senior official,
a senior official's emolument is double that of a higher scholar,
a higher scholar's emolument is double that of a middle scholar,
a middle scholar's emolument is double that of a lower scholar,
a lower scholar's emolument is the same as that of a commoner in government service,
their emolument being sufficient to replace their farming.
A small state has a territory of fifty li square,
the ruler's emolument is ten times that of a minister,
a minister's emolument is twice that of a senior official,
a senior official's emolument is double that of a high-ranking scholar,
a high-ranking scholar's emolument is double that of a middle-ranking scholar,
a middle-ranking scholar's emolument is double that of a low-ranking scholar,
a low-ranking scholar and commoners serving in government receive the same emolument,
which is sufficient to replace their income from farming.
What a farmer reaps,
is one hundred mu per man;
with the manure applied to one hundred mu,
a superior farmer feeds nine people,
the next superior feeds eight people,
a medium farmer feeds seven people,
the next medium feeds six people,
an inferior farmer feeds five people.
Commoners in official positions
have their salaries graded accordingly."
10.3 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"I venture to ask about friendship."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Do not presume on your age,
do not presume on your high position,
do not presume on the status of your brothers to make friends.
In forming a friendship,
one should befriend others for their virtue,
and must not do so with any presumption.
Mèng Xiànzǐ,
In a household of a hundred chariots,
there were five friends:
Yuèzhèng Qiú, Mù Zhòng,
but I have forgotten the other three.
Xiànzǐ befriended these five men,
not because of Xiànzǐ's household status.
If these five men had regarded Xiànzǐ's household status,
they would not have befriended him.
Not only the families of a hundred chariots are like this,
even the rulers of small states also have them.
Duke Huì of Fèi said,
"As for Zǐsī,
I treat him as my teacher;
as for Yán Bān,
I treat him as my friend;
Wáng Shùn and Cháng Xī
are those who serve me."
Not only the rulers of small states are like this,
even the rulers of great states have such cases.
Duke Píng of Jìn with regard to Hài Táng,
when told to enter, he would enter;
when told to sit, he would sit;
when told to eat, he would eat.
Even if it were only coarse food and vegetable soup,
he never failed to eat his fill,
for he dared not do otherwise.
Yet it ends here and no further.
He does not share with him the heavenly position,
nor does he govern with him the heavenly duties,
nor does he partake with him of the heavenly emoluments.
This is the scholar's way of honoring the worthy,
not that of kings and dukes in honoring the worthy.
Shùn paid a visit to the Emperor,
who lodged his son-in-law in the secondary palace,
and also feasted Shùn,
taking turns as host and guest.
This shows that the Son of Heaven
could befriend a common man.
When inferiors respect superiors,
it is called honoring the noble;
when superiors respect inferiors,
it is called esteeming the worthy.
Honoring the noble and esteeming the worthy,
their principle is one and the same.
10.4 Wàn Zhāng said:
"I venture to ask, in social interactions,
what should be the state of mind?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Respectfulness."
Wàn Zhāng said:
" 'To decline and
decline again is disrespectful' -
why is that?"
He said:
"When an elder bestows something,
one says,
'Was what he took
righteous or unrighteous?'
Only after that does one accept it.
To do so would be disrespectful,
therefore I do not decline."
He said:
"I ask not to decline it with words,
but to decline it in my heart,
saying,
'This was taken from the people unjustly,'
and then to decline with some other excuse without accepting it -
would this not be permissible?"
The reply was:
"When the gift is offered in accordance with the Way,
and the presentation is made in accordance with ritual,
then even Confucius would have accepted it."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"If there is someone who robs people outside the capital gates,
but when interacting with others follows the proper way,
and when giving gifts observes the rites,
can such plunder be accepted?"
The reply was:
"It cannot;
The "Announcement to the Prince of Kāng" says:
"Those who kill people to seize their goods,
being reckless and fearless of death,
are detested by all the people."
Such are to be executed without waiting for instruction.
The Yīn dynasty accepted this from the Xià,
the Zhōu dynasty accepted it from the Yīn,
and did not decline it;
now it is even more strictly enforced.
How can it be accepted?"
He said:
"Nowadays the feudal lords take from the people,
like robbery.
But if they properly observe the rules of intercourse,
then the superior man accepts it.
I venture to ask how this is to be explained?"
He said:
"Do you think that if a true king were to arise,
would he treat the present feudal lords as equals and then punish them?
Or would he first instruct them and only punish those who do not reform?
Now, to say that
one who takes what does not belong to him
is a robber
is to carry the analogy to its utmost meaning."
When Confucius served in office in Lǔ,
the people of Lǔ held competitive hunts,
and Confucius also participated in competitive hunts.
If competitive hunts were acceptable,
how much more so accepting their gifts?"
Someone asked:
"Then when Confucius served in office,
was it not to serve the Way?"
The reply was:
"It was to serve the Way."
"If serving the Way, why did he participate in competitive hunts?"
He said:
"Confucius first recorded and rectified the sacrificial vessels,
not using food from all regions for the recorded rectification."
He said:
"Why did he not leave?"
He said:
"He gave it an initial trial.
When the trial was sufficient to proceed,
yet it did not proceed,
then he would leave,
therefore he never stayed anywhere for a full three years."
Confucius had instances of taking office where the Way could be practiced,
instances where he was treated with due courtesy,
and instances where he was supported by the state.
With Jì Huánzǐ,
it was taking office where the Way could be practiced;
with Wèi Línggōng,
it was being treated with due courtesy;
with Wèi Xiàogōng,
it was being supported by the state.
10.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"One takes office not because of poverty,
but there are times when it is because of poverty;
one marries not for the sake of support,
but there are times when it is for the sake of support."
For the poor,
they decline high positions and occupy low ones,
decline wealth and dwell in poverty.
Declining high positions and occupying low ones,
declining wealth and dwelling in poverty—
where is this appropriate?
In guarding gates and striking the night watch.
Confucius once served as a warehouse keeper,
and said,
"Accounts should be kept properly, that is all."
He once served as a livestock keeper,
and said,
"The oxen and sheep should be sturdy
and growing, that is all."
To speak of lofty matters while in a lowly position
is a crime;
to stand in the court of a ruler
yet fail to have one's principles implemented
is a disgrace.
10.6 Wàn Zhāng said:
"Why is it that a scholar does not take refuge with a feudal lord?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"He does not dare.
When a feudal lord has lost his state, and then takes refuge with another feudal lord,
this is in accordance with ritual;
for a scholar to take refuge with a feudal lord,
is not in accordance with ritual."
Wàn Zhāng yuē:
"Jūn kuì zhī sù,
zé shòu zhī hū?"
Yuē:
"Shòu zhī."
"Shòu zhī hé yì yě?"
Yuē:
"Jūn zhī yú méng yě,
gù zhōu zhī."
He said:
"When it is bestowed according to Zhou rituals, I accept it;
when it is given as a personal gift, I do not accept it;
why is this?"
The reply was:
"I dare not."
He asked:
"May I ask why you dare not?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Even gatekeepers and night watchmen
all have regular duties whereby they receive support from their superiors.
Those without regular duties who receive gifts from their superiors
are considered disrespectful."
Wàn Zhāng asked:
"If the ruler sends a gift,
then one accepts it—
may this be done regularly and continuously?"
He said:
"Duke Mù's treatment of Zǐsī
involved frequent inquiries
and repeated gifts of sacrificial meat.
Zǐsī was displeased.
Finally,
he drove the messenger out beyond the main gate,
faced north, bowed twice with his head to the ground, and refused to accept it,
saying:
'From now on I know
the ruler raises Jí like dogs and horses.'"
From then on, there were no more gifts presented in the court.
To admire the worthy but fail to promote them,
and also fail to support them,
can this be called truly admiring the worthy?"
It was said:
"May I ask, if a ruler of a state wishes to support a gentleman,
how can it be considered proper support?"
He said:
"When it was sent with the ruler's command,
I bowed twice and touched my head to the ground to receive it.
Afterwards, when the granary officer sent grain,
and the cook sent meat,
they were not sent with the ruler's command.
Zǐsī considered that sending meat in a tripod
made him repeatedly bow with great haste and trouble,
and this was not the way to treat a gentleman."
Yáo's treatment of Shùn was such that
he made his nine sons serve him,
gave him his two daughters in marriage,
provided officials, cattle, sheep, and granaries fully stocked,
to support Shùn while he was still cultivating the fields.
Later, he raised him and placed him in a high position.
Therefore, it is said that this is how kings and dukes honor the worthy.
10.7 Wàn Zhāng said:
"May I ask, what is the principle behind not visiting the feudal lords?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"When in the state, one is called a minister of the marketplace;
when in the countryside, one is called a minister of the wilds;
both are referred to as commoners.
Commoners who have not presented gifts to become ministers
do not dare to appear before the feudal lords;
this is according to ritual."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"When a commoner
is summoned for service,
he goes to serve;
but when a ruler wishes to see him,
summons him,
he does not go to see him.
Why is this?"
He said:
"To go to perform service,
is right;
to go to see him,
is not right.
Moreover, for what reason
does the ruler wish to see him?"
The reply was:
"Because of his extensive knowledge,
because of his worthiness."
He said:
"If it is because of his extensive learning,
then even the Son of Heaven does not summon his teacher,
let alone the feudal lords.
If it is because of his worthiness,
then I have never heard of someone wishing to see a worthy man and summoning him."
Duke Mù frequently visited Zǐsī,
asking:
"In ancient times, a state of a thousand chariots befriending scholars—
how was that?"
Zǐsī was displeased,
and said:
"The ancients had a saying,
'They served them, so it is said,
how could they be said to have befriended them?'"
Zǐsī's displeasure
was it not because he said,
'By position,
you are
my sovereign;
I
am your subject;
how dare I befriend my sovereign?
By virtue,
you serve me,
how could you befriend me?'
A ruler of a thousand chariots sought to befriend him
but could not succeed,
so how could he be summoned?
When Duke Jǐng of Qí was hunting,
he summoned the gamekeeper with a banner,
but the man did not come,
so the duke intended to kill him.
"A man of purpose does not forget that his end may be in a ditch;
a man of courage does not forget that he may lose his head."
What did Confucius find commendable in this?
He found commendable the refusal to go when summoned improperly.
It was asked,
"May I ask how a gamekeeper should be summoned?"
The reply was,
"With a leather cap,
commoners with a plain silk banner,
officers with a dragon-and-serpent banner,
and high officials with a feathered banner."
Summoning a gamekeeper with the summons for a high official,
the gamekeeper would rather die than dare to go;
summoning a commoner with the summons for a scholar,
how would the commoner dare to go?
How much more so
when summoning a worthy person
with the summons for an unworthy one?
To wish to see a worthy person but not by the proper way,
is like wanting someone to enter yet closing the door to them.
Righteousness
is the path;
propriety
is the gate.
Only the noble person can follow this path
and pass through this gate.
The Book of Songs says:
"The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow;
what the nobleman treads upon,
the common people gaze upon."
Wàn Zhāng said:
"When Confucius
was summoned by the sovereign's command,
he would not wait for his carriage but set out immediately;
was Confucius then wrong?"
The reply was:
"Confucius was holding an official position at the time,
and he was summoned in accordance with that office."
10.8 Mèngzǐ said to Wàn Zhāng:
"The virtuous men of one village
befriend the virtuous men of one village,
the virtuous men of one state
befriend the virtuous men of one state,
the virtuous men of the world
befriend the virtuous men of the world.
If befriending the virtuous men of the world is still not enough,
one then goes further to discuss the men of antiquity."
To recite their poems,
to read their books,
without knowing the person, is that acceptable?
Therefore, we discuss their times.
This is to befriend the ancients.
10.9 King Xuān of Qí asked about high ministers.
Mèngzǐ said:
"What kind of high ministers is Your Majesty asking about?"
The king said:
"Are high ministers not the same?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"They are different.
There are ministers of the royal surname,
and there are ministers of different surnames."
The king said:
"May I ask about the high ministers of the royal house?"
The reply was:
"If the ruler has great faults, they should remonstrate with him.
If after repeated remonstrances he still does not listen,
then they should change his position."
Wáng bó rán biàn hū sè.
Yuē:
"Wáng wù yì yě.
Wáng wèn chén,
chén bù gǎn bù yǐ zhèng duì."
Wáng sè dìng,
rán hòu qǐng wèn yì xìng zhī qīng.
Yuē:
"Jūn yǒu guò zé jiàn,
fǎn fù zhī ér bù tīng,
zé qù."
11.1 Gàozǐ said:
"Human nature is like the willow tree,
and righteousness
is like cups and bowls;
to make human nature into benevolence and righteousness,
is like making the willow tree into cups and bowls."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Can you follow the nature of the willow tree
to make cups and vessels?
Or must you mutilate the willow tree
before making cups and vessels?
If you must mutilate the willow tree
to make cups and vessels,
then must you also mutilate humans to achieve benevolence and righteousness?
He who leads the people of the world to harm benevolence and righteousness
must be one who speaks like you!"
11.2 Gào Zǐ said:
"Human nature
is like swirling water.
If you breach it to the east, it flows east;
if you breach it to the west, it flows west.
Human nature's lack of inherent distinction between good and not good
is just like water's lack of inherent distinction between east and west."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Water truly does not distinguish between east and west,
but does it not distinguish between up and down?
The goodness of human nature
is like water's tendency to flow downward.
There is no person who is not good,
just as there is no water that does not flow downward."
Now take water: if you strike it and make it leap up,
you can cause it to go over your forehead;
if you channel it and force it to flow,
you can make it go up a hill.
Is this the nature of water?
It is the circumstances that make it so.
That people can be made to do what is not good
is because their nature is dealt with in this way.
11.3 Gàozǐ said:
"What is inborn is called nature."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is saying 'what is inborn is called nature'
like saying 'white is called white'?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"The whiteness of white feathers
is like the whiteness of white snow;
the whiteness of white snow
is like the whiteness of white jade, is it not?"
Reply:
"Indeed."
"Then is the nature of a dog
like the nature of an ox,
the nature of an ox
like the nature of a human, is it not?"
11.4 Gào Zǐ said:
"Eating and mating are
human nature.
Benevolence is
internal,
not external;
righteousness is
external,
not internal."
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Why is it said that benevolence is internal and righteousness is external?"
Yuē:
"That person is older and I respect them as elder,
not because there is any elder quality within me;
just as that object is white and I recognize it as white,
following its whiteness which is external,
therefore it is said to be external."
Someone said:
"Regarding whiteness, the whiteness of a white horse
is no different from the whiteness of a white person;
I wonder if the tallness of a tall horse
is no different from the tallness of a tall person?
Moreover, do we call the tall one righteous?
Or do we call the one who makes it tall righteous?"
Another replied:
"I love my younger brother,
but do not love the younger brother of a person from Qín.
This is because I find pleasure in what is mine,
thus it is called internal.
I respect the elders of people from Chǔ,
and also respect my own elders.
This is because I find pleasure in respecting elders,
thus it is called external."
He said:
"Enjoying the roast meat of the Qín people
is no different from enjoying my roast meat.
Things indeed have this similarity,
so does the enjoyment of roast meat also come from without?"
11.5 Mèng Jìzǐ asked Gōngdūzǐ, saying:
"Why is righteousness said to be internal?"
He replied:
"I act out my respect,
therefore it is said to be internal."
"Suppose a villager is one year older than your elder brother,
then whom do you respect?"
He said:
"I respect my elder brother."
"In drinking, who should be the first?"
He said:
"First serve the villagers."
"What is respected lies here,
what is esteemed lies there,
the outcome is external,
not originating from within."
Gōngdūzǐ could not reply,
and reported this to Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Jìng shūfù hū?
Jìng dì hū?
Bǐ jiāng yuē:
'Jìng shūfù.'
Yuē:
'Dì wéi shī,
Zé shuí jìng?'
Bǐ jiāng yuē:
'Jìng dì.'"
The Master said:
"Why should he respect his uncle?"
The other will say:
"Because of his position."
You also say:
"Because of his position.
Constant respect is for the elder brother,
temporary respect is for the villager."
Jìzǐ heard this and said:
"If it's an elder uncle then respect him,
if it's a younger brother then respect him,
this shows that respect is determined externally,
not coming from within."
Gōngdūzǐ said:
"In winter we drink hot water,
in summer we drink cool water -
does that mean drinking and eating are also determined externally?"
11.6 Gōngdūzǐ said:
"Gàozǐ said:
'Human nature is neither good nor bad.'
Some say:
'Human nature can become good,
and can become not good;
therefore when Kings Wén and Wǔ arose,
the people tended toward goodness;
when Kings Yōu and Lì arose,
the people tended toward violence.'"
Someone said:
"Some natures are good,
some natures are not good;
therefore, with Yáo as sovereign, there was Xiàng;
with Gǔsǒu as father, there was Shùn;
with Zhòu as the son of an elder brother,
and moreover as sovereign,
there were Wēizǐ Qǐ and Prince Bǐgān."
Now you say 'human nature is good',
then are all those cases wrong?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Nǎi ruò qí qíng,
zé kěyǐ wéi shàn yǐ,
nǎi suǒwèi shàn yě.
Ruòfú wéi bùshàn,
fēi cái zhī zuì yě."
The heart of compassion,
is possessed by all people;
the heart of shame and dislike,
is possessed by all people;
the heart of respect and reverence,
is possessed by all people;
the heart of approval and disapproval,
is possessed by all people.
The heart of compassion is
benevolence;
the heart of shame and aversion is
righteousness;
the heart of respect and reverence is
propriety;
the heart of right and wrong is
wisdom.
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
are not infused into me from without;
they are inherently possessed by me,
but I have simply not reflected on them.
Therefore, it is said:
'Seek and you will obtain them,
neglect and you will lose them.'
Some differ from others by twofold, fivefold, or an incalculable amount—
it is because they cannot fully develop their natural talents.
The Book of Songs says:
'Heaven gives birth to the multitudes of people,
and to every thing there is its norm.
The people hold fast to their constant nature,
and thus love this excellent virtue.'
Kǒngzǐ yuē:
"Wèi cǐ shī zhě,
qí zhīdào hū!
Gù yǒu wù bì yǒu zé;
mín zhī bǐng yí yě,
gù hào shì yì dé."
11.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"In years of plenty,
most young men are virtuous;
in years of dearth,
most young men are violent,
not that Heaven has bestowed different talents,
but that which ensnares their minds makes them so.
Now take barley:
sow the seeds and cover them with soil,
the ground being the same,
and the planting time also the same,
they grow rapidly and vigorously,
until the summer solstice arrives,
when they all ripen.
Though there may be differences,
this is due to variations in soil fertility,
the nourishment from rain and dew,
and uneven human efforts.
Therefore all things of the same kind
are alike,
so why should there be doubt only when it comes to humans?
Sages are of the same kind as we are.
Hence Longzi said:
'If one weaves sandals without knowing the size of feet,
I know he will not make them like baskets.'
The similarity of sandals
stems from the uniformity of feet under heaven.
As for the mouth in relation to flavors,
there is a common preference;
Yìyá first discovered what our mouths prefer.
If the mouth in relation to flavors
had a nature different from others,
like dogs and horses being of a different kind from us,
then why would everyone in the world
follow Yìyá in matters of taste?
As for flavors,
the whole world agrees on Yìyá,
which shows that all mouths have similar tastes.
The same is true for the ears.
As for sounds,
the whole world agrees on Shī Kuàng,
which shows that all ears have similar perceptions.
The same applies to the eyes.
As for Zǐdū,
there is no one under heaven who does not know his beauty.
Anyone who does not know Zǐdū's beauty
must be blind.
Therefore it is said:
As to the mouth in relation to flavors,
there is a common preference;
as to the ear in relation to sounds,
there is a common appreciation;
as to the eye in relation to colors,
there is a common admiration.
As for the heart,
is it alone without that which is universally the same?
What is that which the heart universally agrees upon?
It is called principle,
and righteousness.
The sages were the first
to attain what our hearts universally agree upon.
Therefore, principle and righteousness delight our hearts,
just as the flavors of grass-fed and grain-fed animals delight our mouths.
11.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"The trees of Niú Mountain were once beautiful,
but because it is on the outskirts of a large state,
axes and hatchets hew them down—
can they remain beautiful?
Yet with the rest they get day and night,
and the moistening by rain and dew,
it is not that there are no new sprouts and shoots growing,
but then cattle and sheep come to graze upon them,
and that is why it appears so barren.
When people see its barrenness,
they think it never had any timber.
But is this the nature of the mountain?
Similarly, in human beings,
how could there be no heart of benevolence and righteousness?
The reason they let go of their good heart
is also like axes acting upon trees.
If one cuts it down every day,
can it maintain its beauty?
The rest it gains day and night,
and the calm air of the morning,
cause it to differ but little from others in its likes and dislikes.
But then what it does in the day
fetters and destroys it.
If fettered and twisted repeatedly,
then his night breath will not be sufficient to be preserved;
if the night breath is not sufficient to be preserved,
then he will not be far removed from birds and beasts.
When people see him behaving like birds and beasts,
they think that he never had any innate capacity—
is this truly the natural disposition of a human being?
Therefore, if it gets its nourishment,
nothing will fail to grow;
if it loses its nourishment,
nothing will fail to perish.
Confucius said:
'Hold it, and it remains;
let it go, and it is lost;
its outgoing and incoming cannot be fixed in time;
none knows the place of its abode.'
Is this not spoken of the mind?"
11.9 Mencius said:
"Do not be perplexed by the king's lack of wisdom.
Even with the most easily growing thing in the world,
if you expose it to the sun for one day,
and then expose it to cold for ten days,
it will never be able to grow.
I see the king but rarely,
and when I retire,
those who expose him to cold arrive.
What can I do with the sprouts of goodness that have begun to grow in him?"
Now, the art of playing weiqi,
though a minor art,
if one does not devote one's whole mind to it,
one cannot master it.
Yì Qiū,
was the best weiqi player in the whole country.
Let Yì Qiū teach two people to play chess.
One of them concentrates his will,
and listens only to Yì Qiū.
Although the other listens,
he has in mind that a swan is about to come,
thinking of taking a bow and arrow to shoot it.
Although he studies together with the first,
he is not equal to him.
Is it because his intelligence is not equal?
The answer is:
"It is not so."
11.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"Fish is
what I desire;
bear's paw
is also what I desire.
If I cannot have both,
I would forsake the fish and choose the bear's paw.
Life
is what I desire,
righteousness
is also what I desire;
when I cannot have both,
I would give up life and choose righteousness.
Life is indeed what I desire,
but there is something I desire more than life,
so I do not cling to life at all costs;
Death is what I detest,
but there are things I detest more than death,
so there are calamities I do not avoid.
If what people desire were nothing greater than life,
then why would they not use any means to preserve it?
If what people detest were nothing worse than death,
then why would they not do anything to avoid calamity?
Thus, there are cases when one would not adopt means leading to survival;
thus, there are cases when one would not do things to avoid calamities.
Therefore, there are things one desires more than life,
and things one detests more than death.
It is not only the virtuous who have such a mind;
all men have it,
but the virtuous are able to avoid losing it.
A bowl of food,
a dish of soup,
obtaining them means life,
not obtaining them means death.
If given with a shout,
a passerby would not accept them;
if given with a kick,
even a beggar would disdain them.
If offered a salary of ten thousand zhòng without regard to propriety and righteousness, one would accept it.
What benefit would ten thousand zhòng bring to me?
Is it for the beauty of magnificent houses,
the service of wives and concubines,
or the gratitude of the impoverished acquaintances I know?
In the past, they would rather die than accept,
but now they do it for the beauty of palaces and houses;
in the past, they would rather die than accept,
but now they do it for the service of wives and concubines;
in the past, they would rather die than accept,
but now they do it so that the poor and needy who know them may be grateful to them;
is this not something that should be stopped?
This is called losing one's original heart."
11.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence is
the human heart;
righteousness is
the human path.
To abandon this path
and not follow it,
to lose this heart
and not know to seek it—
how lamentable!"
When one's chickens and dogs stray,
one knows to seek them;
yet when one's heart strays,
one does not know to seek it.
The way of learning is no other
than to seek the lost heart."
11.12 Mencius said:
"Now suppose there is a man whose fourth finger
is bent and cannot be straightened.
It is not painful nor does it hinder his work.
Yet if there were someone who could straighten it,
he would not consider the journey to Qin or Chu too far,
all because his finger is not like other people's.
If a finger is not as good as others',
one knows to dislike it;
if one's heart is not as good as others',
one does not know to dislike it.
This is called not knowing the proper order of things."
11.13 Mencius said:
"Even a small sapling of a tung or catalpa tree,
if a person wishes to nurture it,
knows how to cultivate it.
But when it comes to their own person,
they do not know how to cultivate it.
Is this because they care for their person less than for the tung or catalpa tree?
It is simply that they do not think deeply enough."
11.14 Mencius said:
"A person, in regard to their body,
loves all parts of it.
Loving all parts of it,
they then nurture all parts of it.
If there is not an inch of skin they do not love,
then there is not an inch of skin they do not nurture.
Therefore, to examine whether it is good or not,
is there any other way?
It is simply to seek it within oneself.
The body has parts of greater and lesser value,
and parts of smaller and larger importance.
Do not let the small harm the large,
nor let the lesser value harm the greater.
He who cultivates the smaller parts becomes a petty person,
while he who cultivates the larger parts becomes a great person.
Now there is a gardener,
who neglects his catalpas and oaks,
and cultivates sour jujubes and thorns,
then he is an inferior gardener.
To care for one finger
but lose the shoulder and back,
without realizing it,
then he is a person with a wolf-like malady.
Those who indulge in eating and drinking
are despised by others,
because they nourish the lesser part
at the expense of the greater.
If those who indulge in eating and drinking
could avoid such loss,
then would mouth and belly
be considered only for a foot or inch of skin?"
11.15 Gōngdūzǐ asked, saying,
"All are similarly men,
some become great men,
some become small men;
how is this?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"Those who follow the great part of themselves
become great men.
Those who follow the small part of themselves
become small men."
It was said:
"All are human beings,
yet some follow their greater parts,
while others follow their lesser parts.
Why is this?"
The reply was:
"The organs of ear and eye do not think,
and are obscured by things.
When one thing interacts with another,
it merely leads them away."
The function of the mind is to think;
thinking leads to its attainment,
while not thinking leads to its loss.
This is what Heaven has bestowed upon us.
First establish what is of greater importance,
then what is of lesser importance cannot take it away.
This is all there is to being a great person.
11.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are heavenly ranks,
and there are human ranks.
Benevolence, righteousness,
loyalty, and faithfulness,
taking delight in goodness without weariness—
these constitute heavenly ranks;
dukes, ministers, and high officials—
these constitute human ranks.
The ancients
cultivated their heavenly nobility,
and human nobility followed.
People today
cultivate their heavenly nobility to seek human nobility;
once they obtain human nobility, they abandon their heavenly nobility.
This is the height of delusion,
and in the end they must lose both.
11.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"To desire honor
is a common aspiration of all people.
Every person has honor within themselves,
but they simply do not reflect upon it.
The honor that people value
is not true honor.
What Zhào Mèng honors,
Zhào Mèng can also debase.
The Book of Songs says:
'I am drunk with wine,
I am satiated with virtue.'
This speaks of being filled with benevolence and righteousness,
therefore one does not covet the rich flavors of others' fine foods;
when widespread fame and praise are bestowed upon oneself,
therefore one does not desire the embroidered robes of others.
11.18 Mèngzǐ said:
"The victory of benevolence over non-benevolence
is like water overcoming fire.
Now those who practice benevolence
are like using one cup of water to save a cartload of burning firewood;"
If it does not extinguish,
it is said that water cannot overcome fire,
this again aligns with the extreme of unkindness,
and in the end, it is bound to perish."
11.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"The five grains
are the finest of all seeds.
But if they are not ripe,
they are not as good as the tares.
So with regard to benevolence, it likewise depends on its being brought to maturity."
11.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"When Yì taught people archery,
he always aimed at drawing the bow to the full;
learners must also aim at drawing the bow to the full.
A master craftsman instructs others
always using the compass and square;
learners must also use the compass and square."
12.1 A man from Rèn asked Wūlúzǐ:
"Which is more important, propriety or food?"
He replied:
"Propriety is more important."
"Which is more important, sex or propriety?"
He replied:
"Propriety is more important."
He said:
"If one eats according to the rites, one will starve to death;
if one does not eat according to the rites, one will get food.
Must one then necessarily follow the rites?
If one goes in person to meet the bride, one will not get a wife;
if one does not go in person to meet the bride, one will get a wife.
Must one then necessarily go in person to meet the bride?"
Wūlúzǐ could not reply.
The next day he went to Zōu
and told Mencius about it.
Mencius said,
"What difficulty is there in answering this?
If you do not measure at the same level,
but compare only the ends,
a piece of wood an inch square can be made taller than a high tower."
When we say that gold is heavier than feathers,
do we mean that one hook of gold
is heavier than a cartload of feathers?
If you compare the importance of food
with the minor aspects of ritual,
why stop at saying merely that food is important?
If you compare the importance of sex
with the minor aspects of ritual,
why stop at saying merely that sex is important?
Wǎng yìng zhī yuē:
'Zhěn xiōng zhī bì ér duó zhī shí,
zé dé shí;
bù zhěn,
zé bùdé shí,
zé jiāng zhěn zhī hū?
Yú dōng jiā qiáng ér lōu qí chǔzǐ,
zé dé qī;
bù lōu,
zé bùdé qī;
zé jiāng lōu zhī hū?'"
12.2 Cáo Jiāo asked:
"Everyone can become a Yáo or a Shùn,
is that true?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yes."
"Jiāo has heard that King Wén was ten chǐ tall,
and Tāng was nine chǐ tall.
Now Jiāo is nine chǐ four cùn tall,
yet only eats grain and does nothing more.
How can I become like them?"
He said:
"What is there to this?
Just do it, that's all.
If there is a person here
whose strength cannot overcome a single chick,
then he is considered a weak person;
if he says he can lift a hundred jun,
then he is considered a strong person.
Therefore, to lift the burden of Wū Huò,
this is simply to be Wū Huò, that's all.
Is it that one is troubled by being unable to do it?
It is simply not doing it.
Walking slowly behind one's elders
is called fraternal duty;
walking quickly ahead of one's elders
is called lack of fraternal duty.
Walking slowly—
is it something people cannot do?
It is what they do not do.
The way of Yáo and Shùn
is nothing but filial piety and fraternal duty.
If you wear the clothes of Yáo,
recite the words of Yáo,
and carry out the actions of Yáo,
then you are simply Yáo.
If you wear Jié's clothes,
recite Jié's words,
and follow Jié's actions,
then you are simply Jié.
He said:
"If I can get an audience with Lord Zōu,
I may borrow lodging,
and wish to stay and receive instruction at your gate."
The reply was:
"The Way is like a great road,
how could it be difficult to know?
The fault lies with people not seeking it.
You should return and seek it,
and you will have more than enough teachers."
12.3 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying,
"Master Gāo says:
'Xiǎopán'
is the poem of a small man."
Mencius said,
"How does he say so?"
He replied,
"It is querulous."
He said:
"How inflexible
is Gāo's interpretation of the Odes!
Suppose there is a man here,
and a man from Yuè draws his bow to shoot him;
he would speak of it with smiles and laughter.
There is no other reason
but that the man is a stranger to him.
When his elder brother bent his bow to shoot,
he would shed tears and persuade him;
for no other reason
than their close kinship.
The resentment in "Xiǎo Biàn"
arises from familial affection.
Cherishing one's kin
is benevolence.
How rigid indeed
is old Gāo's interpretation of the Odes!"
Someone asked:
"Why does 'The Gentle Wind' contain no resentment?"
The reply was:
"In 'The Gentle Wind',
the parent's fault was minor;
in 'The Minor Odes of the Kingdom',
the parent's fault was major.
If one does not resent a parent's major fault,
this means growing more distant;
if one resents a parent's minor fault,
this shows one cannot be stirred to anger."
Being distant and estranged is unfilial;
being unable to be provoked or irritated is also unfilial.
Confucius said:
'Shùn was the most filial,
at fifty he still yearned for his parents.'
12.4 Sòng Kēng was about to go to Chǔ,
when Mèngzǐ met him at Shíqiū,
and said:
"Where are you going, sir?"
He said:
"I have heard that Qin and Chu are at war;
I will go to see the King of Chu
and persuade him to cease hostilities.
If the King of Chu is not pleased,
I will go to see the King of Qin
and persuade him to cease hostilities.
I expect to find agreement with one of the two kings."
He said:
"Kē, I ask not for the details,
but wish to hear the main point.
How shall I persuade him?"
The reply was:
"I shall speak of its disadvantages."
Mèngzǐ said:
"The gentleman's ambition is indeed great,
but the gentleman's approach is unacceptable.
By persuading the kings of Qín and Chǔ with profit,
if the kings of Qín and Chǔ, pleased with profit,
withdraw their armies,
then the officers and soldiers of these armies
will also delight in withdrawal and be pleased with profit."
A minister
who serves his lord with self-interest in mind,
a son
who serves his father with self-interest in mind,
a younger brother
who serves his elder brother with self-interest in mind—
this causes ruler and minister,
father and son, elder and younger brother
to ultimately abandon benevolence and righteousness,
interacting with each other motivated by self-interest.
Yet, for a state not to perish under such circumstances has never been possible.
The gentleman used benevolence and righteousness to persuade the kings of Qín and Chǔ,
and the kings of Qín and Chǔ were pleased with benevolence and righteousness,
thereby disbanding the armies of the three forces.
Thus, the officers of the three forces were happy to disband
and delighted in benevolence and righteousness.
As a minister,
one should embrace benevolence and righteousness to serve his sovereign;
as a son,
one should embrace benevolence and righteousness to serve his father;
as a younger brother,
one should embrace benevolence and righteousness to serve his elder brother,
If sovereign and minister,
father and son,
brothers discard profit
and embrace benevolence and righteousness in their interactions,
yet one who does not become a true king
has never existed.
Why must we speak of profit?"
12.5 Mèngzǐ resided in Zōu,
Jì Rén was acting ruler of Rèn,
and sent gifts to establish relations.
Mèngzǐ received them but did not acknowledge them.
When he was in Pínglù,
Chǔ Zǐ was prime minister,
and sent gifts to establish relations,
Mèngzǐ received them but did not acknowledge them.
Another day, when traveling from Zōu to Rèn,
he saw Jìzǐ;
when traveling from Pínglù to Qí,
he did not see Chǔzǐ.
Wūlúzǐ delightedly said:
"I've found an opening."
He asked:
"When you went to Rèn, you saw Jìzǐ;
when you went to Qí, you did not see Chǔzǐ,
was it because he was prime minister?"
He said:
"No;
the Book of Documents states:
'In sacrifices, the ceremonies are most important.
If the ceremonies are not sufficient for the offerings,
it is said there is no sacrifice,
because the mind is not devoted to the sacrifice.'
This is because it does not constitute a proper sacrifice."
Wūlúzǐ was pleased.
Someone asked him about it.
Wūlúzǐ said:
"Jìzǐ could not go to Zōu,
but Chǔzǐ managed to reach Pínglù."
12.6 Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Those who prioritize reputation and achievement
act for others;
those who put reputation and achievement last
act for themselves.
You, sir, hold one of the three high ministerial positions,
yet your reputation and achievements
have not benefited either ruler or people when you leave.
Would a truly benevolent person necessarily act like this?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Jū xià wèi,
bù yǐ xián shì bùxiào zhě,
Bóyí yě;
wǔ jiù Tāng,
wǔ jiù Jié zhě,
Yīyǐn yě;
bù wù wū jūn,
bù cí xiǎo guān zhě,
Liǔxià Huì yě.
The three masters followed different paths,
yet their direction was the same.
What is this sameness?
It is said:
It is benevolence.
A noble person also embodies benevolence and that is all.
Why must they be the same?
It was said:
"During the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyízǐ was in charge of government,
with Zǐliǔ and Zǐsī as ministers,
yet Lǔ's territorial diminishment became even more severe;
if so, then worthies are of no benefit to the state!"
He said:
"Yú failed to employ Bǎilǐ Xī and perished,
while Duke Mù of Qín employed him and became hegemon.
Not employing the worthy leads to ruin—
how could mere diminution be the result?"
He said:
"In ancient times,
when Wáng Bào lived by the Qí River,
the region west of the Yellow River became skilled at singing;
when Mián Jū lived in Gāotáng,
the region east of Qí became skilled at songs;
the wives of Huá Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng
were skilled at weeping for their husbands,
and thus transformed the customs of the state.
What is within
will inevitably manifest without.
For one who engages in affairs
yet achieves no merit,
I, Kūn, have never witnessed such a case.
Therefore, there are no truly worthy individuals;
if there were, I, Kūn, would certainly recognize them.
It is said:
"When Confucius was the Minister of Crime of Lǔ,
he was not employed,
so he followed along to a sacrifice,
but the roasted meat did not arrive,
and he left without even taking off his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not know thought it was because of the meat,
but those who knew thought it was because of the lack of propriety."
Thus Confucius wished to leave on account of a minor offense,
not wanting to depart without justification.
What the noble man does,
is certainly beyond the understanding of ordinary people."
12.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"The Five Hegemons are
the sinners of the Three Sovereigns;
the feudal lords of today are
the sinners of the Five Hegemons;
the high officials of today are
the sinners of the feudal lords of today."
When the Son of Heaven visited the feudal lords, it was called a tour of inspection;
when the feudal lords attended court before the Son of Heaven, it was called reporting on their administration.
In spring, he inspected the plowing to supply what was deficient;
in autumn, he inspected the harvest to aid those in need.
When one enters its borders,
the land is cultivated,
the fields are well managed,
the elderly are cared for and the worthy are honored,
with outstanding talents in positions of authority,
then there is cause for reward;
the reward is with land.
Upon entering its borders,
the land is barren and desolate,
the elderly are neglected and the virtuous lost,
with extortionate officials in positions of power,
then there is cause for reprimand.
One failure to attend court,
leads to the reduction of their rank;
a second failure to attend court,
results in the reduction of their territory;
a third failure to attend court,
then the six armies are moved against them.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven punishes but does not attack,
while the feudal lords attack but do not punish.
The Five Hegemons,
dragged the feudal lords to attack other feudal lords,
hence it is said:
'The Five Hegemons
are the offenders against the Three Sovereigns.'
Among the Five Hegemons,
Duke Huán was the most illustrious.
At the assembly of Kuíqiū,
the feudal lords bound the sacrificial animal and placed the covenant upon it without smearing blood on their lips.
The first injunction stated:
'Punish the unfilial,
do not change the appointed heir,
do not make a concubine your principal wife.'
The second command said:
'Respect the worthy and nurture the talented,
to make manifest those who have virtue.'
The third command said:
'Revere the aged and be kind to the young,
do not neglect guests and travelers.'
The fourth command said:
'Scholars shall not hold hereditary offices,
official duties shall not be concurrently held,
selecting scholars must ensure competence,
do not arbitrarily execute high officials.'
The fifth command states:
'Do not unjustly divert watercourses,
do not obstruct the purchase of grain,
and do not have enfeoffments without reporting them.'
It says:
'All of us who are in this alliance,
after having sworn the covenant,
shall return to good relations.'
The feudal lords of today
all violate these five prohibitions,
hence it is said:
"The feudal lords of today
are the offenders against the Five Hegemons."
To prolong the ruler's faults
is a minor offense,
but to pander to the ruler's faults
is a major offense.
Nowadays, all high officials pander to the ruler's faults,
hence it is said:
'The high officials of today
are the offenders against the feudal lords of today.'
12.8 The state of Lǔ wanted to make Shènzǐ a general.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To use the people without instructing them
is called bringing disaster upon the people.
Those who bring disaster upon the people
would not be tolerated in the age of Yáo and Shùn.
Even if in one battle you defeated Qí
and thereby possessed Nányáng,
still it would not be acceptable."
Shènzǐ suddenly became displeased and said:
"This is something Huálí does not understand."
He said:
"Let me explain it clearly to you.
The territory of the Son of Heaven is a thousand li square;
if it is not a thousand li,
it is insufficient to host the feudal lords."
The domain of the feudal lords was a hundred li square;
if it were not a hundred li,
it would not be sufficient to preserve the statutes and records of the ancestral temple.
When the Duke of Zhōu was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
it was a hundred li square;
the land was not insufficient,
yet he limited it to a hundred li.
When Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
it was also a territory of one hundred square lǐ;
the land was not insufficient,
yet he was limited to one hundred lǐ.
Now Lǔ has five territories each of a hundred lǐ square.
Do you think that if a true king were to arise,
would Lǔ be among those whose territory would be reduced,
or among those whose territory would be increased?
Merely taking from that one to give to this one
is something even the benevolent would not do,
how much more so is it to kill people in order to seek it?
A gentleman's service to his ruler
lies in guiding him toward the right path,
with the sole aim of benevolence.
12.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who serve rulers today
all say,
'I can expand territory for my ruler,
and fill up treasuries.'
What are called good ministers today,
were called plunderers of the people in ancient times.
If a ruler does not incline toward the Way,
does not set his mind on benevolence,
yet you seek to enrich him,
this is enriching a tyrant like Jié.
"I can form alliances for the ruler,
and ensure victory in every battle."
What are now called good ministers,
were in ancient times called plunderers of the people.
If a ruler does not incline toward the Way,
nor set his mind on benevolence,
yet seeks to have others fight strenuously for him,
this is to assist a Jié.
Following the present path,
without changing the current customs,
even if one were to give him the whole world,
he could not maintain it for a single morning."
12.10 Bái Guī said:
"I wish to take one in twenty,
how would that be?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Your way
is the way of the Mò.
In a country of ten thousand households,
if only one man makes pottery, can it suffice?"
He said:
"It cannot,
for the vessels would not be enough for use."
He said:
"In the land of the Mò,
the five grains do not grow,
only millet grows there;
there are no city walls,
palaces,
ancestral temples,
or the rituals of sacrifice,
no gifts of silk and feasts among feudal lords,
no officials and functionaries,
thus a tax of one in twenty is sufficient."
Now dwelling in the Central Kingdom,
abandoning human relationships,
lacking noble persons,
how can this be permissible?
Even with few potters,
it would still be inadequate to govern a state,
how much more so without noble persons?
Those who wish to make it lighter than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are great Mò and small Mò;
those who wish to make it heavier than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are great Jié and small Jié.
12.11 Bái Guī said:
"My method of managing water is better than Yǔ's."
Mèngzǐ said:
"You are mistaken.
Yǔ's management of water
followed the way of water,
therefore Yǔ made the four seas the reservoir,
but now you make neighboring states your reservoir.
When water flows countercurrent, it is called jiàngshuǐ;
jiàngshuǐ means
floodwater,
which is detested by benevolent people.
You, my friend, are mistaken.
12.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"If a gentleman is not sincere,
how can he maintain steadfastness?"
12.13 The state of Lǔ wanted to make Yuèzhèngzǐ administer the government.
Mèngzǐ said:
"I heard of this,
and was so pleased I could not sleep."
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Is Yuèzhèngzǐ strong?"
The reply was:
"No."
"Has he wisdom and foresight?"
The reply was:
"No."
"Is it because you have learned much?"
He replied,
"No."
"Then why are you so pleased that you cannot sleep?"
He said,
"It is because he is a man who loves goodness."
"Is loving goodness sufficient?"
He said:
"If one is fond of goodness, he excels all under heaven,
let alone the state of Lǔ?
If one is truly fond of goodness,
then within the four seas
all will think nothing of traveling a thousand lǐ
to come and inform him of goodness;
if one is not fond of goodness,
then people will say: 'Hèhè,'
'I already know all that.'"
A harsh voice and an angry countenance
keep others at a distance of a thousand miles.
When gentlemen stop at a thousand miles away,
then slanderous, flattering, and fawning people will arrive.
If one lives with slanderous, flattering, and fawning people,
even if the state desires order,
can it be achieved?
12.14 Chénzǐ said:
"Under what circumstances did the gentlemen of antiquity
take office?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"There are three cases for accepting office,
and three cases for leaving it."
If one greets him with respect and courtesy;
and, speaking, is about to act on his words,
then approach him.
If the courtesy has not diminished,
but his words are not acted upon,
then leave him.
Next,
although one has not yet put his words into practice,
if he is welcomed with respect and according to the rites,
then one should approach him.
When the courtesy declines,
then one should leave him.
Beneath him,
he had no food in the morning,
no food in the evening,
and hunger prevented him from leaving his home.
The ruler, hearing of this,
said:
'On the one hand, I am unable to put his principles into practice,
and on the other, I cannot follow his advice.
To let him suffer hunger in my land
brings me shame.'
To be aided by Zhōu,
is also acceptable,
merely to escape death."
12.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"Shùn arose from the fields;
Fù Yuè was elevated from the building sites;
Jiāo Gé was elevated from among the fish and salt traders;
Guǎn Yíwú was elevated from the hands of the jailers;
Sūnshū Áo was elevated from the sea;
Bǎilǐ Xī was elevated from the marketplace."
Therefore, when Heaven is about to confer a great responsibility on any man,
it will first exercise his mind with suffering,
and his muscles and bones with toil.
It will expose his body to hunger,
and subject him to extreme poverty.
It will confound his undertakings.
By all these methods it will stimulate his mind, harden his nature,
and improve wherever he is incompetent.
People often err,
and then are able to reform;
distressed in mind,
and perplexed in thoughts,
then they arise to effort;
shown in the countenance,
and expressed in words,
then they are understood.
When a state lacks legal experts and loyal ministers within,
and faces no hostile states or external threats without,
it will inevitably perish.
From this we understand that life springs from sorrow and calamity,
while death lurks in ease and pleasure."
12.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are also many methods in teaching.
When I disdain to instruct someone,
that in itself is a form of instruction."
13.1 Mèngzǐ said:
"He who has fully developed his mind
knows his nature.
Knowing his nature,
he knows Heaven.
To preserve one's mind
and nourish one's nature
is the way to serve Heaven."
Whether one dies young or lives long is not a matter of doubt;
one cultivates oneself and awaits the outcome,
this is the way to establish one's destiny.
13.2 Mèngzǐ said:
"Nothing is not destiny,
accept its proper course with compliance;
therefore, one who understands destiny
does not stand beneath a dangerous wall.
Those who die having exhausted their path,
it is proper destiny;
those who die in shackles,
it is not proper destiny."
13.3 Mèngzǐ said:
"Seek and you will obtain it;
neglect and you will lose it.
This shows that seeking is beneficial to obtaining,
for what is sought lies within ourselves.
Though the seeking be according to the proper way,
the obtaining depends on the decree of Heaven.
This shows that seeking is of no benefit to obtaining,
for what is sought lies outside ourselves."
13.4 Mèngzǐ said:
"All things are complete within us.
Turning within and being sincere,
there is no greater joy than this.
Striving to practice reciprocity in conduct,
there is no closer way to seek benevolence."
13.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are those who act without understanding,
practice without examination,
and follow the path all their lives without knowing the Way—
these are the multitude."
13.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"One must not be without shame.
The shame of being without shame,
is indeed shameless."
13.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Shame is of great importance to a person.
Those who engage in cunning and deceitful schemes
have no use for shame.
If one feels no shame at not being equal to others,
how can one ever become their equal?"
13.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"The wise kings of antiquity
loved goodness and forgot their power;
the worthy scholars of antiquity
how could they be otherwise?
They delighted in their principles
and forgot the power of others,
so unless kings and dukes paid them utmost respect and full courtesy,
they could not frequently see them.
Even seeing them could not be done frequently,
how much less could they be made ministers?"
13.9 Mèngzǐ said to Sòng Gōujiàn:
"Do you enjoy traveling?
Let me tell you about traveling.
When people understand you, remain content;
when people do not understand you, remain content."
Sòng Gōujiàn asked:
"How can one achieve such contentment?"
It is said:
"Honoring virtue and delighting in righteousness,
one may then be content and self-possessed.
Thus, a scholar in poverty does not abandon righteousness,
nor in success depart from the Way.
Not abandoning righteousness in poverty,
he thereby retains his integrity;
not departing from the Way in success,
he thus does not disappoint the people.
The ancients,
when they realized their aspirations,
bestowed blessings on the people;
when they did not realize their aspirations,
they cultivated their personal lives and made themselves manifest to the world.
In obscurity, they perfected their own persons;
in prominence, they perfected the whole world."
13.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who awaken only after King Wén are
ordinary people.
As for the outstanding individuals,
they awaken even without King Wén."
13.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"If you add to him the wealth of the houses of Hán and Wèi,
and he still views himself with humility,
then he surpasses others by far."
13.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"Employ the people with the way of ease,
and though they toil, they will not complain.
Kill the people with the way of life,
Even in death, I bear no grudge against my executioner.
13.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"The people of a hegemon
are cheerful and pleased,
while the people of a true king
are content and at ease.
They can be put to death without resentment,
benefited without feeling indebted,
and daily advance in goodness
without knowing who makes them do so."
Where the gentleman passes, transformation occurs;
where he abides, spiritual influence remains;
above and below, he flows in the same stream as Heaven and Earth.
How can this be said to be a small supplement?"
13.14 Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Benevolent words
are not as deeply moving to people as benevolent reputation;
good governance
is not as effective in winning the people as good education.
Good governance makes people fear it;
good education makes people love it.
Good governance gains the people's wealth;
good education gains the people's hearts."
13.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"That which people are capable of without learning
is their innate ability;
that which they know without reflection
is their innate knowledge.
Young children
all know to love their parents;
when they grow up,
they all know to respect their elder brothers.
To love one's parents is
benevolence;
to respect one's elders is
righteousness.
There is no other reason—
these principles extend throughout the world.
13.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"When Shùn dwelt deep in the mountains,
he lived among the trees and rocks,
and roamed with deer and swine.
The difference between him and the wild men of the mountains
was slight;
but when he heard one good word,
saw one good deed,
it was like a river breaking its banks,
so overflowing that nothing could stop it."
13.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"Do not do what you should not do,
and do not desire what you should not desire.
That is all there is to it."
13.18 Mèngzǐ said:
"People's possession of virtue, wisdom, skill, and knowledge
constantly exists in affliction and distress.
Only the solitary minister and the concubine's son,
their hearts are anxious with peril,
their thoughts of calamity are profound,
therefore they become enlightened."
13.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are those who serve a ruler,
serving this ruler
merely to seek favor and pleasure;
there are ministers who stabilize the state,
who take delight in bringing stability to the state;
there are those who are heaven's people,
who wait until their principles can be practiced throughout the world
and then practice them;
there are the great personages,
who rectify themselves and thereby all things are rectified."
13.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"The noble man has three delights,
and ruling the world is not among them.
That both parents are alive,
and brothers are well without mishap,
is the first delight;
that looking up, one has no shame before Heaven,
and looking down, no blush before others,
is the second delight;
To obtain the world's outstanding talents
and educate them
is the third joy.
A gentleman has three joys,
and ruling the world is not among them.
13.21 Mèngzǐ said:
"Vast territories and numerous people
are what the noble person desires,
but his joy does not lie therein;
standing at the center of the world,
bringing stability to the people within the four seas,
the noble person finds joy in this,
but his true nature does not lie therein."
The nature of the noble person,
even when achieving great success, is not augmented by it,
and even when living in poverty, is not diminished by it,
because it is firmly established.
The nature of the noble person,
with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom rooted in the heart,
manifests its vitality
as a pure radiance, visible in the face,
overflowing in the back,
extending to the four limbs,
and the four limbs express it without words.
13.22 Mencius said:
"Bóyí avoided Zhòu,
dwelling by the shores of the northern sea.
Hearing of King Wén's rise, he was stirred
and said:
'Why not go to him?
I have heard that the Earl of the West is good at caring for the elderly.'"
Tàigōng avoided Zhòu,
residing by the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Hearing of King Wén's rise,
he exclaimed:
"Why not return there?
I have heard that the Lord of the West excels at caring for the elderly."
When the world has one who excels at caring for the elderly,
then benevolent people consider him their refuge.
With a homestead of five mǔ,
planting mulberry trees along the walls,
and having women raise silkworms,
the elderly will have enough silk for clothing.
With five hens
and two sows,
if their breeding seasons are not missed,
the elderly will have enough meat without lack.
With a hundred-acre field,
a common man farming it,
a family of eight
can be free from hunger.
It is said that King Wén of Zhōu excelled in providing for the elderly,
by regulating their fields and homesteads,
teaching them planting and animal husbandry,
and guiding their wives and children
to care for their elders.
At fifty, without silk, one is not warm;
at seventy, without meat, one is not satisfied.
If not warm and not satisfied,
it is called suffering from cold and hunger.
Among King Wén's people,
there were no elders suffering from cold and hunger—
this is what it means."
13.23 Mèngzǐ said:
"Cultivate their fields well,
lighten their taxes and levies,
and the people can be made prosperous.
Eat according to the seasons,
use according to ritual,
and wealth will be more than enough."
Without water and fire, the people cannot survive.
When knocking on someone's door at dusk
to ask for water and fire,
there is none who will not give them—
such is their abundance.
When a sage governs the world,
he ensures that grains are as plentiful as water and fire.
If grains are as abundant as water and fire,
how could the people be lacking in benevolence?
13.24 Mencius said:
"When Confucius ascended the Eastern Mountain,
he considered Lǔ small;
when he ascended Mount Tài,
he considered the world small.
Therefore, one who has seen the ocean finds it difficult to be impressed by other waters,
and one who has studied at the gate of a sage finds it difficult to be impressed by other words."
There is an art to observing water,
one must observe its waves.
The sun and moon have their brilliance,
and any crevice that can hold light will be illuminated.
Flowing water, as a substance,
does not advance until it fills the hollows;
the noble person's aspiration for the Way,
does not reach its goal until it is fully expressed.
13.25 Mèngzǐ said:
"He who rises at cockcrow
and diligently does good
is a follower of Shùn;
he who rises at cockcrow
and diligently seeks profit
is a follower of Zhí.
To know the difference between Shùn and Zhí,
there is no other way
but to distinguish between profit and good."
13.26 Mencius said:
"Yángzǐ advocates egoism.
He would not pluck out a single hair from his body
even if it would benefit the whole world.
Mòzǐ advocates universal love.
He would rub smooth his whole body from head to heel
if it would benefit the world.
Zǐmò holds to the middle course.
Holding to the middle course is close to being right.
To hold fast to the mean without exercising discretion
is like holding to one extreme.
The reason I dislike holding to one extreme
is that it injures the Way,
taking one point and neglecting all others."
13.27 Mèngzǐ said:
"The hungry find any food sweet,
the thirsty find any drink sweet;
this is because they have not attained the proper taste of food and drink,
but are harmed by hunger and thirst.
Is it only the mouth and belly that suffer from hunger and thirst?
The human mind also suffers harm.
