If one can prevent the harm of hunger and thirst from becoming harm to the mind,
then not being equal to others will not be a cause for worry."
13.28 Mèngzǐ said:
"Liǔxià Huì would not exchange his integrity
for the position of the Three Dukes."
13.29 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who act
are like digging a well;
if they dig nine fathoms
yet do not reach the spring,
it is still an abandoned well."
13.30 Mèngzǐ said:
"Yáo and Shùn
acted according to their nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
cultivated it in themselves;
the Five Hegemons
borrowed it.
If one borrows it for a long time without returning it,
how can one know it is not truly theirs?"
13.31 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Yī Yǐn said:
'I do not associate with the unrighteous.'
He exiled Tài Jiǎ to Tóng,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When Tài Jiǎ became virtuous,
he restored him,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When a worthy serves as a minister,
if his ruler is unworthy,
can he indeed be exiled?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Yǒu Yī Yǐn zhī zhì,
zé kě;
wú Yī Yǐn zhī zhì,
zé cuàn yě."
13.32 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'He does not eat the bread of idleness.'
Yet gentlemen do not farm and still eat—
why is this?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Jūnzǐ jū shì guó yě,
qí jūn yòng zhī,
zé ān fù zūn róng;
qí zǐdì cóng zhī,
zé xiào tì zhōng xìn.
'Bù sùcān xī',
shú dà yú shì?"
13.33 Prince Diàn asked:
"What does a scholar do?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Exalts his will."
He asked:
"What is meant by exalting one's will?"
He said:
"It is simply about benevolence and righteousness.
To kill an innocent person
is not benevolent;
to take what does not belong to you
is not righteous.
Where does one dwell?
In benevolence.
Where does the path lie?
In righteousness.
Dwelling in benevolence and following righteousness,
the affairs of the great person are complete."
13.34 Mencius said:
"Zhòngzǐ, if given the state of Qí
unjustly, would not accept it.
Everyone believes this of him,
but this is the righteousness of refusing
a basket of rice and a bowl of soup."
What greater misfortune is there for a person than to lack the bonds of parents and relatives,
sovereign and minister,
superior and inferior?
To trust in greater matters based on
their minor aspects,
how can this be acceptable?"
13.35 Táo Yìng wèn yuē:
"Shùn wéi tiānzǐ,
Gāo Yáo wéi shì,
Gǔ Sǒu shā rén,
zé rú zhī hé?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Zhí zhī ér yǐ yǐ."
"Rán zé Shùn bù jìn yú?"
He said:
"How could Shùn prevent it?
It was something he had received from Yao."
"Then what should Shùn have done?"
He replied:
"Shùn would have regarded abandoning the empire
as discarding a worn-out sandal.
He would have secretly carried his father on his back and fled,
dwelling along the seacoast,
joyful throughout his life,
happy and forgetting about the empire."
13.36 Mencius traveled from Fàn to Qí,
and upon seeing the king of Qí's son from afar,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Residence transforms the demeanor,
nourishment transforms the physique,
how great is the influence of residence!
Is he not also a man's son like any other?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Wángzǐ's palaces, carriages, horses, and clothing
are mostly the same as others',
yet the prince is as he is
because his dwelling makes him so;
how much more so for one who dwells in the broadest dwelling under heaven?
When the lord of Lǔ went to Sòng,
he called out at the Diézé Gate.
The guard said:
"This is not my lord,
why does his voice so resemble my lord's?"
This is for no other reason
than that their dwellings are similar."
13.37 Mèngzǐ yuē:
“Shí ér fú ài,
shǐ jiāo zhī yě;
ài ér bú jìng,
shòu chù zhī yě.
Gōngjìng zhě,
bì zhī wèi jiāng zhě yě.
Gōngjìng ér wú shí,
jūnzǐ bù kě xū jū.”
13.38 Mèngzǐ said:
"Physical form and appearance
are natural endowments;
only the sage can fully realize their potential through these forms."
13.39 King Xuān of Qí wanted to shorten the mourning period.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Would observing a one-year mourning period
still be better than abolishing it altogether?"
Mencius said:
"This is like someone twisting his elder brother's arm,
and you telling him
'just do it gently and slowly,'
when you should instead be teaching him filial piety and fraternal duty."
A prince had a mother who died,
and his tutor requested for him several months of mourning.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"What about such a case?"
The reply was:
"This was a case where wishing to complete the mourning was impossible.
Even adding one day
is better than having none,
this refers to those who, when nothing prevents them, still do not observe mourning."
13.40 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are five ways in which the superior man teaches:
Some he transforms like timely rain;
Some he perfects in virtue;
Some he develops their talents;
Some he answers their questions;
Some he sets an example for private cultivation.
These five ways
are how the superior man teaches."
13.41 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"The Way is lofty and beautiful,
like ascending to heaven,
it seems unattainable;
why not make it something that can be reached
so that people may strive for it daily?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"A great craftsman does not alter or abandon the marking line for an unskilled worker,
Yì does not change his draw strength for a poor archer.
The gentleman draws the bow but does not release the arrow,
yet it seems to leap forward.
He stands in the middle of the path,
and those who are capable follow him."
13.42 Mèngzǐ said:
"When the Way prevails in the world,
one follows the Way with one's person;
when the Way does not prevail in the world,
one sacrifices one's person for the Way;
I have never heard of sacrificing the Way to accommodate people."
13.43 Gōngdūzǐ said:
"Téng Gēng, being at the gate,
seemed to be among those to be treated with courtesy,
yet you did not respond to him.
Why is this?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Xié guì ér wèn,
xié xián ér wèn,
xié zhǎng ér wèn,
xié yǒu xūn láo ér wèn,
xié gù ér wèn,
jiē suǒ bù dá yě.
Téng Gèng yǒu èr yān."
13.44 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who stop where they should not stop
will stop at nothing.
Those who are negligent where they should be generous
will be negligent in everything.
Those who advance too hastily
will retreat just as quickly."
13.45 Mèngzǐ said:
"The gentleman, regarding things,
loves them but is not benevolent toward them;
regarding the people,
he is benevolent toward them but does not feel affection for them.
He feels affection for his family and is benevolent toward the people;
he is benevolent toward the people and loves things."
13.46 Mencius said:
"The wise have nothing they do not know,
but they consider urgent tasks as the priority;
the benevolent have no one they do not love,
but they consider attending to the worthy as the urgent task.
Yáo and Shùn's wisdom did not extend to all things,
because they gave priority to the most urgent matters.
Yáo and Shùn's benevolence
did not extend to loving all people indiscriminately,
but prioritized their own kin and the virtuous.
If one cannot observe the three-year mourning period,
yet scrutinizes the finer details of the three-month and five-month mourning rites;
if one gobbles food and gulps drink,
yet inquires about not using teeth to bite meat,
this is called not knowing what is essential.
14.1 Mencius said:
"How unkind
King Hui of Liáng was!
The kind
extend from those they love to those they do not love,
while the unkind
extend from those they do not love to those they love."
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"What does this mean?"
"King Huì of Liàng, for the sake of territory,
ruined his people by waging war,
suffered a great defeat,
and intended to resume it,
fearing he might not prevail,
thus drove his beloved sons and brothers to die for it.
This is what is called
extending from what he did not love to what he loved."
14.2 Mèngzǐ said:
"In the Spring and Autumn period there were no righteous wars.
Some were better than others,
that is all.
A punitive expedition
is when the superior attacks the inferior;
states of equal rank do not launch punitive expeditions against each other."
14.3 Mèngzǐ said:
"If one were to believe everything in the Book of Documents,
it would be better not to have the Book of Documents.
In the case of the 'Wǔ Chéng' chapter,
I accept only two or three passages.
A benevolent man has no enemy under heaven.
When the most benevolent attacks the most unbenevolent,
how could the blood have flowed so as to float the pestles?"
14.4 Mencius said:
"There are those who say:
'I am skilled at deploying troops,
I am skilled at waging war.'
This is a great crime.
If a ruler loves benevolence,
he will have no enemy in the world.
When he campaigns south, the northern tribes complain;
when he campaigns east, the western tribes complain,
saying:
'Why does he put us last?'
When King Wǔ launched his campaign against the Yīn,
he had three hundred armored chariots
and three thousand tiger warriors.
The king declared:
"Do not fear!
We come to bring you peace,
not to oppose the common people."
They kowtowed till their foreheads hit the ground like crumbling horns.
The word 'correction' means to rectify.
Each desires to rectify himself;
what need is there for war?"
14.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"A carpenter or wheelwright
can give others the compass and square,
but cannot make them skillful."
14.6 Mencius said:
"When Shùn ate parched grain and wild herbs,
it was as if he would do so for life;
but when he became the Son of Heaven,
dressed in embroidered robes,
playing the qin,
with the two daughters
attending him, it was as if these were his natural possessions."
14.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Now I understand
the gravity of killing someone's relative:
if you kill someone's father,
others will kill your father;
if you kill someone's elder brother,
others will kill your elder brother.
Thus it is not that you kill them yourself,
but it is almost the same."
14.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"In ancient times, the establishment of passes
was intended to guard against violence;
nowadays, the establishment of passes
is intended to perpetrate violence."
14.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"If one does not practice the Way personally,
it will not be followed even by his wife and children;
if one employs others not in accordance with the Way,
he cannot make even his wife and children follow it."
14.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who are abundant in wealth
cannot be ruined even in a famine year;
those who are abundant in virtue
cannot be corrupted even in an evil age."
14.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"A man fond of fame
can yield a state of a thousand chariots;
but if he is not that kind of man,
the sight of a basket of rice and a bowl of soup will show in his countenance."
14.12 Mencius said:
"If the benevolent and worthy are not trusted,
then the state will be empty;
if there is no propriety and righteousness,
then the high and low will be in disorder;
if there is no governance,
then resources and expenditures will be insufficient."
14.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"There have been cases
of the unvirtuous gaining a state;
but
there has never been a case of the unvirtuous gaining the empire."
14.14 Mencius said:
"The people are the most important,
the altars of the gods of earth and grain come next,
and the ruler is of lesser importance.
Therefore, he who gains the allegiance of the multitude of the people becomes the Son of Heaven,
he who gains the allegiance of the Son of Heaven becomes a feudal lord,
he who gains the allegiance of a feudal lord becomes a minister.
If the feudal lords endanger the altars of soil and grain,
they should be replaced.
When the sacrificial animals have been prepared,
the sacrificial grains have been cleansed,
and the sacrifices are offered at the proper times,
yet there are still droughts or floods,
then the altars of soil and grain should be replaced.
14.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"The sage is
the teacher for a hundred generations;
Bóyí and Liǔxià Huì were such men.
Therefore, those who have heard of the character of Bóyí,
the corrupt become pure,
and the timid become resolute;
Those who hear of the virtues of Liǔxià Huì,
the mean become generous,
the narrow-minded become broad-minded.
He rose up more than a hundred generations ago,
yet those who hear of him a hundred generations later are all inspired to rise up.
If he were not a sage, could he be like this?
How much more so for those who received his personal instruction?
14.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence is
humanity.
Combining these in speech,
this is the Way."
14.17 Mencius said:
"When Confucius left the state of Lǔ,
he said:
'Slowly, slowly I make my departure—
this is the way to leave the state of one's parents.'
When he left the state of Qí,
he departed immediately after rinsing the rice—
this is the way to leave a foreign state."
14.18 Mencius said:
"The gentleman's distress between Chén and Cài
was because he had no interaction with either the high or the low."
14.19 Mò Jī said:
"Jī is greatly disapproved of by mouths."
Mèngzǐ said:
"It does no harm.
A scholar dislikes this multitude of mouths."
The Book of Songs says:
"Anxious is my heart,
resented by the petty crowd."
This refers to Confucius.
"He did not vent his anger,
nor did he lose his reputation."
This refers to King Wén.
14.20 Mencius said:
"The wise instruct others
with their own clarity to make them clear;
nowadays people try to make others clear
with their own confusion."
14.21 Mencius said to Gāozǐ:
"The narrow path over the mountain, when
persistently used becomes a road;
when left unused for a while,
it gets blocked by wild grass.
Now wild grass has blocked your heart."
14.22 Gāo Zǐ said:
"Yǔ's music
is superior to King Wén's music."
Mèngzǐ said:
"How do you argue this?"
He replied:
"By the worn-out bell clapper."
Mèngzǐ said:
"How is that sufficient?
The ruts at the city gate -
are they made by the strength of two horses?"
14.23 The state of Qí suffered a famine.
Chén Zhēn said:
"All the people of the state thought that you, Master,
would again request the opening of the Táng granary for them,
but I am afraid it cannot be done again."
Mèngzǐ said:
"This is to be Féng Fù.
There was a man of Jìn named Féng Fù,
who was good at fighting tigers,
and finally became a virtuous man.
He went to the countryside,
where a crowd was chasing a tiger.
The tiger stood at bay in a mountain recess,
and no one dared to approach it.
Upon seeing Féng Fù,
he hurried forward to greet him.
Féng Fù rolled up his sleeves and alighted from the carriage.
The crowd was pleased with him,
but those who considered themselves scholars laughed at him.
14.24 Mèngzǐ said:
"The mouth's desire for flavors,
the eyes' desire for colors,
the ears' desire for sounds,
the nose's desire for smells,
the four limbs' desire for ease and comfort -
these are matters of nature,
but they are also subject to fate.
The noble person does not call them matters of nature."
Benevolence in the relationship between father and son,
righteousness in the relationship between ruler and minister,
propriety in the relationship between host and guest,
wisdom in the relationship between the worthy,
and the sage's relationship with the Way of Heaven—
these are all matters of destiny.
Yet there is also nature involved,
so the noble person does not simply attribute them to destiny.
14.25 Hào Shēng Bùhài asked, saying:
"What sort of person is Yuèzhèngzǐ?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"He is a good man,
a sincere man."
"What is meant by 'good'?
What is meant by 'sincere'?"
He said:
"Desirable is called good,
having it in oneself is called true,
being filled with it is called beautiful,
being filled with it and having radiance is called great,
being great and transforming with it is called sage,
being sage and unknowable is called divine.
Yuèzhèngzǐ
is between the second
and below the fourth."
14.26 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who flee from the Mohists inevitably turn to the Yangists,
and those who flee from the Yangists inevitably turn to the Confucians.
When they turn,
simply accept them.
Those who now debate with the Yangists and Mohists
are like chasing a stray pig:
after it has already entered its pen,
they still go and tie it up."
14.27 Mèngzǐ said:
"There is the levy of cloth and silk,
the levy of grain and rice,
and the levy of labor service.
The noble man employs one of these,
and postpones the other two.
If he employs two of them,
the people will have starvation deaths;
if he employs all three,
fathers and sons will be separated."
14.28 Mèngzǐ said:
"The treasures of a feudal lord are three:
land, people, and governance.
He who treasures pearls and jade,
calamity will surely reach his person."
14.29 Penchéng Kuò took office in Qí,
Mèngzǐ said:
"Penchéng Kuò is doomed!"
Penchéng Kuò was killed,
and a disciple asked:
"How did you, Master, know that he would be killed?"
He replied:
"In his character,
he had minor talents,
but had not learned the great Way of the noble person;
this was enough to bring about his own death."
14.30 When Mencius went to Téng,
he lodged at the Upper Palace.
There was a pair of unfinished straw sandals on the window ledge,
but the keeper of the lodging could not find them when he searched for them.
Someone asked Mencius, saying,
"Is it thus that your followers pilfer?"
He said:
"Do you think he came to steal sandals?"
The reply was:
"Probably not."
"In establishing my school,
I do not pursue those who leave,
nor reject those who come.
If they come with such intention,
I simply accept them."
14.31 Mèngzǐ said:
"All people have things they cannot bear to do,
extending this to what they can bear
is benevolence;
all people have things they will not do,
extending this to what they will do,
is righteousness.
If one can fill the mind that desires not to harm others,
then benevolence becomes inexhaustible;
If a person can expand the mind that refrains from tunneling or climbing over walls,
then righteousness will be inexhaustible;
if a person can expand the reality of not accepting being addressed as "ěr" or "rǔ",
there will be no place he goes where he does not act righteously.
When a scholar speaks where he should not speak,
he is using speech to fish for something;
when he does not speak where he should speak,
he is using silence to fish for something—
these are both of the same category as tunneling or climbing over walls."
14.32 Mencius said:
"Words that are near at hand but carry far-reaching significance
are good words.
Principles that are simple to uphold yet widely applicable
are good principles.
The words of a noble person,
though not going beyond common matters,
contain the Way within them.
What the noble person upholds
is the cultivation of their own character,
and thereby the whole world is brought to order."
People make the mistake of abandoning their own fields
to weed the fields of others,
demanding much from others,
but imposing little upon themselves.
14.33 Mèngzǐ said:
"Yáo and Shùn
acted according to their nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
returned to it through self-cultivation.
One who in moving and bearing himself makes all his gestures and every turn of his body accord with the rules of propriety,
is an example of the highest degree of virtue.
To mourn for the dead with the most heartfelt grief,
is not for the sake of the living.
To keep persistently in the way of virtue without swerving from it,
is not with a view to emolument.
In his words to be always sincere,
is not in order to display correctness of conduct.
The superior man performs the law of right,
and only waits for the appointment of Heaven.
14.34 Mèngzǐ said:
"When speaking to great men,
one should look down upon them,
not viewing their imposing appearance.
Halls several ren high,
eaves extending several feet,
if I achieved my ambitions, I would not do this.
Food spread out over a square zhang,
with hundreds of serving concubines,
if I achieved my ambitions, I would not do this.
Indulging in extravagant drinking,
galloping about in hunting,
with a thousand chariots following behind—
were I to achieve my ambitions, I would not engage in such things.
What lies in others
are all things I do not pursue;
what resides within me
are all in accordance with the ancient ways.
Why then should I stand in awe of them?"
14.35 Mèngzǐ said:
"There is no better way to nourish the heart than to reduce desires.
If a person has few desires,
even if some qualities are lacking,
they will be few;
if a person has many desires,
even if some qualities are present,
they will be few."
14.36 Zēng Xī was fond of date-plums,
but Zēngzǐ could not bear to eat them.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying,
"Which is more delicious, minced meat and roast meat or date-plums?"
Mencius said,
"Minced meat and roast meat, of course!"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
"Then why did Zēngzǐ eat minced meat
but not eat date-plums?"
The reply was:
"Minced meat is what everyone enjoys,
date-plums were his personal preference.
We avoid using personal names but not surnames,
for surnames are shared by many,
while names belong to individuals alone."
14.37 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"When Confucius was in Chén,
he said,
'Why not return!
The young scholars of our party are ardent but rough;
they are ambitious and progressive,
yet they do not forget their original aspirations.'
When Confucius was in Chén,
why did he think of the ardent scholars of Lǔ?"
Mèngzǐ yuē:
"Kǒngzǐ
'bùdé zhōngdào ér yǔ zhī,
bì yě kuángjuàn hū!
Kuáng zhě jìnqǔ,
juàn zhě yǒusuǒ bù wéi yě.'
Kǒngzǐ qǐ bù yù zhōngdào zāi?
Bùkě bì dé,
gù sī qí cì yě."
"I venture to ask, what must one be like to be called a wild enthusiast?"
The reply was,
"Such as Qín Zhāng, Zēng Xī, and Mù Pí—
these were what Confucius called wild enthusiasts."
"Why were they called wild enthusiasts?"
The reply was,
"They had grand aspirations,
saying,
'The ancients!
The ancients!'
But when examining their actions,
they did not match their words."
Even the ardent are not to be found;
I wish to associate with those who disdain impurity,
but this is being fastidious,
which is still a lesser choice.
Confucius said:
'Those who pass by my gate without entering my house,
and whom I do not regret—
are only the village worthies!
Village worthies
are the thieves of virtue.'"
He said:
"What kind of person can be called a village honest man?"
He replied:
"Why are they so boastful?"
Their words do not match their actions,
their actions do not match their words,
yet they say:
"The ancients, the ancients."
Why walk alone and desolate?
Born in this age,
be for this age.
To be good is enough.
Those who furtively flatter the world
are the village honest men."
Wànzǐ yuē:
"Yī xiāng jiē chēng yuán rén yān,
wú suǒ wǎng ér bù wéi yuán rén,
Kǒngzǐ yǐwéi dé zhī zéi,
hé zāi?"
It is said:
"To criticize him, there is nothing to point out;
to reprove him, there is nothing to reprove.
He conforms to the common customs,
harmonizes with the corrupt age.
In his dwelling, he appears loyal and trustworthy;
in his conduct, he seems honest and pure.
The multitude all delight in him,
and he considers himself to be right.
Yet he cannot be admitted into the Way of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore, it is said."
"Thief of virtue," Confucius said:
"I detest what appears similar but is not:
I detest darnel,
fearing it will be confused with seedlings;
I detest flattery,
fearing it will be confused with righteousness;
I detest glib talk,
fearing it will be confused with trustworthiness.
He hated the tunes of Zhèng,
fearing lest they should corrupt the classical music;
he hated the color purple,
fearing lest it should confound the vermilion;
he hated the village honest man,
fearing lest he should confound true virtue.
The noble person simply returns to the norm.
When the norm is correct,
then the common people will flourish;
when the common people flourish,
then there will be no wickedness.
14.38 Mèngzǐ said:
"From Yáo and Shùn to Tāng,
it was over five hundred years;
like Yǔ and
Gāo Yáo, they saw and knew them;
like Tāng, he heard and knew them.
From Tāng to King Wén,
it was over five hundred years.
Men like Yī Yǐn and Lái Zhū saw and knew him;
men like King Wén heard and knew him.
From King Wén to Confucius,
it was over five hundred years.
Men like Tàigōng Wàng and Sǎn Yíshēng saw and knew him;
men like Confucius heard and knew him.
From the time of Confucius to the present day,
over a hundred years have passed,
yet the age of the sage
seems not so distant,
and the proximity to the sage’s homeland
is so very close.
Nevertheless, there is none like him,
then indeed there is none like him.
